selfTest.q: 1. సెక్షన్ 70 ఏ మూడు షరతులను కోరుతుంది?
selfTest.a: క్లెయిమ్ చేసేవాడు మరొకరి కోసం చట్టబద్ధంగా ఏదైనా చేశాడు లేదా అందజేశాడు. దాన్ని దానంగా ఉద్దేశించలేదు. మరొకరు ప్రయోజనాన్ని అనుభవించారు.

selfTest.q: 2. ఒక పొరుగువాడు సద్భావనతో మీ సరుకులను అగ్ని నుంచి కాపాడుతాడు. అతను డబ్బు అడగగలడా?
selfTest.a: లేదు. అతను ఉచితంగా చేశాడు (Illustration (b)).

selfTest.q: 3. అధికారులు ప్రభుత్వ కాంట్రాక్టుల రూపాన్ని పాటించలేదని రాష్ట్రం సెక్షన్ 70 నుంచి తప్పించుకోగలదా?
selfTest.a: లేదు. పనిని స్వచ్ఛందంగా అంగీకరించి అనుభవిస్తే చెల్లించాలి ( B.K. Mondal ).

selfTest.q: 4. ఒక వ్యాపారి పొరపాటున మీ ఇంట్లో సరుకులు వదిలితే, మీరు వెంటనే తిరిగి ఇచ్చేస్తారు. మీరు చెల్లించాలా?
selfTest.a: లేదు. మీరు వాటిని అంగీకరించలేదు, అనుభవించలేదు. స్వచ్ఛంద అంగీకారంపైనే బాధ్యత పుడుతుంది ( B.K. Mondal ; Illustration (a)).

selfTest.q: 5. చెల్లుబాటయ్యే కాంట్రాక్టు రేట్లను నిర్ణయించినప్పుడు సరఫరాదారు సెక్షన్ 70 కింద క్వాంటమ్ మెరిట్ క్లెయిమ్ చేయగలడా?
selfTest.a: లేదు. కాంట్రాక్టు రేటే వర్తిస్తుంది ( Alopi Parshad ; MTNL v. Tata Communications ).

law-of-contract-i-u4-t3.subtitle: Section 69 of the Indian Contract Act, 1872

en.inOneMinute: Sometimes a person must pay another's debt to save his own interest. Section 69 gives him a right to be paid back by the person who should have paid. Two things must be present. The payer has a real interest in the payment, and the other person is bound by law to pay. The payer must pay "therefore", that is, because of that interest. In exams, the two conditions and the Act's illustration of the Bengal lease earn the marks. In real life, it protects a tenant, buyer or co-owner who pays a landlord's or seller's dues to stop a forced sale.
legalProvision: Section 69. Reimbursement of person paying money due by another, in payment of which he is interested. A person who is interested in the payment of money which another is bound by law to pay, and who therefore pays it, is entitled to be reimbursed by the other. Illustration. B holds land in Bengal, on a lease granted by A, the zamindar. The revenue payable by A to the Government being in arrear, his land is advertised for sale by the Government. Under the revenue law, the consequence of such sale will be the annulment of B's lease. B, to prevent the sale and the consequent annulment of his own lease, pays to the Government the sum due from A. A is bound to make good to B the amount so paid.
Related provisions

Section 43 (second and third paragraphs). Each promisor may compel contribution. —Each of two or more joint promisors may compel every other joint promisor to contribute equally with himself to the performance of the promise, unless a contrary intention appears from the contract. Sharing of loss by default in contribution. —If any one of two or more joint promisors makes default in such contribution, the remaining joint promisors must bear the loss arising from such default in equal shares.

Section 145. Implied promise to indemnify surety. In every contract of guarantee there is an implied promise by the principal debtor to indemnify the surety, and the surety is entitled to recover from the principal debtor whatever sum he has rightfully paid under the guarantee, but, no sums which he has paid wrongfully.
Section 72, Illustration (a). A and B jointly owe 100 rupees to C, A alone pays the amount to C, and B, not knowing this fact, pays 100 rupees over again to C. C is bound to repay the amount to B.
In simple words

A person who is interested in the payment of money that another is bound by law to pay, and who pays it for that reason, gets the money back from the other. In the illustration, B, the lessee , pays the revenue that A, the zamindar, owed, to stop a sale that would end B's lease. A must make good to B what B paid. "In arrear" means unpaid after it fell due.
en.meaning:
Section 69 is one of the five situations of quasi contract . The Act does not define "interested". It does not need to, because the section describes the whole claim: an interested person pays what another must pay by law, and the other reimburses him. Why the law has this rule. The reason is fairness. The payer saved the debtor from the result of his own default. If the law let the debtor keep that saving for free, the debtor would be made richer at the payer's cost. This is unjust enrichment , and the law prevents it. Not a promise. The claim does not come from any promise by the debtor. It comes from the law. English source. The English earlier form of the rule is Exall v. Partridge (1799). See Diagram 1 for the parties in the Act's own illustration. Diagram 1. The boxes are the parties. The arrows say what each one does. The dotted arrow shows what the law gives B. flowchart LR A["A, the zamindar
owes land revenue, unpaid"] G["The Government
advertises A's land for sale"] B["B, the lessee
a sale would annul his lease"] A -->|"owes revenue"| G B -->|"pays the revenue due from A,
to save his lease"| G B -.->|"s. 69: A must make good
the amount paid"| A N["If B had no interest and paid out of kindness:
no right to be reimbursed"] B --- N Text description A, the zamindar, owes land revenue to the Government and has not paid. The Government advertises A's land for sale; the sale would annul the lease of B, the lessee. B pays the Government the revenue due from A, to save his lease. The Government's claim for that revenue ends. Under Section 69, A must make good to B the amount paid. If B had no interest and paid only out of kindness, he would have no right to be reimbursed.
keyPoints: Section 69 reimburses a person who pays money that another was bound by law to pay. The payer must be interested in the payment; a legal proprietary interest is not needed ( Seksaria ). The payment must be made "therefore", to protect that interest. The other person's duty may come from a statute, a contract or a decree. The right is to the sum paid and nothing more. A volunteer with no interest has no claim. The debtor's promise is not needed; the right comes from the law.

caseLaws.name: Govindram Gordhandas Seksaria v
caseLaws.facts: State of Gondal (1949) Facts. The State of Gondal sold two Bombay mills (the Currimbhoy and Mahomedbhoy Mills) to Seksaria, who sub-sold them to a company. Municipal taxes of Rs. 1,24,092-1-0 were outstanding on the mills. Neither the seller nor the debenture trustees in possession paid. On 23 February 1939 the company paid Rs. 78,466-12-0 to the Municipality to avoid a forced sale, and claimed reimbursement. Principle. "Interested" does not require a legal proprietary interest. "Bound by law to pay" extends "to any obligation which is an effective bond in law", including one arising by contract. The company recovered under Section 69. Privy Council, 19 December 1949 : (1950) 52 Bom LR 450. Why it matters. It gives the widest reading of the two conditions of Section 69. Radha Madhub Samonta v. Sasti Ram Sen (1899) Facts. The plaintiff bought a putni (a kind of tenure) at a sale in May 1892. On 12 May 1894 the sale was set aside, and the zamindar's appeal against that order was pending. During the appeal the zamindar demanded the rent that had fallen due, and on 16 May 1895 the plaintiff paid about Rs. 2,000. He then sued the defaulting putnidars (the tenure holders) for reimbursement under Section 69. Principle. Maclean CJ said: "It is difficult to say that, at the time the plaintiff made the payment, he was not interested." He was not "a mere volunteer". The putnidars' liability for the rent "cannot be disputed", so they were bound by law to pay. (1899) ILR 26 Cal 826 (Calcutta High Court, 22 February 1899). Why it matters. A doubtful title does not defeat the payer's interest. Exall v. Partridge (1799) Facts. Exall left his carriage at the premises of Partridge, a coachbuilder, for repair. The landlord seized the carriage as distress for rent that Partridge and his co-tenants owed. Exall paid the rent to recover the carriage and sued Partridge and the others. (1799) 8 TR 308 (Court of King's Bench). Principle. The payment was compulsory and not voluntary, so Exall could recover the money. Why it matters. It is the English forerunner of Section 69.

selfTest.q: 1. What two conditions does Section 69 require?
selfTest.a: The payer must be interested in the payment, and the other person must be bound by law to pay the money.

selfTest.q: 2. Can a stranger who pays a debt out of kindness recover under Section 69?
selfTest.a: No. He has no interest in the payment, so the section does not apply.

selfTest.q: 3. In the Act's illustration, why is B entitled to be reimbursed?
selfTest.a: B paid the Government the revenue that A owed, to prevent a sale that would end B's lease. B was interested and A was bound by law to pay.

selfTest.q: 4. Does "bound by law to pay" cover a duty that arises from a contract?
selfTest.a: Yes. It extends to any obligation which is an effective bond in law, including one under a contract ( Seksaria ).

selfTest.q: 5. Mohan pays ₹1,20,000 of Lata's property tax to save his lease. How much can he recover?
selfTest.a: ₹1,20,000, the sum he paid. Section 69 gives reimbursement, not profit or damages.

legalProvision: Section 69. Reimbursement of person paying money due by another, in payment of which he is interested. A person who is interested in the payment of money which another is bound by law to pay, and who therefore pays it, is entitled to be reimbursed by the other. Illustration. B holds land in Bengal, on a lease granted by A, the zamindar. The revenue payable by A to the Government being in arrear, his land is advertised for sale by the Government. Under the revenue law, the consequence of such sale will be the annulment of B's lease. B, to prevent the sale and the consequent annulment of his own lease, pays to the Government the sum due from A. A is bound to make good to B the amount so paid.

Section 43 (second and third paragraphs). Each promisor may compel contribution. —Each of two or more joint promisors may compel every other joint promisor to contribute equally with himself to the performance of the promise, unless a contrary intention appears from the contract. Sharing of loss by default in contribution. —If any one of two or more joint promisors makes default in such contribution, the remaining joint promisors must bear the loss arising from such default in equal shares.

Section 145. Implied promise to indemnify surety. In every contract of guarantee there is an implied promise by the principal debtor to indemnify the surety, and the surety is entitled to recover from the principal debtor whatever sum he has rightfully paid under the guarantee, but, no sums which he has paid wrongfully.
Section 72, Illustration (a). A and B jointly owe 100 rupees to C, A alone pays the amount to C, and B, not knowing this fact, pays 100 rupees over again to C. C is bound to repay the amount to B.

law-of-contract-i-u4-t5.subtitle: Sections 71, 168 and 169 of the Indian Contract Act, 1872

en.inOneMinute: You find a wallet on the road and take it home. You do not become its owner. The law treats you as a bailee , a person who looks after another's goods. You must take care of the goods and return them to the owner. In return, you have a right to keep the goods until your expenses are paid. You may sue for a reward only if the owner offered one. In some cases you may sell the goods. In exams, the duties, Section 168, Section 169 and the loose-or-attached rule earn the marks. In real life, it settles who may keep a lost phone, a bracelet or a ring.
legalProvision: Section 71. Responsibility of finder of goods. A person who finds goods belonging to another, and takes them into his custody, is subject to the same responsibility as a bailee.

Section 168. Right of finder of goods, may sue for specific reward offered. The finder of goods has no right to sue the owner for compensation for trouble and expense voluntarily incurred by him to preserve the goods and to find out the owner; but he may retain the goods against the owner until he receives such compensation; and, where the owner has offered a specific reward for the return of goods lost, the finder may sue for such reward, and may retain the goods until he receives it.

Section 169. When finder of thing commonly on sale may sell it. When a thing which is commonly the subject of sale is lost, if the owner cannot with reasonable diligence be found, or if he refuses, upon demand, to pay the lawful charges of the finder, the finder may sell it— (1) when the thing is in danger of perishing or of losing the greater part of its value, or, (2) when the lawful charges of the finder, in respect of the thing found, amount to two-thirds of its value.
Related provisions (the bailee 's duties that Section 71 applies)

Section 151. Care to be taken by bailee. In all cases of bailment the bailee is bound to take as much care of the goods bailed to him as a man of ordinary prudence would, under similar circumstances, take of his own goods of the same bulk, quality and value as the goods bailed.

Section 152. Bailee when not liable for loss, etc., of thing bailed. The bailee, in the absence of any special contract, is not responsible for the loss, destruction or deterioration of the thing bailed, if he has taken the amount of care of it described in section 151.

Section 154 (first sentence). If the bailee makes any use of the goods bailed which is not according to the conditions of the bailment, he is liable to make compensation to the bailor for any damage arising to the goods from or during such use of them.

Section 160. It is the duty of the bailee to return, or deliver according to the bailor's directions, the goods bailed, without demand, as soon as the time for which they were bailed has expired, or the purpose for which they were bailed has been accomplished.

Section 161. If, by the default of the bailee, the goods are not returned, delivered or tendered at the proper time, he is responsible to the bailor for any loss, destruction or deterioration of the goods from that time.

Section 163. In the absence of any contract to the contrary, the bailee is bound to deliver to the bailor, or according to his directions, any increase or profit which may have accrued from the goods bailed. Illustration. A leaves a cow in the custody of B to be taken care of. The cow has a calf. B is bound to deliver the calf as well as the cow to A.

Section 25(2) and Illustration (c). An agreement made without consideration is void, unless ... (2) it is a promise to compensate, wholly or in part, a person who has already voluntarily done something for the promisor ... (c) A finds B's purse and gives it to him. B promises to give A Rs. 50. This is a contract.
In simple words

Section 71: a person who finds another's goods and takes them into his keeping has the same responsibility as a bailee. Section 168: the finder cannot sue the owner for the trouble and expense he voluntarily took to preserve the goods and find the owner. He may keep the goods until he is paid. If the owner offered a specific reward, the finder may sue for it, and keep the goods until it is paid. Section 169: the finder may sell a thing commonly sold only if (a) the owner cannot be found with reasonable effort, or refuses to pay the finder's lawful charges, and (b) the thing may perish or lose most of its value, or the charges reach two-thirds of its value. Bailee's sections: ordinary care (Sections 151, 152), no unauthorised use (Section 154), return in time (Sections 160, 161), hand over any increase (Section 163). Section 25(2): a later promise by the owner to pay the finder is a valid contract even without fresh consideration .
en.meaning:
A finder of goods is a person who finds goods belonging to another and takes them into his custody. Section 71 does not make him a bailee by contract. There is no contract between him and the owner. The Act treats him as a bailee so that the full set of bailee's duties applies to him. Why the law has this rule. The reason is fairness to both sides. The owner has lost his goods through no wish of his own, and he should get them back unharmed. The finder is a stranger who took on a burden, so the law gives him rights to protect him. Where it fits. This is one of the five quasi-contractual situations in Chapter V of the Act, "Of Certain Relations Resembling Those Created by Contract". See Diagram 1 for the finder's position from finding to the end. Diagram 1. Read from the top. After the care stage, the path splits: either the owner is found, or he is not. flowchart TD F["1. Finds goods of another
and takes them into custody
s. 71: a bailee's responsibility"] C["2. Ordinary care, no use,
tries to trace the owner
ss. 151, 152, 154"] F --> C C -->|"owner found"| R["Returns the goods with any increase
ss. 160, 161, 163"] R --> L["s. 168: may keep the goods until expenses are paid;
may sue only for a specific reward offered"] C -->|"owner not found,
or refuses lawful charges"| S["s. 169: may sell a thing commonly sold
only if perishing, or charges reach
two-thirds of its value"] Text description Step 1: the finder finds goods belonging to another and takes them into custody; he now has a bailee's responsibility under Section 71. Step 2: he takes ordinary care, does not use the goods, and tries to trace the owner (Sections 151, 152, 154). If the owner is found, the finder returns the goods with any increase (Sections 160, 161, 163); he may keep them until his expenses are paid, and may sue for a specific reward if one was offered (Section 168). If the owner cannot be found, or refuses the lawful charges, the finder may sell a thing commonly sold only if it is perishing or the charges reach two-thirds of its value (Section 169).
keyPoints: A finder who takes goods into custody has the responsibility of a bailee (Section 71). He must take ordinary care, not use the goods, and return them with any increase. He cannot sue for his trouble and expense, but may keep the goods until he is paid (Section 168). He may sue for a reward only if a specific reward was offered. He may sell only a thing commonly sold, and only in the cases of Section 169. His title is good against everyone but the true owner ( Armory v. Delamirie ). Loose goods in a public place go to the finder; goods attached to land go to the landowner. A promise of payment made after the goods are returned is enforceable (Section 25(2)).

caseLaws.name: Armory v
caseLaws.facts: Delamirie (1722) Facts. A chimney sweeper's boy took a jewel he had found to a goldsmith's shop. The apprentice took out the stones and returned only the socket. The boy sued the master in trover (an old action for the value of goods wrongly kept). Principle. A finder gets no absolute ownership but may keep the jewel "against all but the rightful owner", and may sue in trover. The master answers for his apprentice's neglect. (1722) 1 Strange 505 : 93 ER 664 (King's Bench, Pratt CJ, 31 July 1722). Why it matters. It is the basic authority on the finder's title. Bridges v. Hawkesworth (1851) Facts. A customer found banknotes on the floor of a shop and gave them to a partner of the firm, for the owner. After three years nobody had claimed them, and the shopkeeper refused to return them. (1851) 21 LJ QB 75. Principle. The finder had a better claim than the shopkeeper. The notes were never in the shopkeeper's custody before they were found. Why it matters. It gives the rule for loose goods in a place open to the public. South Staffordshire Water Co. v. Sharman (1896) Facts. A workman who was cleaning a pool on the company's land found two gold rings in the mud at the bottom. The company claimed them. [1896] 2 QB 44. Principle. A landowner has a better right than the finder to things that lie in or are attached to his land. Why it matters. It marks the difference between loose goods and goods attached to the land. Hannah v. Peel (1945) Facts. A soldier found a brooch on a window frame in a house that the military had requisitioned. He gave it to the police. The owner of the house, who had never lived there, had it returned to him and sold it for £66. [1945] KB 509. Principle. The finder won, because the brooch was lost, was not attached to the land, and the owner had never occupied the house. Why it matters. It shows when a landowner has no better right than the finder. Parker v. British Airways Board (1982) Facts. A passenger found a gold bracelet in an airline lounge at Heathrow and handed it to an employee. The airline sold it for £850 when no owner came forward. [1982] QB 1004 (Court of Appeal). Principle. The finder's rights beat the occupier's unless the occupier showed an intention to control the place and the things in it. The finder must act honestly and take reasonable steps to find the owner. Why it matters. It is the modern statement of the finder's rights against an occupier.

selfTest.q: 1. Does a finder become the owner of lost goods?
selfTest.a: No. He is treated as a bailee, and his right to the goods is good against everyone except the true owner.

selfTest.q: 2. Can a finder sue the owner for his expenses?
selfTest.a: No. He may keep the goods until the owner pays, but he can sue only for a specific reward that the owner offered (Section 168).

selfTest.q: 3. When may a finder sell the goods?
selfTest.a: Only if the thing is commonly sold, the owner cannot be found or refuses the lawful charges, and the thing is perishing or the charges reach two-thirds of its value (Section 169).

selfTest.q: 4. A finder takes ordinary care of a found phone, but it is stolen from his locked cupboard. Is he liable?
selfTest.a: No. A bailee who takes the care described in Section 151 is not liable for the loss (Section 152).

selfTest.q: 5. A found cow gives birth to a calf while with the finder. Who gets the calf?
selfTest.a: The owner. The finder must deliver any increase from the goods (Section 163).

legalProvision: Section 71. Responsibility of finder of goods. A person who finds goods belonging to another, and takes them into his custody, is subject to the same responsibility as a bailee.

Section 168. Right of finder of goods, may sue for specific reward offered. The finder of goods has no right to sue the owner for compensation for trouble and expense voluntarily incurred by him to preserve the goods and to find out the owner; but he may retain the goods against the owner until he receives such compensation; and, where the owner has offered a specific reward for the return of goods lost, the finder may sue for such reward, and may retain the goods until he receives it.

Section 169. When finder of thing commonly on sale may sell it. When a thing which is commonly the subject of sale is lost, if the owner cannot with reasonable diligence be found, or if he refuses, upon demand, to pay the lawful charges of the finder, the finder may sell it— (1) when the thing is in danger of perishing or of losing the greater part of its value, or, (2) when the lawful charges of the finder, in respect of the thing found, amount to two-thirds of its value.
సంబంధిత నిబంధనలు (సెక్షన్ 71 వర్తింపజేసే బెయిలీ బాధ్యతలు)

Section 151. Care to be taken by bailee. In all cases of bailment the bailee is bound to take as much care of the goods bailed to him as a man of ordinary prudence would, under similar circumstances, take of his own goods of the same bulk, quality and value as the goods bailed.

Section 152. Bailee when not liable for loss, etc., of thing bailed. The bailee, in the absence of any special contract, is not responsible for the loss, destruction or deterioration of the thing bailed, if he has taken the amount of care of it described in section 151.

Section 154 (first sentence). If the bailee makes any use of the goods bailed which is not according to the conditions of the bailment, he is liable to make compensation to the bailor for any damage arising to the goods from or during such use of them.

Section 160. It is the duty of the bailee to return, or deliver according to the bailor's directions, the goods bailed, without demand, as soon as the time for which they were bailed has expired, or the purpose for which they were bailed has been accomplished.

Section 161. If, by the default of the bailee, the goods are not returned, delivered or tendered at the proper time, he is responsible to the bailor for any loss, destruction or deterioration of the goods from that time.

Section 163. In the absence of any contract to the contrary, the bailee is bound to deliver to the bailor, or according to his directions, any increase or profit which may have accrued from the goods bailed. Illustration. A leaves a cow in the custody of B to be taken care of. The cow has a calf. B is bound to deliver the calf as well as the cow to A.

Section 25(2) and Illustration (c). An agreement made without consideration is void, unless ... (2) it is a promise to compensate, wholly or in part, a person who has already voluntarily done something for the promisor ... (c) A finds B's purse and gives it to him. B promises to give A Rs. 50. This is a contract.
సరళంగా చెప్పాలంటే

సెక్షన్ 71: మరొకరి వస్తువులను కనుగొని తన అధీనంలోకి తీసుకున్న వ్యక్తికి బెయిలీకి ఉన్న బాధ్యతే ఉంటుంది. సెక్షన్ 168: వస్తువులను కాపాడడానికి, యజమానిని కనుగొనడానికి తాను స్వచ్ఛందంగా పడిన శ్రమ, చేసిన ఖర్చు కోసం కనుగొన్నవారు యజమానిపై దావా వేయలేరు. తనకు చెల్లించే వరకు వస్తువులను ఉంచుకోవచ్చు. యజమాని ఒక నిర్దిష్ట బహుమతి ప్రకటించి ఉంటే, దాని కోసం దావా వేయవచ్చు, అది చెల్లించే వరకు వస్తువులను ఉంచుకోవచ్చు. సెక్షన్ 169: సాధారణంగా అమ్మకానికి వచ్చే వస్తువును కనుగొన్నవారు అమ్మవచ్చు, కానీ (a) సహేతుకమైన ప్రయత్నంతో యజమాని దొరకకపోతే, లేదా యజమాని కనుగొన్నవారి చట్టబద్ధమైన ఖర్చులను చెల్లించడానికి నిరాకరిస్తే, మరియు (b) వస్తువు పాడైపోయే ప్రమాదంలో ఉంటే లేదా దాని విలువలో ఎక్కువ భాగం కోల్పోయే ప్రమాదంలో ఉంటే, లేదా ఖర్చులు దాని విలువలో మూడింట రెండు వంతులకు చేరితే మాత్రమే. బెయిలీ సెక్షన్లు: సాధారణ జాగ్రత్త (సెక్షన్లు 151, 152), అనుమతి లేని వాడకం వద్దు (సెక్షన్ 154), సమయానికి తిరిగి ఇవ్వడం (సెక్షన్లు 160, 161), ఏదైనా పెరుగుదలను అప్పగించడం (సెక్షన్ 163). సెక్షన్ 25(2): యజమాని తర్వాత కనుగొన్నవారికి డబ్బు ఇస్తానని చేసిన వాగ్దానం, కొత్త ప్రతిఫలం లేకపోయినా, చెల్లుబాటయ్యే కాంట్రాక్టు.
te.meaning:
పోయిన వస్తువులను కనుగొన్నవారు (finder of goods) అంటే మరొకరికి చెందిన వస్తువులను కనుగొని తన అధీనంలోకి తీసుకున్న వ్యక్తి. సెక్షన్ 71 అతన్ని కాంట్రాక్టు ద్వారా బెయిలీని చేయదు. అతనికి, యజమానికి మధ్య కాంట్రాక్టు లేదు. బెయిలీ బాధ్యతలన్నీ అతనికి వర్తించేలా చట్టం అతన్ని బెయిలీగా పరిగణిస్తుంది. చట్టం ఈ నియమం ఎందుకు పెట్టింది. కారణం ఇద్దరికీ న్యాయం. యజమాని తన ఇష్టం లేకుండానే వస్తువులు పోగొట్టుకున్నాడు, అవి పాడవకుండా అతనికి తిరిగి రావాలి. కనుగొన్నవారు ఒక భారాన్ని తలకెత్తుకున్న అపరిచితుడు, కాబట్టి అతన్ని రక్షించడానికి చట్టం అతనికి హక్కులు ఇస్తుంది. ఇది ఎక్కడ వస్తుంది. చట్టంలోని అధ్యాయం V, "Of Certain Relations Resembling Those Created by Contract " లోని ఐదు క్వాసి-కాంట్రాక్టు సందర్భాల్లో ఇది ఒకటి. కనుగొన్నప్పటి నుంచి చివరి వరకు కనుగొన్నవారి స్థితిని చిత్రం 1 లో చూడండి. Diagram 1. పై నుంచి చదవండి. జాగ్రత్త దశ తర్వాత దారి రెండుగా చీలుతుంది: యజమాని దొరుకుతాడు, లేదా దొరకడు. flowchart TD F["1. మరొకరి వస్తువులను కనుగొని
అధీనంలోకి తీసుకుంటాడు
సె. 71: బెయిలీ బాధ్యత"] C["2. సాధారణ జాగ్రత్త, వాడకం లేదు,
యజమానిని వెతుకుతాడు
సె. 151, 152, 154"] F --> C C -->|"యజమాని దొరికాడు"| R["ఏదైనా పెరుగుదలతో సహా తిరిగి ఇస్తాడు
సె. 160, 161, 163"] R --> L["సె. 168: ఖర్చులు చెల్లించే వరకు ఉంచుకోవచ్చు;
ప్రకటించిన నిర్దిష్ట బహుమతికి మాత్రమే దావా"] C -->|"యజమాని దొరకలేదు,
లేదా ఖర్చులు నిరాకరించాడు"| S["సె. 169: సాధారణంగా అమ్మే వస్తువును
పాడైపోతుంటే, లేదా ఖర్చులు విలువలో
మూడింట రెండు వంతులకు చేరితే మాత్రమే అమ్మవచ్చు"] వచన వివరణ దశ 1: మరొకరి వస్తువులను కనుగొన్నవారు వాటిని అధీనంలోకి తీసుకుంటారు; సెక్షన్ 71 కింద అతనికి బెయిలీ బాధ్యత వస్తుంది. దశ 2: సాధారణ జాగ్రత్త తీసుకుంటాడు, వస్తువులను వాడడు, యజమానిని వెతుకుతాడు (సెక్షన్లు 151, 152, 154). యజమాని దొరికితే, ఏదైనా పెరుగుదలతో సహా వస్తువులను తిరిగి ఇస్తాడు (సెక్షన్లు 160, 161, 163); ఖర్చులు చెల్లించే వరకు ఉంచుకోవచ్చు, నిర్దిష్ట బహుమతి ప్రకటించి ఉంటే దాని కోసం దావా వేయవచ్చు (సెక్షన్ 168). యజమాని దొరకకపోతే, లేదా చట్టబద్ధమైన ఖర్చులను నిరాకరిస్తే, సాధారణంగా అమ్మకానికి వచ్చే వస్తువును, అది పాడైపోతుంటే లేదా ఖర్చులు దాని విలువలో మూడింట రెండు వంతులకు చేరితే మాత్రమే అమ్మవచ్చు (సెక్షన్ 169).

selfTest.q: 1. పోయిన వస్తువులను కనుగొన్నవారు వాటి యజమాని అవుతారా?
selfTest.a: కాదు. అతన్ని బెయిలీగా పరిగణిస్తారు, ఆ వస్తువులపై అతని హక్కు నిజమైన యజమాని తప్ప అందరికీ వ్యతిరేకంగా చెల్లుతుంది.

selfTest.q: 2. కనుగొన్నవారు తన ఖర్చుల కోసం యజమానిపై దావా వేయగలరా?
selfTest.a: లేదు. యజమాని చెల్లించే వరకు వస్తువులను ఉంచుకోవచ్చు, కానీ యజమాని ప్రకటించిన నిర్దిష్ట బహుమతి కోసం మాత్రమే దావా వేయవచ్చు (సెక్షన్ 168).

selfTest.q: 3. కనుగొన్నవారు వస్తువులను ఎప్పుడు అమ్మవచ్చు?
selfTest.a: వస్తువు సాధారణంగా అమ్మకానికి వచ్చేదై, యజమాని దొరకకపోతే లేదా చట్టబద్ధమైన ఖర్చులను నిరాకరిస్తే, వస్తువు పాడైపోతుంటే లేదా ఖర్చులు దాని విలువలో మూడింట రెండు వంతులకు చేరితే మాత్రమే (సెక్షన్ 169).

selfTest.q: 4. దొరికిన ఫోన్‌ను కనుగొన్నవారు సాధారణ జాగ్రత్తతో ఉంచారు, కానీ తాళం వేసిన బీరువా నుంచి అది దొంగిలించబడింది. అతను బాధ్యుడా?
selfTest.a: కాదు. సెక్షన్ 151 లో చెప్పిన జాగ్రత్త తీసుకున్న బెయిలీ నష్టానికి బాధ్యుడు కాదు (సెక్షన్ 152).

selfTest.q: 5. కనుగొన్నవారి దగ్గర ఉండగా దొరికిన ఆవు దూడకు జన్మనిచ్చింది. దూడ ఎవరికి?
selfTest.a: యజమానికి. వస్తువుల నుంచి వచ్చిన ఏ పెరుగుదలనైనా కనుగొన్నవారు అప్పగించాలి (సెక్షన్ 163).

law-of-contract-i-u4-t6.subtitle: Section 72 of the Indian Contract Act, 1872

en.inOneMinute: If you pay money by mistake, or hand over goods because you are forced to, the person who received them must give them back. Section 72 says so in one sentence. You do not have to prove that the receiver did anything wrong. In exams, the double payment by joint debtors, the illegal railway charge, and the rule that "mistake" covers both fact and law earn the marks. In real life, it is the basis of refunds of excess payments and of taxes collected without authority.
legalProvision: Section 72. Liability of person to whom money is paid, or thing delivered, by mistake or under coercion. A person to whom money has been paid, or anything delivered, by mistake or under coercion, must repay or return it. Illustrations (a) A and B jointly owe 100 rupees to C, A alone pays the amount to C, and B, not knowing this fact, pays 100 rupees over again to C. C is bound to repay the amount to B. (b) A railway company refuses to deliver up certain goods to the consignee, except upon the payment of an illegal charge for carriage. The consignee pays the sum charged in order to obtain the goods. He is entitled to recover so much of the charge as was illegally excessive.
Related provisions

Section 43 (second paragraph). Each promisor may compel contribution. —Each of two or more joint promisors may compel every other joint promisor to contribute equally with himself to the performance of the promise, unless a contrary intention appears from the contract.

Section 15. "Coercion" defined. "Coercion" is the committing, or threatening to commit, any act forbidden by the Indian Penal Code (45 of 1860) or the unlawful detaining, or threatening to detain, any property, to the prejudice of any person whatever, with the intention of causing any person to enter into an agreement.

Section 21. Effect of mistakes as to law. A contract is not voidable because it was caused by a mistake as to any law in force in India; but a mistake as to a law not in force in India has the same effect as a mistake of fact.

Section 65. When an agreement is discovered to be void, or when a contract becomes void, any person who has received any advantage under such agreement or contract is bound to restore it, or to make compensation for it to the person from whom he received it. Illustration (a). A pays B 1,000 rupees in consideration of B's promising to marry C, A's daughter. C is dead at the time of the promise. The agreement is void, but B must repay A the 1,000 rupees.
In simple words

Section 72: whoever receives money, or any thing, that was paid or delivered by mistake or under coercion must repay the money or return the thing. Illustration (a): a joint debt paid twice by mistake. The creditor must repay the second payment. Illustration (b): goods held back until an illegal charge is paid. The consignee (the person to whom goods are sent) recovers the part of the charge that was more than the law allowed. Section 43: each joint promisor may make the others contribute equally.
en.meaning:
Section 72 is the last of the five quasi-contractual situations. It has two grounds. The first is a payment or delivery made by mistake . The second is a payment or delivery made under coercion . In both, the receiver has something that the giver never meant to give freely. Why the law has this rule. The reason is unjust enrichment . The receiver should not keep what he had no right to take. The section does not ask whether the receiver was honest. It asks only whether the payment came from a mistake or from compulsion. See Diagram 1 for the questions that a court asks. Diagram 1. Start at the top. If the answer to a box ends the claim, stop at the result beside it. Otherwise follow the arrow down to the next box. flowchart TD Q1["1. Was money paid, or a thing delivered,
to the person who now holds it?"] Q1 -->|"No"| X1["Section 72 does not apply"] Q1 -->|"Yes"| Q2["2. By mistake, of fact or of law,
or under coercion in the wide sense?"] Q2 -->|"No"| X2["A free and informed payment:
the receiver need not return it"] Q2 -->|"Yes"| Q3["3. Was the sum legally due
from the giver anyway?"] Q3 -->|"Yes"| X3["Not recoverable:
he paid only what he owed"] Q3 -->|"No"| R["The receiver must repay the money
or return the thing"] Text description Question 1: was money paid, or a thing delivered, to the person who now holds it? If no, Section 72 does not apply. Question 2: was it paid or delivered by mistake, whether of fact or of law, or under coercion in the wide sense of compulsion? If no, it was a free and informed payment, and the receiver need not return it. Question 3: was the sum legally due from the giver anyway, for example under a contract? If yes, it cannot be recovered, because the giver paid only what he owed. If all the tests are met, the receiver must repay the money or return the thing.
keyPoints: Money paid or goods delivered by mistake or under coercion must be repaid or returned (Section 72). Mistake covers both fact and law ( Shiba Prasad Singh ; Kanhaiya Lal ). Coercion in Section 72 means any compulsion, not just the technical meaning in Section 15. The receiver's good faith is not the test. A sum that was legally due cannot be recovered. Joint debtors who pay twice: the receiver repays the second payer (Illustration (a)), and contribution follows under Section 43.

caseLaws.name: Sales Tax Officer, Banaras v
caseLaws.facts: Kanhaiya Lal Mukundlal Saraf (1958) Facts. A Banaras firm dealing in bullion and in forward contracts in silver paid sales tax for 1948-49, 1949-50 and 1950-51. The Allahabad High Court later held the tax on forward transactions ultra vires (beyond the power of the State). The firm sought a refund of Rs. 1,365-12-0. Principle. "Mistake" in Section 72 "comprises within its scope a mistake of law as well as a mistake of fact". It made no difference that the State had spent the money. AIR 1959 SC 135 (Supreme Court, Bhagwati J, 23 September 1958). Why it matters. It is the leading Supreme Court case on refunds under Section 72. Sri Sri Shiba Prasad Singh v. Maharaja Srish Chandra Nandi (1949) Facts. A coal mining lease in the Jharia estate was granted on 22 October 1898. Under the lease, the higher royalty rates (5 annas and 2 annas 6 pies a ton) were payable only while railway freight stayed low. Freight rose on 1 April 1921, so only the lower rates (3 annas and 1 anna 6 pies) were due from then. The lessee went on paying the higher rates until 30 September 1923, Rs. 63,680 more than was due. When the lessor sued for royalties in 1936, the lessee claimed to set off the excess. Principle. Section 72 "makes no distinction between mistakes of fact and mistakes of law". A payment by mistake is one "not legally due and which could not have been enforced". The Privy Council dismissed the lessor's suit with costs. (1949) LR 76 IA 244 : (1950) 52 Bom LR 17 (Privy Council, 18 July 1949). Why it matters. It settled that mistake of law is within Section 72. Moses v. Macferlan (1760) Facts. Moses endorsed notes to Macferlan on a promise that Macferlan would not sue him on them. Macferlan sued him in the Court of Conscience, and Moses had to pay. Moses then sued to recover the money. Principle. The action for money had and received lies wherever the defendant is obliged by natural justice and equity to refund the money. Why it matters. It is the English root of the principle that Section 72 applies.

selfTest.q: 1. Does Section 72 cover a mistake of law?
selfTest.a: Yes. The Privy Council in Shiba Prasad Singh and the Supreme Court in Kanhaiya Lal held that mistake covers both fact and law.

selfTest.q: 2. Is the meaning of coercion in Section 72 the same as in Section 15?
selfTest.a: No. Section 72 uses the word in its wide, ordinary sense of compulsion.

selfTest.q: 3. A and B jointly owe 100 rupees to C. A pays, and B pays again by mistake. What must C do?
selfTest.a: C must repay the second payment to B (Section 72, Illustration (a)).

selfTest.q: 4. The State spent tax money that it had collected under a law later struck down. Can it refuse a refund on that ground?
selfTest.a: No. In Kanhaiya Lal the Supreme Court held that spending the money made no difference.

selfTest.q: 5. A tenant pays the full rent that his lease requires and later regrets it. Can he recover under Section 72?
selfTest.a: No. The rent was legally due, so it was not paid "by mistake".

సెక్షన్ 72: పొరపాటున లేదా బలవంతం కింద చెల్లించిన డబ్బును, లేదా అప్పగించిన ఏ వస్తువునైనా పొందిన వ్యక్తి, ఆ డబ్బును తిరిగి చెల్లించాలి లేదా ఆ వస్తువును తిరిగి ఇవ్వాలి. Illustration (a): ఒక ఉమ్మడి అప్పు పొరపాటున రెండుసార్లు చెల్లించబడింది. అప్పిచ్చినవాడు రెండో చెల్లింపును తిరిగి ఇవ్వాలి. Illustration (b): చట్టవిరుద్ధమైన ఛార్జీ చెల్లించే వరకు వస్తువులను ఆపి ఉంచారు. Consignee (వస్తువులు ఎవరికి పంపబడ్డాయో ఆ వ్యక్తి) చట్టం అనుమతించిన దాని కంటే ఎక్కువగా ఉన్న ఛార్జీ భాగాన్ని తిరిగి పొందుతాడు. సెక్షన్ 43: ప్రతి ఉమ్మడి వాగ్దానకర్త మిగతావారిని సమానంగా వాటా ఇచ్చేలా చేయవచ్చు.

ఐదు క్వాసి-కాంట్రాక్టు సందర్భాల్లో సెక్షన్ 72 చివరిది. దీనికి రెండు ఆధారాలు ఉన్నాయి. మొదటిది పొరపాటు వల్ల చేసిన చెల్లింపు లేదా అప్పగింత. రెండోది బలవంతం (coercion) కింద చేసిన చెల్లింపు లేదా అప్పగింత. రెండింటిలోనూ, ఇచ్చినవారు స్వేచ్ఛగా ఇవ్వాలని ఎప్పుడూ అనుకోనిది పొందినవారి దగ్గర ఉంటుంది. చట్టం ఈ నియమం ఎందుకు పెట్టింది. కారణం అన్యాయమైన సంపన్నత . తీసుకునే హక్కు లేనిదాన్ని పొందినవారు ఉంచుకోకూడదు. పొందినవారు నిజాయితీపరుడా కాదా అని సెక్షన్ అడగదు. చెల్లింపు పొరపాటు వల్ల జరిగిందా, బలవంతం వల్ల జరిగిందా అని మాత్రమే అడుగుతుంది. కోర్టు అడిగే ప్రశ్నలను చిత్రం 1 లో చూడండి. law-of-contract-i-u4-t7.subtitle: Reasonable payment for work done or goods supplied: sections 65 and 70 of the Indian Contract Act, 1872

en.inOneMinute: Quantum meruit is Latin for "as much as he has earned". The syllabus calls it "quantum merit". It is a claim for a reasonable price for work done or goods supplied, when no contract price binds the parties. The contract may be void, the price may never have been fixed, or the other side may have stopped the work. The claim is for the value of what was given. It is not a claim for profit, and it is not a claim for damages. In exams, the grounds, the limit (no claim where a valid contract fixes the price) and Alopi Parshad earn the marks. In real life, it pays freelancers, builders and professionals whose paperwork failed.
legalProvision: The Act has no section called " quantum meruit ". The claim rests on Sections 65 and 70 and on the law of implied contract .

Section 65. Obligation of person who has received advantage under void agreement, or contract that becomes void. When an agreement is discovered to be void, or when a contract becomes void, any person who has received any advantage under such agreement or contract is bound to restore it, or to make compensation for it to the person from whom he received it. Illustrations (b) A contracts with B to deliver to him 250 maunds of rice before the first of May. A delivers 130 maunds only before that day, and none after. B retains the 130 maunds after the first of May. He is bound to pay A for them. (c) A, a singer, contracts with B, the manager of a theatre, to sing at his theatre for two nights in every week during the next two months, and B engages to pay her a hundred rupees for each night's performance. On the sixth night, A wilfully absents herself from the theatre, and B, in consequence, rescinds the contract. B must pay A for the five nights on which she had sung. (d) A contracts to sing for B at a concert for 1,000 rupees, which are paid in advance. A is too ill to sing. A is not bound to make compensation to B for the loss of the profits which B would have made if A had been able to sing, but must refund to B the 1,000 rupees paid in advance.

Section 70. Obligation of person enjoying benefit of non-gratuitous act. Where a person lawfully does anything for another person, or delivers anything to him, not intending to do so gratuitously, and such other person enjoys the benefit thereof, the latter is bound to make compensation to the former in respect of, or to restore, the thing so done or delivered.

Section 73 (third paragraph). Compensation for failure to discharge obligation resembling those created by contract. —When an obligation resembling those created by contract has been incurred and has not been discharged, any person injured by the failure to discharge it is entitled to receive the same compensation from the party in default, as if such person had contracted to discharge it and had broken his contract.
In simple words

Section 65: when an agreement turns out to be void , or a contract becomes void, a person who has received any benefit under it must give it back, or pay for it. Illustration (b): B keeps 130 of the 250 maunds of rice, so he must pay for them. A maund is an old Indian unit of weight. Section 70: a person who lawfully does something for another, not meaning it as a gift, is paid compensation if the other enjoys the benefit. Section 73, third paragraph: when an obligation resembling a contract is not discharged, the injured person gets the same compensation as if there had been a contract and it had been broken.
en.meaning:
The Latin phrase quantum meruit means "as much as he has earned". The syllabus spells it "quantum merit"; it means the same claim. The Supreme Court's words. In Alopi Parshad and Sons Ltd. v. Union of India (1960) the Court said: "Compensation quantum meruit is awarded for work done or services rendered, when the price thereof is not fixed by a contract". It added that "Quantum meruit is but reasonable compensation awarded on implication of a contract to remunerate". Why the law has this rule. The reason is unjust enrichment . If a person has taken the benefit of another's work or goods, he should pay a fair price for it. The law fixes that price by the value of the work, not by any promise. Where it fits. It is one of the claims based on quasi-contract (Sections 65 and 70), and it also serves as a remedy when a contract is broken. See Diagram 1 for when the claim lies. Diagram 1. Go down the boxes in order. A "No" answer sends you to the result beside the box. flowchart TD Q1["1. Work done or goods supplied, expecting payment,
for the other person's benefit? (s. 70)"] Q1 -->|"No"| X1["No claim"] Q1 -->|"Yes"| Q2["2. No valid contract that fixes
the price for this work?"] Q2 -->|"No: a valid contract fixes the price"| X2["Claim lies under the contract,
not as quantum meruit"] Q2 -->|"Yes"| Q3["3. Contract void, no price fixed,
other party stopped the work,
or a part accepted?"] Q3 -->|"No"| X3["No basis for the claim"] Q3 -->|"Yes"| Q4["4. Did the other person accept and enjoy it,
or prevent the work being finished?"] Q4 -->|"No: claimant walked away
from an entire contract"| X4["No claim"] Q4 -->|"Yes"| R["Reasonable price for the work done
or goods supplied"] Text description Question 1: did the claimant do work or supply goods expecting to be paid, for the other person's benefit (Section 70)? If no, there is no claim. Question 2: is there no valid contract that fixes the price for this work? If a valid contract fixes the price, the claim lies under the contract and not as quantum meruit. Question 3: is the reason one of these: the contract is void, no price was fixed, the other party stopped the work, or a part was accepted? If no, there is no basis for the claim. Question 4: did the other person accept and enjoy the work or goods, or prevent the work from being finished? If no, because the claimant walked away from an entire contract, there is no claim. If all answers favour the claimant, he recovers a reasonable price for the work done or goods supplied.
keyPoints: Quantum meruit means "as much as he has earned": a reasonable price for work done or goods supplied. It is available where a contract is void, no price was fixed, the other party stopped the work, or part performance was accepted. It is not available where a valid contract fixes the price. It measures the value of the benefit, not profit and not damages. A party who abandons an entire contract halfway cannot claim for the part done. The claimant cannot have both quantum meruit and damages for the same work.

caseLaws.name: Alopi Parshad and Sons Ltd
caseLaws.facts: v. Union of India (1960) Facts. Agents supplied ghee to the Government for the Army under a written agreement that fixed their rates. They claimed more when wartime costs rose, and arbitrators awarded extra sums. The High Court set the award aside. Principle. "Compensation quantum meruit is awarded for work done or services rendered, when the price thereof is not fixed by a contract." An express stipulation cannot be displaced by assuming that it is not reasonable. AIR 1960 SC 588 : (1960) 2 SCR 793 (Supreme Court, 20 January 1960); the agents' appeal was dismissed with costs. Why it matters. It is the leading Indian case on the limit of quantum meruit. Craven-Ellis v. Canons Ltd. (1936) Facts. A managing director performed services under an agreement that was void, because those who made it had no authority to bind the company. He sued for payment. [1936] 2 KB 403. Principle. Greer L.J. said that the obligation to pay reasonable remuneration is "imposed by a rule of law, and not by an inference of fact". Why it matters. It shows that quantum meruit does not need a valid contract. Planché v. Colburn (1831) Facts. An author had written a large part of a book for £100 when the publisher abandoned the project. The author sued. (1831) 8 Bing 14. Principle. He recovered a reasonable sum for the work done, because the other side had prevented completion. Why it matters. It supports quantum meruit when the other party stops the work. Sumpter v. Hedges (1898) Facts. A builder agreed to build two houses and stables for £560. He did work worth £333 and then abandoned the contract. [1898] 1 QB 673. Principle. He could not recover on the contract, and he could not claim quantum meruit unless the owner did something from which a new promise to pay could be inferred. Why it matters. It marks the limit for a party who abandons an entire contract. State of West Bengal v. B.K. Mondal and Sons (1962) Facts. A contractor built storage sheds and other buildings for the State's Civil Supplies department at officers' request in 1944. The contracts did not meet the form required by Section 175(3) of the Government of India Act, 1935. Principle. The State had to pay compensation under Section 70 for work it accepted. AIR 1962 SC 779 (Supreme Court, 5 December 1961). Why it matters. It applies the reasonable-payment idea to a Government contract.

selfTest.q: 1. What does quantum meruit mean?
selfTest.a: It means "as much as he has earned". It is a claim for a reasonable price for work done or goods supplied.

selfTest.q: 2. Can an agent claim quantum meruit when a valid contract fixes his remuneration?
selfTest.a: No. The express contract rate governs ( Alopi Parshad ).

selfTest.q: 4. A builder abandons an entire lump-sum contract halfway. Can he claim for the work done?
selfTest.a: Not on the contract, and not as quantum meruit, unless the owner did something from which a new promise to pay can be inferred ( Sumpter v. Hedges ).

selfTest.q: 5. A singer is too ill to sing at a concert for which she was paid in advance. What must she do?
selfTest.a: Refund the advance. She owes no compensation for the organiser's lost profits (Section 65, Illustration (d)).

Compensation for failure to discharge obligation resembling those created by contract. —When an obligation resembling those created by contract has been incurred and has not been discharged, any person injured by the failure to discharge it is entitled to receive the same compensation from the party in default, as if such person had contracted to discharge it and had broken his contract.

సెక్షన్ 65: ఒక ఒప్పందం చెల్లనిది (void) అని తేలినప్పుడు, లేదా ఒక కాంట్రాక్టు చెల్లనిదిగా మారినప్పుడు, దాని కింద ఏదైనా ప్రయోజనం పొందిన వ్యక్తి దాన్ని తిరిగి ఇవ్వాలి, లేదా దానికి డబ్బు చెల్లించాలి. Illustration (b): 250 maunds బియ్యంలో 130 ను B ఉంచుకున్నాడు, కాబట్టి వాటికి అతను చెల్లించాలి. Maund అనేది పాత భారతీయ బరువు కొలమానం. సెక్షన్ 70: మరొకరి కోసం బహుమతిగా కాకుండా చట్టబద్ధంగా ఏదైనా చేసిన వ్యక్తికి, ఆ మరొకరు దాని ప్రయోజనాన్ని అనుభవిస్తే, పరిహారం వస్తుంది. సెక్షన్ 73, మూడో పేరా: కాంట్రాక్టును పోలిన బాధ్యతను నెరవేర్చకపోతే, కాంట్రాక్టు ఉండి అది ఉల్లంఘించబడితే వచ్చేంత పరిహారమే నష్టపోయిన వ్యక్తికి వస్తుంది.
te.meaning:
Quantum meruit అనే లాటిన్ పదబంధానికి అర్థం "as much as he has earned" (అతను సంపాదించినంత). సిలబస్ దీన్ని "quantum merit" అని రాస్తుంది; అర్థం అదే క్లెయిమ్. సుప్రీం కోర్టు మాటలు. Alopi Parshad and Sons Ltd. v. Union of India (1960) లో కోర్టు ఇలా చెప్పింది: "Compensation quantum meruit is awarded for work done or services rendered, when the price thereof is not fixed by a contract". "Quantum meruit is but reasonable compensation awarded on implication of a contract to remunerate" అని కూడా చెప్పింది. చట్టం ఈ నియమం ఎందుకు పెట్టింది. కారణం అన్యాయమైన సంపన్నత . ఒక వ్యక్తి మరొకరి పని లేదా వస్తువుల ప్రయోజనాన్ని తీసుకుంటే, దానికి న్యాయమైన ధర చెల్లించాలి. చట్టం ఆ ధరను ఏ వాగ్దానంతోనూ కాకుండా, పని విలువతో నిర్ణయిస్తుంది. ఇది ఎక్కడ వస్తుంది. ఇది క్వాసి-కాంట్రాక్టు పై ఆధారపడిన క్లెయిమ్‌లలో ఒకటి (సెక్షన్లు 65, 70). కాంట్రాక్టు ఉల్లంఘించబడినప్పుడు పరిష్కారంగా కూడా పనిచేస్తుంది. క్లెయిమ్ ఎప్పుడు వస్తుందో చిత్రం 1 లో చూడండి. Diagram 1. పెట్టెలను వరుసగా కిందికి చదవండి. "కాదు" అనే జవాబు మిమ్మల్ని పక్కన ఉన్న ఫలితానికి పంపుతుంది. flowchart TD Q1["1. చెల్లింపు ఆశించి, అవతలి వ్యక్తి ప్రయోజనం కోసం
పని చేశారా లేదా వస్తువులు ఇచ్చారా? (సె. 70)"] Q1 -->|"కాదు"| X1["క్లెయిమ్ లేదు"] Q1 -->|"అవును"| Q2["2. ఈ పనికి ధరను నిర్ణయించే

లేదా పని పూర్తి కాకుండా అడ్డుకున్నాడా?"] Q4 -->|"కాదు: క్లెయిమ్ చేసేవారు

సహేతుకమైన ధర"] వచన వివరణ ప్రశ్న 1: అవతలి వ్యక్తి ప్రయోజనం కోసం, చెల్లింపు ఆశించి క్లెయిమ్ చేసేవారు పని చేశారా లేదా వస్తువులు సరఫరా చేశారా (సెక్షన్ 70)? లేకపోతే క్లెయిమ్ లేదు. ప్రశ్న 2: ఈ పనికి ధరను నిర్ణయించే చెల్లుబాటయ్యే కాంట్రాక్టు లేదా? చెల్లుబాటయ్యే కాంట్రాక్టు ధరను నిర్ణయిస్తే, క్లెయిమ్ కాంట్రాక్టు కింద వస్తుంది, quantum meruit గా కాదు. ప్రశ్న 3: కారణం వీటిలో ఒకటా: కాంట్రాక్టు చెల్లనిది, ధర నిర్ణయించలేదు, అవతలి పక్షం పనిని ఆపింది, లేదా ఒక భాగాన్ని స్వీకరించారు? లేకపోతే క్లెయిమ్‌కు ఆధారం లేదు. ప్రశ్న 4: అవతలి వ్యక్తి పనిని లేదా వస్తువులను స్వీకరించి అనుభవించాడా, లేదా పని పూర్తి కాకుండా అడ్డుకున్నాడా? లేకపోతే, క్లెయిమ్ చేసేవారు entire కాంట్రాక్టును వదిలేశారు కాబట్టి, క్లెయిమ్ లేదు. అన్ని జవాబులూ క్లెయిమ్ చేసేవారికి అనుకూలమైతే, చేసిన పనికి లేదా సరఫరా చేసిన వస్తువులకు సహేతుకమైన ధర వస్తుంది.

selfTest.q: 1. Quantum meruit అంటే ఏమిటి?
selfTest.a: "as much as he has earned" అని అర్థం. చేసిన పనికి లేదా సరఫరా చేసిన వస్తువులకు సహేతుకమైన ధర కోసం చేసే క్లెయిమ్.

selfTest.q: 2. చెల్లుబాటయ్యే కాంట్రాక్టు తన వేతనాన్ని నిర్ణయించినప్పుడు ఒక ఏజెంట్ quantum meruit క్లెయిమ్ చేయగలడా?
selfTest.a: లేదు. స్పష్టమైన కాంట్రాక్టు రేటే వర్తిస్తుంది ( Alopi Parshad ).

selfTest.q: 4. ఒక బిల్డర్ మొత్తం ధర (lump-sum) entire కాంట్రాక్టును మధ్యలో వదిలేస్తాడు. చేసిన పనికి క్లెయిమ్ చేయగలడా?
selfTest.a: కాంట్రాక్టుపై కాదు, quantum meruit గా కూడా కాదు, చెల్లిస్తాననే కొత్త వాగ్దానాన్ని ఊహించగలిగేది యజమాని ఏదైనా చేస్తే తప్ప ( Sumpter v. Hedges ).

selfTest.q: 5. ముందుగా డబ్బు తీసుకున్న కచేరీలో ఒక గాయని అనారోగ్యం వల్ల పాడలేకపోయింది. ఆమె ఏం చేయాలి?
selfTest.a: ముందుగా తీసుకున్న డబ్బు తిరిగి ఇవ్వాలి. నిర్వాహకుడి పోయిన లాభాలకు ఆమె పరిహారం ఇవ్వనక్కర్లేదు (సెక్షన్ 65, Illustration (d)).

Diagram 2. ప్రతి నిలువు వరుస ఒక క్లెయిమ్. అది దేనిపై ఆధారపడుతుందో, ఏం చెల్లిస్తుందో చూడడానికి కిందికి చదవండి.

law-of-contract-i-u4-t8.subtitle: Sections 39, 53 to 55, 64, 65 and 73 to 75 of the Indian Contract Act, 1872, and the Specific Relief Act, 1963

en.inOneMinute: When a party breaks a contract, the other party does not have to just accept it. The law gives him a set of remedies . He may end the contract and get back what he gave. He may claim money . He may ask the court to make the other side perform , or to stop him from doing something. The ordinary remedy is damages (Section 73). The others are rescission with restoration (Sections 39, 64, 65) and compensation (Section 75), an agreed sum (Section 74), quantum meruit , specific performance and injunction (Specific Relief Act, 1963). In exams, a clear list of remedies with the section for each, and the choice between them, earn the marks. In real life, the right choice depends on what the injured party actually wants: his money, or the thing promised.
legalProvision: Section 39. When a party to a contract has refused to perform, or disabled himself from performing, his promise in its entirety, the promisee may put an end to the contract, unless he has signified, by words or conduct, his acquiescence in its continuance.

Section 64 (part). When a person at whose option a contract is voidable rescinds it, the other party thereto need not perform any promise therein contained in which he is promisor. The party rescinding a voidable contract shall, if he have received any benefit thereunder from another party to such contract, restore such benefit, so far as may be, to the person from whom it was received.

Section 65. When an agreement is discovered to be void, or when a contract becomes void, any person who has received any advantage under such agreement or contract is bound to restore it, or to make compensation for it to the person from whom he received it.

Section 73 (first two paragraphs). When a contract has been broken, the party who suffers by such breach is entitled to receive, from the party who has broken the contract, compensation for any loss or damage caused to him thereby, which naturally arose in the usual course of things from such breach, or which the parties knew, when they made the contract, to be likely to result from the breach of it. Such compensation is not to be given for any remote and indirect loss or damage sustained by reason of the breach.

Section 74 (first part). … the party complaining of the breach is entitled, whether or not actual damage or loss is proved to have been caused thereby, to receive from the party who has broken the contract reasonable compensation not exceeding the amount so named or, as the case may be, the penalty stipulated for.
Section 75. A person who rightfully rescinds a contract is entitled to compensation for any damage which he has sustained through the non-fulfilment of the contract.

Specific Relief Act, 1963, Section 10. The specific performance of a contract shall be enforced by the court subject to the provisions contained in sub-section (2) of section 11, section 14 and section 16.

Specific Relief Act, Section 42 (main part). Where a contract comprises an affirmative agreement to do a certain act, coupled with a negative agreement, express or implied, not to do a certain act, the circumstance that the court is unable to compel specific performance of the affirmative agreement shall not preclude it from granting an injunction to perform the negative agreement.
In simple words

Section 39: if the other side refuses to perform the whole contract, you may end it, unless you have accepted that it continues. Sections 53 and 55: if one side prevents performance, or fails to perform on time where time is essential, the contract becomes voidable at the other's option, and he may claim compensation. Sections 64 and 65: when a contract is ended, each side must give back what it received. Section 73: damages for natural and foreseen loss, not remote loss. Section 74: if a sum is named for breach, reasonable compensation up to that sum. Section 75: a party who rightly ends the contract can also claim damages. Specific Relief Act: the court may order specific performance (Section 10), award compensation with or instead of it (Section 21), order refund of earnest money where it is refused (Section 22), and grant an injunction (Sections 36 to 42).
en.meaning:
A remedy is the relief the law gives to a party whose right has been broken. A breach of contract happens when a party fails or refuses to perform his promise, or disables himself from performing it. A breach may be actual (on or after the due date) or anticipatory (before the due date). Where the remedies come from. The Indian Contract Act deals with the effects of breach mainly in Sections 39, 53 to 55, 64, 65 and 73 to 75. The Specific Relief Act, 1963 adds the remedies a court gives "in kind": specific performance and injunction . Why there are several remedies. Injured parties want different things. One wants out of the contract and his money back. One wants compensation for a loss. One wants the very thing promised. One wants the other side stopped. Sections 64, 65"] E --> E3["Compensation on rescission
Section 75"] M --> M1["Damages
Section 73"] M --> M2["Agreed sum or penalty
Section 74"] M --> M3["Quantum meruit
Sections 65, 70"] T --> T1["Specific performance
SRA Sections 10, 14, 16, 20, 21"] T --> T2["Injunction
SRA Sections 36 to 42"] Text description Breach of contract leads to three groups. End the contract: rescission (Sections 39, 53, 55, 64) with restitution (Sections 64, 65) and compensation (Section 75). Money: damages (Section 73), agreed sum (Section 74), quantum meruit (Sections 65, 70). The thing itself: specific performance (Specific Relief Act Sections 10, 14, 16, 20, 21) and injunction (Sections 36 to 42).
keyPoints: A breach gives the injured party a choice . It does not end the contract by itself (Section 39). Damages under Section 73 are the ordinary remedy. Rescission comes with restoration (Sections 64, 65) and compensation (Section 75). Section 74 limits compensation to the sum named; the court awards what is reasonable. Quantum meruit gives a reasonable price for work done. Specific performance is now enforced subject to Sections 11(2), 14 and 16 of the Specific Relief Act. Injunction can enforce a negative promise (Section 42). Inconsistent remedies, such as rescission and specific performance, cannot be claimed together.

caseLaws.name: Hadley v
caseLaws.facts: Baxendale (1854) Facts. A Gloucester mill's crank shaft broke. The owners sent it by carrier to Greenwich as a pattern for a new one. The carrier delayed delivery, and the mill lost profits. Principle. Damages are those arising naturally from the breach, or reasonably in the contemplation of both parties when they contracted. (1854) 9 Exch 341; 156 ER 145. Why it matters. It is the source of the rule on remote loss in Section 73. Hochster v. De la Tour (1853) Facts. A courier was engaged from 1 June 1852. On 11 May his employer wrote that he would not need him. The courier sued on 22 May. Principle. The injured party may sue as soon as the other party clearly refuses to perform, without waiting for the due date. (1853) 2 E & B 678. Why it matters. It shows the injured party's choice on an anticipatory breach. Fateh Chand v. Balkishan Dass (1963) Facts. A buyer paid Rs. 1,000 earnest money and Rs. 24,000 towards the price of a Delhi property and failed to complete. The contract said Rs. 25,000 would be forfeited. Principle. Section 74 applies to a clause forfeiting money already paid. The seller could keep only the Rs. 1,000. AIR 1963 SC 1405. Why it matters. It shows how the law limits what the wronged party may keep. K.S. Vidyanadam v. Vairavan (1997) Facts. A buyer agreed on 15 December 1978 to buy a house for Rs. 60,000 within six months. He sent a notice only on 11 July 1981, after prices had risen. Principle. Even where time is not of the essence in a land sale, the buyer must act within a reasonable time. Specific performance was refused. AIR 1997 SC 1751. Why it matters. Delay can defeat specific performance. Saradamani Kandappan v. S. Rajalakshmi (2011) Facts. A 1981 agreement to sell land fixed dated instalments and made time the essence. The buyer missed later instalments, and the sellers cancelled. Principle. Where the contract makes time for payment the essence, default justifies cancellation, even for immovable property. A refund with interest was ordered. (2011) 12 SCC 18. Why it matters. It shows when cancellation and refund replace specific performance. Katta Sujatha Reddy v. Siddamsetty Infra Projects (2022) Facts. A purchaser sought specific performance of 1997 agreements to buy land near Hyderabad. Principle. The 2022 judgment held the 2018 amendment to Section 10 prospective. It was recalled in review in 2024, and the review did not decide that question. Why it matters. The effect of the 2018 amendment on older contracts is not settled by this case.

selfTest.q: 2. Can a party who rescinds also claim damages?
selfTest.a: Yes. Section 75 gives compensation to a person who rightfully rescinds.

selfTest.q: 3. What did the 2018 amendment change in Section 10 of the Specific Relief Act?
selfTest.a: It made specific performance something the court "shall" enforce, subject to Sections 11(2), 14 and 16.

selfTest.q: 4. Sita paid ₹50,000 in advance for 100 bags at ₹2,000. Ravi refuses on the due date, when the market price is ₹2,300. What can Sita recover if she ends the contract?
selfTest.a: Her ₹50,000 advance and damages of ₹30,000.

selfTest.q: 5. Can the injured party both rescind and claim specific performance?
selfTest.a: No. The two are inconsistent.

legalProvision: Section 39. When a party to a contract has refused to perform, or disabled himself from performing, his promise in its entirety, the promisee may put an end to the contract, unless he has signified, by words or conduct, his acquiescence in its continuance.

Section 64 (part). When a person at whose option a contract is voidable rescinds it, the other party thereto need not perform any promise therein contained in which he is promisor. The party rescinding a voidable contract shall, if he have received any benefit thereunder from another party to such contract, restore such benefit, so far as may be, to the person from whom it was received.

Section 65. When an agreement is discovered to be void, or when a contract becomes void, any person who has received any advantage under such agreement or contract is bound to restore it, or to make compensation for it to the person from whom he received it.

Section 73 (first two paragraphs). When a contract has been broken, the party who suffers by such breach is entitled to receive, from the party who has broken the contract, compensation for any loss or damage caused to him thereby, which naturally arose in the usual course of things from such breach, or which the parties knew, when they made the contract, to be likely to result from the breach of it. Such compensation is not to be given for any remote and indirect loss or damage sustained by reason of the breach.

Section 74 (first part). … the party complaining of the breach is entitled, whether or not actual damage or loss is proved to have been caused thereby, to receive from the party who has broken the contract reasonable compensation not exceeding the amount so named or, as the case may be, the penalty stipulated for.
Section 75. A person who rightfully rescinds a contract is entitled to compensation for any damage which he has sustained through the non-fulfilment of the contract.

Specific Relief Act, 1963, Section 10. The specific performance of a contract shall be enforced by the court subject to the provisions contained in sub-section (2) of section 11, section 14 and section 16.

Specific Relief Act, Section 42 (main part). Where a contract comprises an affirmative agreement to do a certain act, coupled with a negative agreement, express or implied, not to do a certain act, the circumstance that the court is unable to compel specific performance of the affirmative agreement shall not preclude it from granting an injunction to perform the negative agreement.

సెక్షన్ 39: ఎదుటి పక్షం మొత్తం కాంట్రాక్టును అమలు చేయనంటే, మీరు దాన్ని ముగించవచ్చు , అది కొనసాగడానికి మీరు అంగీకరిస్తే తప్ప. సెక్షన్లు 53, 55: ఒక పక్షం అమలును అడ్డుకుంటే, లేదా సమయం ముఖ్యమైన చోట సమయానికి అమలు చేయకపోతే, కాంట్రాక్టు ఎదుటి పక్షం ఇష్టప్రకారం voidable అవుతుంది, అతను పరిహారం కోరవచ్చు. సెక్షన్లు 64, 65: కాంట్రాక్టు ముగిసినప్పుడు, ప్రతి పక్షం తాను పొందినది తిరిగి ఇవ్వాలి . సెక్షన్ 73: సహజ నష్టానికి, ముందే ఊహించిన నష్టానికి నష్టపరిహారం ; దూరపు నష్టానికి కాదు. సెక్షన్ 74: ఉల్లంఘనకు ఒక మొత్తం పేర్కొంటే, ఆ మొత్తం వరకు సహేతుక పరిహారం . సెక్షన్ 75: కాంట్రాక్టును సరైన కారణంతో ముగించిన పక్షం నష్టపరిహారం కూడా కోరవచ్చు. Specific Relief Act: కోర్టు specific performance ఆదేశించవచ్చు (సెక్షన్ 10), దానితో పాటు గానీ దాని బదులు గానీ పరిహారం ఇవ్వవచ్చు (సెక్షన్ 21), దాన్ని తిరస్కరించిన చోట బయానా తిరిగి ఇవ్వమని ఆదేశించవచ్చు (సెక్షన్ 22), injunction ఇవ్వవచ్చు (సెక్షన్లు 36 నుంచి 42).
te.meaning:
పరిష్కారం (remedy) అంటే హక్కు భంగమైన పక్షానికి చట్టం ఇచ్చే ఉపశమనం. ఒక పక్షం తన వాగ్దానాన్ని అమలు చేయడంలో విఫలమైనప్పుడు గానీ, నిరాకరించినప్పుడు గానీ, అమలు చేయలేని స్థితికి తనను తాను తెచ్చుకున్నప్పుడు గానీ కాంట్రాక్టు ఉల్లంఘన జరుగుతుంది. ఉల్లంఘన వాస్తవ (actual; గడువు తేదీన లేదా తర్వాత) కావచ్చు, లేదా ముందస్తు (anticipatory; గడువు తేదీకి ముందు) కావచ్చు. పరిష్కారాలు ఎక్కడి నుంచి వస్తాయి. భారత కాంట్రాక్టు చట్టం ఉల్లంఘన ప్రభావాలను ప్రధానంగా సెక్షన్లు 39, 53 నుంచి 55, 64, 65, 73 నుంచి 75 లో చెబుతుంది. కోర్టు "ఉన్నది ఉన్నట్లు" ఇచ్చే పరిష్కారాలను Specific Relief Act, 1963 జోడిస్తుంది: specific performance , injunction . ఎన్నో పరిష్కారాలు ఎందుకు. నష్టపోయిన పక్షాలకు వేర్వేరు అవసరాలు ఉంటాయి. ఒకరు కాంట్రాక్టు నుంచి బయటపడి తన డబ్బు తిరిగి కావాలనుకుంటారు. ఒకరు నష్టానికి పరిహారం కావాలనుకుంటారు. ఒకరు వాగ్దానం చేసిన వస్తువే కావాలనుకుంటారు. ఒకరు ఎదుటి పక్షాన్ని ఆపాలనుకుంటారు. Diagram 1 చూడండి (పరిష్కారాలు, అవి సాధించేదాని ప్రకారం వర్గీకరించి). selfTest.q: 2. రద్దు చేసిన పక్షం నష్టపరిహారం కూడా కోరవచ్చా?
selfTest.a: అవును. సరైన కారణంతో రద్దు చేసిన వ్యక్తికి సెక్షన్ 75 పరిహారం ఇస్తుంది.

selfTest.q: 3. Specific Relief Act సెక్షన్ 10 లో 2018 సవరణ ఏమి మార్చింది?
selfTest.a: సెక్షన్లు 11(2), 14, 16 కి లోబడి, specific performance ను కోర్టు "shall" అమలు చేయాలని చేసింది.

selfTest.q: 4. ₹2,000 చొప్పున 100 బస్తాలకు సీత ₹50,000 అడ్వాన్స్ చెల్లించింది. మార్కెట్ ధర ₹2,300 ఉన్న గడువు తేదీన రవి నిరాకరించాడు. సీత కాంట్రాక్టు ముగిస్తే ఏమి పొందవచ్చు?
5. నష్టపోయిన పక్షం రద్దు చేసి, specific performance కూడా కోరవచ్చా?
selfTest.a: లేదు. రెండూ పరస్పర విరుద్ధం.

law-of-contract-i-u4-t10.subtitle: Section 74 of the Indian Contract Act, 1872, read with section 73

en.inOneMinute: Sometimes a contract fixes in advance what a party must pay if he breaks it. That is a liquidated sum, or, if it is meant to frighten, a penalty . Sometimes the contract says nothing, and the court works out the loss after the breach. Those are unliquidated damages, under Section 73. Section 74 governs every sum named for breach. The injured party gets reasonable compensation, never more than the sum named . Indian law does not split the named sum into a valid "liquidated damages" clause and a void "penalty" clause. Both are treated alike ( Fateh Chand , 1963). Loss is still essential, and where loss can be proved it must be proved ( Kailash Nath , 2015). In exams, Section 74, Fateh Chand , Kailash Nath , the upper limit and proof of loss earn the marks. In real life, the rule decides how much a seller can keep of an advance, or how much a buyer can deduct for late delivery.
legalProvision: Section 74. When a contract has been broken, if a sum is named in the contract as the amount to be paid in case of such breach, or if the contract contains any other stipulation by way of penalty, the party complaining of the breach is entitled, whether or not actual damage or loss is proved to have been caused thereby, to receive from the party who has broken the contract reasonable compensation not exceeding the amount so named or, as the case may be, the penalty stipulated for. Explanation. A stipulation for increased interest from the date of default may be a stipulation by way of penalty. Exception. When any person enters into any bail-bond, recognizance or other instrument of the same nature, or, under the provisions of any law, or under the orders of the Central Government or of any State Government, gives any bond for the performance of any public duty or act in which the public are interested, he shall be liable, upon breach of the condition of any such instrument, to pay the whole sum mentioned therein. Explanation. A person who enters into a contract with Government does not necessarily thereby undertake any public duty, or promise to do an act in which the public are interested.

Section 73 (summary). Compensation is given for loss that naturally arose in the usual course of things from the breach, or that the parties knew, when they made the contract, to be likely to result from it. It is not given for remote and indirect loss.
In simple words

Section 74: if the contract names a sum for breach, or contains any other penalty (such as forfeiting money already paid), the court gives reasonable compensation , and the sum named is the ceiling . Explanation: a jump in interest on default may be a penalty. Exception: bail-bonds, recognizances and bonds for a public duty are payable in full . A contract with the Government is not, by itself, a public duty. Section 73: where nothing is named, the court assesses the loss itself.
en.meaning:
Liquidated damages are a sum the contract fixes in advance as payable on breach, as a genuine pre-estimate of the likely loss. Unliquidated damages are not fixed in advance. The court assesses them after the breach, under Section 73 . A penalty is a sum fixed mainly to frighten a party into performing ( in terrorem ). It is out of proportion to any likely loss. Earnest money is a deposit paid when the contract is made, as a sign that the payer means to perform. It usually goes towards the price. The English background. Under English common law, a genuine pre-estimate was enforced in full as liquidated damages , and a penalty was not enforced at all. In Fateh Chand v. Balkishan Dass (1963), the Supreme Court said Section 74 is "an attempt to eliminate the somewhat elaborate refinements" of that English distinction. India has one rule for both : reasonable compensation not exceeding the sum named. Why the law has this rule. Damages compensate and do not punish. A party should not get a windfall just because the contract named a large figure. But a fair pre-estimate saves the trouble of proving a loss that is hard to measure. See Diagram 1 (how a court applies Section 74). Diagram 1. Yes: is it a bail-bond or public duty bond? Yes: whole sum payable (Exception). No: was there any loss? No: nothing (Kailash Nath). Yes: can the loss be proved? Yes: actual proved loss, capped at the sum named. No, hard to prove, and the sum is a genuine pre-estimate: the sum may be awarded (ONGC v. Saw Pipes). Never above the sum named (MTNL).
keyPoints: Section 74 applies to a named sum and to any penalty , including forfeiture. The court awards reasonable compensation . The sum named is the upper limit . India does not distinguish liquidated damages from a penalty ( Fateh Chand ). Loss is a sine qua non. Where loss can be proved, it must be proved ( Kailash Nath ). Proof is excused where loss is hard to prove and the sum is a genuine pre-estimate ( ONGC v. Saw Pipes ). Forfeiture of reasonable earnest money: two lines of authority. Increased interest on default may be a penalty. An acceleration clause for a real debt is not. Bail-bonds and public duty bonds are payable in full . Unliquidated damages are assessed by the court under Section 73 .

caseLaws.name: Fateh Chand v
caseLaws.facts: Balkishan Dass (1963) Facts. A buyer agreed to buy a Delhi property for Rs. 1,12,500, paid Rs. 1,000 earnest money and Rs. 24,000 towards the price, and failed to complete. The contract said Rs. 25,000 would be forfeited. Principle. Section 74 applies to every stipulation by way of penalty, including forfeiture of money paid. Only reasonable compensation up to the sum named is given. AIR 1963 SC 1405. Why it matters. It removed the English distinction in India. The seller kept only the Rs. 1,000. Maula Bux v. Union of India (1969) Facts. A supplier of potatoes, and of poultry, eggs and fish, to the Government gave deposits of Rs. 10,000 and Rs. 8,500 as security. On his default, the Government forfeited them without proving loss. Principle. Reasonable earnest money may be forfeited. But a security deposit is not earnest money. Where loss can be measured in money, it must be proved. AIR 1970 SC 1955. Why it matters. It limits forfeiture of deposits to real, proved loss. ONGC Ltd. v. Saw Pipes Ltd. (2003) Facts. Saw Pipes supplied casing pipes late. The contract fixed liquidated damages at 1% per week of delay, up to 10%, and ONGC deducted them. Principle. A genuine pre-estimate is payable without proof of actual loss, unless the other side shows it is unreasonable. (2003) 5 SCC 705. Why it matters. It explains when proof of loss is not required. Kailash Nath Associates v. DDA (2015) Facts. DDA forfeited ₹78 lakh earnest money (25% of a ₹3.12 crore bid). It later re-auctioned the plot for ₹11.78 crore. Principle. Loss is a sine qua non under Section 74. Where loss can be proved, it must be proved. Section 74 applies to forfeiture of earnest money. (2015) 4 SCC 136. Why it matters. It is the leading summary of Section 74. DDA, with no loss, had to refund. Construction and Design Services v. Delhi Development Authority (2015) Facts. A contractor was late in building a sewage pumping station. DDA claimed the agreed compensation for delay. Principle. Loss may be presumed for a delayed public utility project. Where only a maximum is fixed, the court may award part as reasonable compensation. Half the claim was awarded. Supreme Court, decided 4 February 2015. Why it matters. It shows how the burden of proof works. Mahanagar Telephone Nigam Ltd. v. Tata Communications Ltd. (2019) Facts. A purchase order capped liquidated damages at 12%. MTNL deducted more from the bills. Principle. A higher amount than the contract fixes cannot be awarded. The excess had to be refunded. Why it matters. It applies the upper limit under Section 74. K.R. Suresh v. R. Poornima (2025) Facts. Under a 2007 agreement to sell property for ₹55,50,000, the buyer paid ₹20,00,000 and failed to pay the balance. The vendors forfeited the advance. Principle. The earnest money clause was not penal, so Section 74 did not apply. Even if it did, the vendors' proved losses exceeded the sum forfeited. 2025 INSC 617. Why it matters. It is the latest Supreme Court word on earnest money.

selfTest.q: 1. What is the upper limit of compensation under Section 74?
selfTest.a: The sum named in the contract, or the penalty stipulated .

selfTest.q: 2. Does Indian law treat liquidated damages and a penalty differently?
selfTest.a: No. Section 74 gives reasonable compensation up to the sum named in both ( Fateh Chand ).

selfTest.q: 3. A contract fixes ₹500 for each month of delay. The seller is six months late and the buyer's loss is ₹6,500. What can the buyer recover?
selfTest.a: At most ₹3,000, because the sum named is the upper limit.

selfTest.q: 4. Is any compensation payable under Section 74 if there is no loss at all?
selfTest.a: No. Loss is a sine qua non ( Kailash Nath ).

selfTest.q: 5. Which instruments are enforced for the whole sum?
selfTest.a: Bail-bonds, recognizances and bonds for a public duty (the Exception to Section 74).

Section 73 (సారాంశం). ఉల్లంఘన నుంచి సాధారణ పరిస్థితుల్లో సహజంగా వచ్చిన నష్టానికి, లేదా కాంట్రాక్టు చేసుకున్నప్పుడు జరగవచ్చని పక్షాలకు తెలిసిన నష్టానికి పరిహారం ఇస్తారు. దూరపు, పరోక్ష నష్టానికి ఇవ్వరు.
సులభమైన మాటల్లో

సెక్షన్ 74: ఉల్లంఘనకు కాంట్రాక్టు ఒక మొత్తం పేర్కొంటే, లేదా వేరే ఏదైనా జరిమానా (ఇప్పటికే చెల్లించిన డబ్బును జప్తు చేయడం వంటిది) ఉంటే, కోర్టు సహేతుక పరిహారం ఇస్తుంది. పేర్కొన్న మొత్తం గరిష్ట పరిమితి . Explanation: ఉల్లంఘన జరిగినప్పటి నుంచి వడ్డీ పెంచడం జరిమానా కావచ్చు . Exception: బెయిల్ బాండ్లు, recognizances, ప్రజా విధికి ఇచ్చే బాండ్ల మొత్తాన్ని పూర్తిగా చెల్లించాలి. ప్రభుత్వంతో కాంట్రాక్టు చేసుకున్నంత మాత్రాన అది ప్రజా విధి కాదు. సెక్షన్ 73: ఏ మొత్తమూ పేర్కొనని చోట, కోర్టే నష్టాన్ని అంచనా వేస్తుంది.
te.meaning:
Liquidated damages (ముందే నిర్ణయించిన నష్టపరిహారం ) అంటే జరగబోయే నష్టానికి నిజాయితీగా ముందుగా వేసిన అంచనాగా (genuine pre-estimate), ఉల్లంఘనపై చెల్లించాల్సినదిగా కాంట్రాక్టు ముందుగానే నిర్ణయించిన మొత్తం. Unliquidated damages (నిర్ణయించని నష్టపరిహారం) ముందుగా నిర్ణయించినవి కావు . ఉల్లంఘన తర్వాత సెక్షన్ 73 కింద కోర్టు వాటిని అంచనా వేస్తుంది. జరిమానా (penalty) అంటే ఒక పక్షాన్ని భయపెట్టి కాంట్రాక్టు అమలు చేయించడానికే ( in terrorem ) ప్రధానంగా నిర్ణయించిన మొత్తం. జరగవచ్చిన ఏ నష్టానికీ ఇది సరితూగదు. బయానా (earnest money) అంటే కాంట్రాక్టు చేసుకునేటప్పుడు, చెల్లించేవాడు కాంట్రాక్టు అమలు చేయాలనుకుంటున్నాడని చూపడానికి చెల్లించే డిపాజిట్. సాధారణంగా ఇది ధరలో భాగంగా లెక్కకు వస్తుంది. ఇంగ్లీష్ నేపథ్యం. ఇంగ్లీష్ common law కింద, నిజాయితీ అంచనాను liquidated damages గా పూర్తిగా అమలు చేసేవారు, జరిమానాను అసలు అమలు చేసేవారు కాదు. Fateh Chand v. Balkishan Dass (1963) లో, సెక్షన్ 74 ఆ ఇంగ్లీష్ తేడాలోని "somewhat elaborate refinements" ను తొలగించే ప్రయత్నమని సుప్రీంకోర్టు చెప్పింది. భారతదేశంలో రెండింటికీ ఒకే నియమం : పేర్కొన్న మొత్తానికి మించని సహేతుక పరిహారం. చట్టం ఈ నియమం ఎందుకు పెట్టింది. నష్టపరిహారం నష్టాన్ని పూడుస్తుంది, శిక్షించదు. కాంట్రాక్టులో పెద్ద సంఖ్య రాసినంత మాత్రాన ఒక పక్షానికి అనుకోని లాభం రాకూడదు. కానీ కొలవడం కష్టమైన నష్టాన్ని నిరూపించే శ్రమను న్యాయమైన ముందస్తు అంచనా తప్పిస్తుంది.
