law-of-contract-i-u4-t9.subtitle: Sections 73 and 75 of the Indian Contract Act, 1872

en.inOneMinute: Damages are money paid to a party who has suffered by a breach of contract. The aim is to put him, as far as money can, where he would have been if the contract had been performed. Damages compensate . They do not punish . Section 73 sets the limits. The loss must arise naturally from the breach, or be one the parties knew was likely when they made the contract. Remote and indirect loss is not paid. The kinds of damages are general (ordinary), special, nominal, exemplary, liquidated and unliquidated . Damages for mental distress are not given in an ordinary commercial contract. In exams, the kinds of damages with an example each, the rule in Hadley v. Baxendale , the market-price measure and the Act's illustrations earn the marks. In real life, they decide how much a wronged party can actually recover.
legalProvision: Section 73. When a contract has been broken, the party who suffers by such breach is entitled to receive, from the party who has broken the contract, compensation for any loss or damage caused to him thereby, which naturally arose in the usual course of things from such breach, or which the parties knew, when they made the contract, to be likely to result from the breach of it. Such compensation is not to be given for any remote and indirect loss or damage sustained by reason of the breach. Compensation for failure to discharge obligation resembling those created by contract. When an obligation resembling those created by contract has been incurred and has not been discharged, any person injured by the failure to discharge it is entitled to receive the same compensation from the party in default, as if such person had contracted to discharge it and had broken his contract. Explanation. In estimating the loss or damage arising from a breach of contract, the means which existed of remedying the inconvenience caused by the non-performance of the contract must be taken into account.

Section 74 (first part). When a contract has been broken, if a sum is named in the contract as the amount to be paid in case of such breach, or if the contract contains any other stipulation by way of penalty, the party complaining of the breach is entitled, whether or not actual damage or loss is proved to have been caused thereby, to receive from the party who has broken the contract reasonable compensation not exceeding the amount so named or, as the case may be, the penalty stipulated for.
In simple words

Section 73, first paragraph: pay for loss that arises naturally from the breach (first limb), and for loss both parties knew was likely when they contracted (second limb). Section 73, second paragraph: do not pay for remote and indirect loss. Section 73, third paragraph: the same rule applies to quasi-contractual obligations. Explanation: count what the injured party could have done to reduce the loss. Section 74: if the contract names a sum for breach, the court gives reasonable compensation up to that sum.
The Act gives eighteen illustrations, (a) to (r), to Section 73. The table in section 9 below groups them by the rule each one shows.
en.meaning:
Damages are the compensation, in money, that the law awards to a person for loss caused to him by a breach of contract. The Act uses the word "compensation". "Damages" is the word used in courts and exam questions. The aim is compensation, not punishment. The injured party should be no worse off and no better off than if the contract had been performed. That is why: he gets his actual, proved loss, not a reward; he cannot claim remote loss; he cannot claim loss he could have avoided (mitigation); a penalty clause is cut down to reasonable compensation (Section 74). Four questions decide whether a loss is recoverable (see Diagram 1 ): Diagram 1. Ask the four questions in order. flowchart TD L["A loss after a breach"] --> Q1{"1. Caused by the breach?"} Q1 -- "No" --> X1["Not recoverable"] Q1 -- "Yes" --> Q2{"2. Arose naturally, OR both parties
knew it was likely when contracting?"} Q2 -- "No" --> X2["Remote and indirect · not paid
Section 73, para 2"] Q2 -- "Yes" --> Q3{"3. Loss and amount proved?"} Q3 -- "No" --> X3["Nominal damages only"] Q3 -- "Yes" --> Q4{"4. Could reasonable steps
have reduced it?"} Q4 -- "Yes" --> X4["Avoidable part cut
Explanation to Section 73"] Q4 -- "No" --> OK["Compensation for the loss
Section 73"] X4 --> OK Text description 1 Was the loss caused by the breach? No: nothing. 2 Did it arise naturally, or did both parties know it was likely when contracting? No: remote, not paid. 3 Is the loss and its amount proved? No: nominal damages only. 4 Could reasonable steps have reduced it? Yes: avoidable part cut. Result: compensation for the proved, natural or foreseen, unavoidable loss. Was the loss caused by the breach? Did it arise naturally , or did both parties know it was likely when they contracted? If not, it is remote. Has the claimant proved the loss and its amount? If not, only nominal damages . Could he have reduced it by reasonable steps? If yes, the avoidable part is cut.
keyPoints: Damages compensate for loss caused by the breach. They do not punish. Section 73 pays for natural loss and for loss both parties knew was likely, but not for remote and indirect loss. The kinds are general, special, nominal, exemplary, liquidated and unliquidated . Special damages need knowledge of the special circumstances when the contract was made . Nominal damages are given when breach is proved but no loss. Exemplary damages are generally not given in contract. No damages for mental agony in an ordinary commercial contract. Hadley v. Baxendale (1854) is the source of the two limbs of Section 73. For goods, the measure is the market price against the contract price at the date of breach .

caseLaws.name: Hadley v
caseLaws.facts: Baxendale (1854) Facts. A Gloucester mill's crank shaft broke. The owners sent it by carrier to Greenwich as a pattern for a new one. The carrier delayed delivery, and the mill lost profits. Principle. Damages are those arising naturally from the breach, or reasonably in the contemplation of both parties when they contracted. Special circumstances count only if communicated. (1854) 9 Exch 341; 156 ER 145. Why it matters. Its two limbs are written into Section 73. Karsandas H. Thacker v. Saran Engineering Co. (1965) Facts. A seller agreed to supply 200 tons of scrap iron at Rs. 100 a ton, then said he could not deliver. The buyer had agreed to resell to a third party. Principle. The seller was not liable for the buyer's payment to the third party, because that contract was not communicated. The buyer proved no market-price loss. AIR 1965 SC 1981. Why it matters. It applies Section 73 to remote loss and to the measure of damages. Victoria Laundry (Windsor) Ltd. v. Newman Industries Ltd. (1949) Facts. A boiler for a laundry was delivered late. The laundry claimed ordinary lost profits and the profits of special Government dyeing contracts. Principle. Ordinary profits were recoverable. The special profits were not, because the supplier did not know of those contracts. [1949] 2 KB 528. Why it matters. It applies the two limbs to a business loss. C. Czarnikow Ltd. v. Koufos (The Heron II) (1967) Facts. A ship carrying sugar to Basra arrived late, after the sugar price had fallen. Principle. The test of remoteness in contract is whether the loss was "not unlikely" to result. [1969] 1 AC 350. Why it matters. It states how likely a loss must be under the second limb. Jamal v. Moolla Dawood, Sons & Co. (1915) Facts. Buyers failed to take 23,500 shares on 30 December 1911. The seller sold them later. Principle. The measure is the contract price minus the market price on the date of breach. (1915) LR 43 IA 6 (PC). Why it matters. It fixes the date at which the loss is measured. Ghaziabad Development Authority v. Union of India (2000) Facts. A housing authority failed to allot plots as promised. ₹50,000 was awarded for "mental agony". Principle. Damages for mental agony are not given for breach of an ordinary commercial contract. The award was set aside. (2000) 6 SCC 113. Why it matters. It limits damages for mental distress in contract.

selfTest.q: 1. What are the two limbs of the rule in Hadley v. Baxendale?
selfTest.a: Loss arising naturally from the breach, and loss both parties reasonably contemplated, when contracting, as the probable result of breach.

selfTest.q: 2. Ravi fails to deliver 100 bags of rice at ₹2,000. The market price on the due date is ₹2,300. What are the general damages?
3. When can special damages be recovered?
selfTest.a: Only if the special circumstances were known to both parties when the contract was made.

selfTest.q: 4. Are exemplary damages normally awarded for breach of contract?
selfTest.a: No. Contract damages compensate. Textbooks list breach of promise to marry and wrongful dishonour of a cheque as exceptions.

selfTest.q: 5. What are nominal damages?
selfTest.a: A small sum given when a breach is proved but no real loss is shown.

Kind What it covers Condition Example
General (ordinary) Loss that naturally follows from the breach Proof of loss ₹30,000 market difference on rice
Special Loss from unusual circumstances Known to both parties when contracting ₹50,000 wedding profit, if Ravi knew
Nominal A small sum to mark the breach Breach proved, no loss proved Market price fell to ₹1,800
Exemplary Punishment of the wrongdoer Not part of contract law, except rare textbook cases Breach of a promise to marry
Mental distress Anguish, vexation Not in an ordinary commercial contract Ghaziabad Development Authority (2000)
Liquidated A sum fixed in the contract Section 74: reasonable compensation up to that sum ₹1,000 for each day of delay
Unliquidated A sum the court assesses Section 73 Most claims

When an obligation resembling those created by contract has been incurred and has not been discharged, any person injured by the failure to discharge it is entitled to receive the same compensation from the party in default, as if such person had contracted to discharge it and had broken his contract. Explanation. In estimating the loss or damage arising from a breach of contract, the means which existed of remedying the inconvenience caused by the non-performance of the contract must be taken into account.

Section 74 (first part). When a contract has been broken, if a sum is named in the contract as the amount to be paid in case of such breach, or if the contract contains any other stipulation by way of penalty, the party complaining of the breach is entitled, whether or not actual damage or loss is proved to have been caused thereby, to receive from the party who has broken the contract reasonable compensation not exceeding the amount so named or, as the case may be, the penalty stipulated for.
సులభమైన మాటల్లో

సెక్షన్ 73, మొదటి పేరా: ఉల్లంఘన నుంచి సహజంగా వచ్చే నష్టానికి (మొదటి భాగం), కాంట్రాక్టు చేసుకున్నప్పుడు జరగవచ్చని ఇరుపక్షాలకూ తెలిసిన నష్టానికి (రెండో భాగం) పరిహారం ఇవ్వాలి. సెక్షన్ 73, రెండో పేరా: దూరపు, పరోక్ష నష్టానికి పరిహారం ఇవ్వకూడదు . సెక్షన్ 73, మూడో పేరా: quasi- contract బాధ్యతలకూ ఇదే నియమం వర్తిస్తుంది. Explanation: నష్టాన్ని తగ్గించడానికి నష్టపోయిన పక్షం ఏమి చేయగలిగేవాడో లెక్కలోకి తీసుకోండి. సెక్షన్ 74: ఉల్లంఘనకు కాంట్రాక్టులో ఒక మొత్తం పేర్కొంటే, ఆ మొత్తానికి మించకుండా కోర్టు సహేతుక పరిహారం ఇస్తుంది.
సెక్షన్ 73 కి చట్టం (a) నుంచి (r) వరకు పద్దెనిమిది illustrations ఇచ్చింది. కింది 9వ భాగంలోని పట్టిక, ఒక్కొక్కటి ఏ నియమాన్ని చూపిస్తుందో దాని ప్రకారం వాటిని వర్గీకరిస్తుంది.
te.meaning:
నష్టపరిహారం అంటే కాంట్రాక్టు ఉల్లంఘన వల్ల ఒక వ్యక్తికి కలిగిన నష్టానికి చట్టం డబ్బు రూపంలో ఇచ్చే పరిహారం. చట్టం "compensation" అనే మాట వాడుతుంది. కోర్టుల్లో, పరీక్ష ప్రశ్నల్లో "damages" అనే మాట వాడతారు. లక్ష్యం నష్టాన్ని పూడ్చడం, శిక్షించడం కాదు. కాంట్రాక్టు అమలైతే ఉండే స్థితి కంటే నష్టపోయిన పక్షం దిగువన గానీ ఎగువన గానీ ఉండకూడదు. అందుకే: అతనికి నిజమైన, నిరూపించిన నష్టం వస్తుంది, బహుమతి కాదు; దూరపు నష్టాన్ని కోరలేడు; తాను తప్పించుకోగలిగిన నష్టాన్ని కోరలేడు (mitigation); జరిమానా ( penalty ) షరతును సహేతుక పరిహారానికి తగ్గిస్తారు (సెక్షన్ 74). ఒక నష్టం వస్తుందా రాదా అని నాలుగు ప్రశ్నలు నిర్ణయిస్తాయి ( Diagram 1 చూడండి): Diagram 1. నాలుగు ప్రశ్నలను వరుసగా అడగండి. flowchart TD L["ఉల్లంఘన తర్వాత ఒక నష్టం"] --> Q1{"1. ఉల్లంఘన వల్లే వచ్చిందా?"} Q1 -- "కాదు" --> X1["రాదు"] Q1 -- "అవును" --> Q2{"2. సహజంగా వచ్చిందా, లేదా కాంట్రాక్టు
చేసుకున్నప్పుడే ఇరుపక్షాలకూ తెలుసా?"} Q2 -- "కాదు" --> X2["దూరపు, పరోక్ష నష్టం · రాదు
సెక్షన్ 73, పేరా 2"] Q2 -- "అవును" --> Q3{"3. నష్టం, దాని మొత్తం నిరూపించారా?"} Q3 -- "లేదు" --> X3["నామమాత్ర నష్టపరిహారం మాత్రమే"] Q3 -- "అవును" --> Q4{"4. సహేతుక చర్యలతో
తగ్గించగలిగేవాడా?"} Q4 -- "అవును" --> X4["తప్పించుకోగలిగిన భాగం తీసివేస్తారు
సెక్షన్ 73 Explanation"] Q4 -- "లేదు" --> OK["నష్టానికి పరిహారం
సెక్షన్ 73"] X4 --> OK వచన వివరణ 1 నష్టం ఉల్లంఘన వల్లేనా? 2 సహజంగా వచ్చిందా, లేదా ఇరుపక్షాలకూ తెలుసా? లేకపోతే దూరపు నష్టం. 3 నిరూపించారా? లేకపోతే నామమాత్రం. 4 సహేతుక చర్యలతో తగ్గించగలిగేవాడా? అవునైతే ఆ భాగం తీసివేస్తారు. ఆ నష్టం ఉల్లంఘన వల్లే వచ్చిందా? అది సహజంగా వచ్చిందా, లేదా కాంట్రాక్టు చేసుకున్నప్పుడు జరగవచ్చని ఇరుపక్షాలకూ తెలుసా ? లేకపోతే అది దూరపు నష్టం. క్లెయిమ్ చేసినవాడు నష్టాన్నీ దాని మొత్తాన్నీ నిరూపించాడా ? లేకపోతే నామమాత్ర నష్టపరిహారం మాత్రమే. సహేతుక చర్యలతో అతను దాన్ని తగ్గించగలిగేవాడా ? అవునైతే, తప్పించుకోగలిగిన భాగం తీసివేస్తారు.

selfTest.q: 1. Hadley v. Baxendale నియమంలోని రెండు భాగాలు ఏవి?
selfTest.a: ఉల్లంఘన నుంచి సహజంగా వచ్చే నష్టం; కాంట్రాక్టు చేసుకున్నప్పుడు ఉల్లంఘన వల్ల జరగవచ్చని ఇరుపక్షాలూ సహేతుకంగా ఊహించిన నష్టం.

selfTest.q: 2. ₹2,000 చొప్పున 100 బస్తాల బియ్యాన్ని రవి డెలివరీ చేయలేదు. గడువు తేదీ నాటి మార్కెట్ ధర ₹2,300. సాధారణ నష్టపరిహారం ఎంత?
3. ప్రత్యేక నష్టపరిహారం ఎప్పుడు వస్తుంది?
selfTest.a: కాంట్రాక్టు చేసుకున్నప్పుడే ప్రత్యేక పరిస్థితులు ఇరుపక్షాలకూ తెలిసి ఉంటేనే.

selfTest.q: 4. కాంట్రాక్టు ఉల్లంఘనకు సాధారణంగా శిక్షాత్మక నష్టపరిహారం ఇస్తారా?
selfTest.a: లేదు. కాంట్రాక్టు నష్టపరిహారం నష్టాన్ని పూడుస్తుంది. పెళ్లి వాగ్దానం ఉల్లంఘన, చెక్కును తప్పుగా తిరస్కరించడం మినహాయింపులుగా పాఠ్యపుస్తకాలు చెబుతాయి.

selfTest.q: 5. నామమాత్ర నష్టపరిహారం అంటే ఏమిటి?
selfTest.a: ఉల్లంఘన నిరూపితమై, నిజమైన నష్టం చూపించనప్పుడు ఇచ్చే చిన్న మొత్తం.

visuals.html:
అంశం మొత్తం
జూన్ 1 నాటి మార్కెట్ ధర బస్తా ₹2,300
కాంట్రాక్టు ధర బస్తా ₹2,000
తేడా బస్తా ₹300
పరిమాణం 100 బస్తాలు
సాధారణ నష్టపరిహారం 100 × ₹300 = ₹30,000

పరిస్థితి ఫలితం
బియ్యం ఈ పెళ్లి ఆర్డర్ కోసమని కాంట్రాక్టు చేసుకున్నప్పుడే రవికి తెలుసు ఆ నష్టం ఇరుపక్షాల ఊహలో ఉంది. నష్టపరిహారం = ₹30,000 + ₹50,000 = ₹80,000
పెళ్లి ఆర్డర్ గురించి రవికి తెలియదు ₹50,000 దూరపు నష్టం. నష్టపరిహారం ₹30,000 మాత్రమే

Illustration క్లుప్తంగా వాస్తవాలు ఫలితం
(a), (c), (d), (g), (h) సరుకు, ఓడ, లేదా అద్దె డెలివరీ కాలేదు, తీసుకోలేదు, లేదా చెల్లించలేదు డెలివరీ లేదా ఉల్లంఘన సమయంలో కాంట్రాక్టు ధరకూ మార్కెట్ ధరకూ తేడా
(b) ఓడ బయలుదేరలేదు; A సమానంగా మంచి షరతులపై వేరే రవాణా ఏర్పాటు చేసుకున్నాడు ఏర్పాటు చేసుకోవడంలో శ్రమ, ఖర్చు
(e) పడవ ఆలస్యంగా బయలుదేరింది, చేరేలోపు జనుము ధర పడిపోయింది సమయానికి చేరితే ఉండే ధర మైనస్ నిజంగా చేరినప్పటి ధర
(f) మరమ్మతు చేశారు, కానీ కాంట్రాక్టు ప్రకారం కాదు కాంట్రాక్టుకు తగ్గట్టు చేయడానికి అయ్యే ఖర్చు
(i) యంత్రం లేక మిల్లు ఆగిందని తెలిసీ రవాణాదారు ఆలస్యం చేశాడు ఆలస్య కాలంలో మిల్లు సగటు లాభం, కోల్పోయిన ప్రభుత్వ కాంట్రాక్టు కాదు
(j), (l), (m) తిరిగి అమ్మడం, మరొకరికి అద్దెకివ్వడం, లేదా మరొకరికి ఇచ్చిన వారంటీ గురించి ప్రతివాదికి తెలుసు కోల్పోయిన లాభం; తిరిగి కట్టే ఖర్చు, కోల్పోయిన అద్దె, చెల్లించిన పరిహారం; ఉప-కొనుగోలుదారుకు చెల్లించిన మొత్తం
(k), (o), (p), (q) మూడో వ్యక్తి కాంట్రాక్టు, తిరిగి అమ్మడం, లేదా ప్రత్యేక వాడకం గురించి ప్రతివాదికి తెలియదు ధర లేదా మార్కెట్ తేడా మాత్రమే, అదనపు నష్టం కాదు
(n) ఆ రోజు డబ్బు చెల్లించలేదు; అప్పిచ్చినవాడు నాశనమయ్యాడు అసలు, వడ్డీ మాత్రమే
(r) ఓడ బయలుదేరలేదు; ప్రయాణికుడు ఆలస్యంగా చేరి డబ్బు కోల్పోయాడు వడ్డీతో డిపాజిట్, ఆగిన ఖర్చు, అదనపు చార్జీ; ఆలస్యంగా చేరడం వల్ల వచ్చిన నష్టం కాదు

రకం దేనికి షరతు ఉదాహరణ
సాధారణ (general) ఉల్లంఘన నుంచి సహజంగా వచ్చే నష్టం నష్టానికి రుజువు బియ్యం మీద ₹30,000 మార్కెట్ తేడా
ప్రత్యేక (special) అసాధారణ పరిస్థితుల వల్ల నష్టం కాంట్రాక్టు చేసుకున్నప్పుడే ఇరుపక్షాలకూ తెలుసు రవికి తెలిస్తే ₹50,000 పెళ్లి లాభం
నామమాత్ర (nominal) ఉల్లంఘనను సూచించే చిన్న మొత్తం ఉల్లంఘన నిరూపితం, నష్టం నిరూపితం కాలేదు మార్కెట్ ధర ₹1,800 కి పడింది
శిక్షాత్మక (exemplary) ఉల్లంఘించినవాడికి శిక్ష కాంట్రాక్టు చట్టంలో భాగం కాదు, అరుదైన పాఠ్యపుస్తక సందర్భాలు తప్ప పెళ్లి వాగ్దానం ఉల్లంఘన

law-of-contract-i-u4-t11.subtitle: Explanation to section 73 of the Indian Contract Act, 1872

en.inOneMinute: When a contract is broken, the injured party must act sensibly. He must take reasonable steps to keep his loss small . He cannot sit still, let the loss grow, and then bill the wrongdoer for all of it. Loss that reasonable steps would have avoided is not paid . The rule comes from the Explanation to Section 73 : in estimating the loss, "the means which existed of remedying the inconvenience" must be taken into account. It is a limit on what he can claim , not a duty anyone can sue him for. Reasonable costs of mitigating are recoverable, and gains made by mitigating are deducted. In exams, the meaning, the rules (reasonable steps, nothing extraordinary, costs, gains, burden of proof) and the cases ( Murlidhar Chiranjilal , Jamal , British Westinghouse , Payzu ) earn the marks. In real life, the rule decides how much of a large loss a court will actually award.
legalProvision: Section 73 (first two paragraphs). When a contract has been broken, the party who suffers by such breach is entitled to receive, from the party who has broken the contract, compensation for any loss or damage caused to him thereby, which naturally arose in the usual course of things from such breach, or which the parties knew, when they made the contract, to be likely to result from the breach of it. Such compensation is not to be given for any remote and indirect loss or damage sustained by reason of the breach.

Explanation. In estimating the loss or damage arising from a breach of contract, the means which existed of remedying the inconvenience caused by the non-performance of the contract must be taken into account.

Illustration (a). A contracts to sell and deliver 50 maunds of saltpetre to B, at a certain price to be paid on delivery. A breaks his promise. B is entitled to receive from A, by way of compensation, the sum, if any, by which the contract price falls short of the price for which B might have obtained 50 maunds of saltpetre of like quality at the time when the saltpetre ought to have been delivered.

Illustration (b). A hires B's ship to go to Bombay, and there take on board, on the first of January, a cargo, which A is to provide, and to bring it to Calcutta, the freight to be paid when earned. B's ship does not go to Bombay, but A has opportunities of procuring suitable conveyance for the cargo upon terms as advantageous as those on which he had chartered the ship. A avails himself of those opportunities, but is put to trouble and expense in doing so. A is entitled to receive compensation from B in respect of such trouble and expense.
In simple words

Section 73 pays for loss that arises naturally from the breach, and for loss both sides knew was likely. It does not pay for remote loss. The Explanation says: count what the injured party could have done to reduce the loss. Illustration (a) measures the loss by the price at which the buyer might have bought elsewhere, so he is expected to buy elsewhere. Illustration (b) shows the other side: the reasonable trouble and expense of mitigating is paid by the wrongdoer. Illustrations (c), (d), (g) and (h) also measure loss by the market price, which shows what the injured party could have got elsewhere.
en.meaning:
Mitigation means taking reasonable steps to reduce the loss caused by a breach. The Supreme Court stated the rule in Murlidhar Chiranjilal v. Harishchandra Dwarkadas (1961). It said there are two settled principles under Section 73 read with its Explanation: the injured party is to be placed, as far as money can do it, in as good a situation as if the contract had been performed; but he has a duty to take all reasonable steps to mitigate the loss, and he cannot claim any part of the damage that is due to his neglect to take such steps. The Privy Council said the same earlier in Jamal v. Moolla Dawood, Sons & Co. (1915). Why the law has this rule. Fairness. The wrongdoer should pay for the loss his breach caused, not for the part the injured party could easily have avoided. It is not a true "duty". The injured party is not liable to anyone for failing to mitigate. The wrongdoer cannot sue him. He only loses the right to recover the avoidable part of the loss. See Diagram 1 (from breach to the claim: where mitigation fits). Diagram 1. Damages are fixed at the date of breach. Sita waits to 1 July and pays ₹2,600; extra ₹30,000 is avoidable and not paid. Reasonable cost of mitigation, ₹2,000 lorry, is added. Any gain from mitigation is set off. Claim allowed ₹32,000. Burden of proving failure to mitigate is on the wrongdoer.
keyPoints: The injured party must take reasonable steps to reduce his loss (Explanation to Section 73). Avoidable loss cannot be recovered. He need not take extraordinary or risky steps, or accept a lower-status job. The reasonable cost of mitigation is recoverable (illustration (b)). A gain made by mitigating is set off against the damages. The wrongdoer must prove the failure to mitigate. For goods, the loss is fixed at the date of breach . Delay is at the injured party's risk. Failure to mitigate only reduces the damages. No one can sue for it.

caseLaws.name: Murlidhar Chiranjilal v
caseLaws.facts: Harishchandra Dwarkadas (1961) Facts. A seller failed to supply canvas under a contract for delivery at Kanpur, to be sent to Calcutta. The buyer claimed damages at the Calcutta price. Principle. Under Section 73 and its Explanation, the buyer must take all reasonable steps to mitigate. Damages are the Kanpur market price on the date of breach minus the contract price. The buyer did not prove the Kanpur price and got nothing. AIR 1962 SC 366. Why it matters. It is the Supreme Court authority on the duty to mitigate. Jamal v. Moolla Dawood, Sons & Co. (1915) Facts. Buyers failed to take 23,500 shares on 30 December 1911. The seller sold them later, mostly at higher prices. Principle. The loss is the difference between the contract price and the market price on the date of breach. Later market movements are the seller's own risk. (1915) LR 43 IA 6; ILR 43 Cal 493 (PC). Why it matters. It fixes the date of assessment and states the duty to mitigate. British Westinghouse Electric and Manufacturing Co. v. Underground Electric Railways Co. of London (1912) Facts. Turbines supplied for a power station were less efficient than promised. The buyers replaced them with better turbines from another maker. Principle. The injured party must take all reasonable steps to reduce his loss, but need not take steps a prudent person would not ordinarily take. A gain from reasonable mitigation is set off. [1912] AC 673. Why it matters. It states the main rules of mitigation and was relied on by the Supreme Court in Murlidhar Chiranjilal . Payzu Ltd. v. Saunders (1919) Facts. A seller refused to continue supplying on credit but offered the same goods at the same price for cash. The buyer refused and bought elsewhere at a higher price. Principle. The buyer should have accepted the reasonable offer. His damages were limited to what he would have lost by accepting it. [1919] 2 KB 581. Why it matters. Mitigation may include accepting an offer from the wrongdoer. Harichand & Co. v. Gosho Kabushiki Kaisha (1924) Facts. The buyer refused goods on 5 April 1921. The sellers resold only on 25 May 1921, while the market kept falling. Principle. Undue delay in reselling in a falling market is a failure to mitigate. The sellers got only the market difference on the day after the breach. (1924) 26 Bom LR 921; AIR 1925 Bom 28. Why it matters. It applies the rule to an Indian sale of goods. Prafulla Ranjan Sarkar v. Hindusthan Building Society Ltd. (1959) Facts. A society's Secretary was dismissed with only one month's salary. The court found he was entitled to nine months' notice. Principle. Failure to mitigate is a question of fact, and the burden of proving it is on the defendant. With no evidence from the defendant, he got nine months' salary in full. AIR 1960 Cal 214. Why it matters. It places the burden of proof on the wrongdoer.

selfTest.q: 1. Where is the duty to mitigate found in the Act?
selfTest.a: In the Explanation to Section 73.

selfTest.q: 2. Sita could buy rice on the due date at ₹2,300 a bag, but waited and paid ₹2,600. The contract price was ₹2,000 for 100 bags. How much does Ravi pay?
selfTest.a: ₹30,000, that is (₹2,300 − ₹2,000) × 100. The extra ₹30,000 was avoidable.

selfTest.q: 3. Can the wrongdoer sue the injured party for failing to mitigate?
selfTest.a: No. Failure to mitigate only reduces the damages by the avoidable part.

selfTest.q: 4. What happens to a gain made while mitigating?
selfTest.a: It is set off against the damages ( British Westinghouse ).

selfTest.q: 5. Who must prove that the injured party failed to mitigate?
selfTest.a: The wrongdoer (defendant) ( Prafulla Ranjan Sarkar ).

సెక్షన్ 73 ఉల్లంఘన వల్ల సహజంగా వచ్చే నష్టానికీ, జరగవచ్చని ఇరుపక్షాలకూ తెలిసిన నష్టానికీ పరిహారం ఇస్తుంది. దూరపు నష్టానికి ఇవ్వదు. Explanation ఇలా చెబుతుంది: నష్టాన్ని తగ్గించడానికి నష్టపోయిన పక్షం ఏమి చేయగలిగేవాడో లెక్కలోకి తీసుకోండి. Illustration (a) నష్టాన్ని కొనుగోలుదారు బయట కొనుక్కోగలిగిన ధరతో కొలుస్తుంది. అంటే అతను బయట కొనుక్కుంటాడని ఆశిస్తుంది. Illustration (b) మరో వైపు చూపిస్తుంది: నష్టాన్ని తగ్గించుకోవడానికి పడిన సహేతుకమైన శ్రమ, ఖర్చు ఉల్లంఘించినవాడే చెల్లిస్తాడు. Illustrations (c), (d), (g), (h) కూడా నష్టాన్ని మార్కెట్ ధరతో కొలుస్తాయి. నష్టపోయిన పక్షం బయట ఏమి పొందగలిగేవాడో అది చూపిస్తుంది.

Moolla Dawood, Sons & Co. selfTest.q: 1. నష్టం తగ్గించుకునే బాధ్యత చట్టంలో ఎక్కడ ఉంది?
selfTest.a: సెక్షన్ 73 కి ఉన్న Explanation లో.

selfTest.q: 2. డెలివరీ తేదీన సీత బస్తా ₹2,300 కు బియ్యం కొనగలిగేది, కానీ ఆగి ₹2,600 చెల్లించింది. 100 బస్తాలకు కాంట్రాక్టు ధర ₹2,000. రవి ఎంత చెల్లిస్తాడు?
3. నష్టం తగ్గించుకోనందుకు ఉల్లంఘించినవాడు నష్టపోయిన పక్షం మీద దావా వేయగలడా?
selfTest.a: లేదు. నష్టం తగ్గించుకోకపోతే, తప్పించుకోగలిగిన భాగం మేరకు నష్టపరిహారం తగ్గుతుంది, అంతే.

selfTest.q: 4. నష్ట నివారణలో వచ్చిన లాభం ఏమవుతుంది?
selfTest.a: నష్టపరిహారం నుంచి మినహాయించబడుతుంది ( British Westinghouse ).

selfTest.q: 5. నష్టపోయిన పక్షం నష్టం తగ్గించుకోలేదని ఎవరు నిరూపించాలి?
selfTest.a: ఉల్లంఘించినవాడు (ప్రతివాది) ( Prafulla Ranjan Sarkar ).

Section 70 gives a remedy when a lawful act is done for another person, provided:

Explanation. Section 70 requires the act to be non-gratuitous and the other person to have knowingly enjoyed its benefit.

In illustration (b) to Section 70, A saves B's property from fire. A is entitled to compensation:

Explanation. If circumstances show A intended to act gratuitously, no compensation is due, regardless of the benefit B received.

In State of West Bengal v. B.K. Mondal & Sons, the Supreme Court held that Section 70 applies:

Explanation. The Court held Section 70 does not require any contract at all — it applies precisely where no valid contract exists but a benefit was accepted.

en.meaning:
Under Section 71, a person who finds goods and takes them into custody has:

Explanation. Section 71 treats the finder as a bailee, subject to the full bailment framework of the Act.

Under Section 168, a finder's right to sue for a reward exists only if:

Explanation. The finder can sue for a reward only if the owner had publicly offered one; otherwise there is only a right of lien for expenses.

Under Section 169, a finder may sell a thing commonly sold only when:

Explanation. Section 169 applies to a thing commonly sold and needs both sets of conditions: the owner cannot be found or refuses to pay the charges, and the thing is in danger of perishing or losing most of its value, or the charges are two-thirds of its value.

In Bridges v. Hawkesworth, the court held that the finder of banknotes lying loose in a shop was entitled to them because:

en.meaning:
Under Section 72, money paid or goods delivered by mistake or under coercion:

Explanation. Section 72 requires repayment or return. The recipient's good faith is not the test.

In illustration (a) to Section 72, B pays a jointly-owed debt a second time because he did not know A had already paid. C must:

Explanation. Since B paid under a genuine mistake of fact, C is bound to refund the duplicate payment to B.

In Sales Tax Officer, Banaras v. Kanhaiya Lal Mukundlal Saraf, the Supreme Court held that "mistake" under Section 72 covers:

Explanation. The Court followed the Privy Council in Shiba Prasad Singh: "mistake" in Section 72 covers a mistake of law as well as a mistake of fact.

en.meaning:
"Quantum meruit" literally means:

Explanation. Quantum meruit means "as much as he has earned" — a claim for the reasonable value of work or goods actually provided.

A quantum meruit claim can arise when an agreement is discovered to be void, under:

Explanation. Section 65 requires restoration of, or compensation for, any advantage received under an agreement later discovered to be void.

In Craven-Ellis v. Canons Ltd., the court awarded quantum meruit even though:

Explanation. The persons who made the agreement had no authority to bind the company, so the agreement was void. The Court of Appeal still allowed the managing director a reasonable sum for the services he had rendered.

Quantum meruit is available to an innocent party when the other party's breach prevents completion of the contract because:

The statutory basis for the duty to mitigate is found in:

Explanation. The Explanation to Section 73 requires that means of remedying inconvenience be taken into account when estimating loss.

Loss that the injured party could have avoided through reasonable steps is:

Explanation. Avoidable loss is excluded from the damages calculation once a reasonable alternative existed.

The standard expected of an injured party in mitigating loss is:

Explanation. The injured party must take only reasonable steps — not unusual, risky, or financially dangerous ones.

Part A — Short Answer Quasi Contract. (Tested twice — March/April 2017 and March/April 2018) Quasi Contract Unjust Enrichment. Quasi Contract Quantum Meruit. (Tested twice — March/April 2017 and March/April 2018) Quantum Meruit Remote Damages. Kinds of Damages Explain the duty to mitigate damages. Duty to Mitigate Part B — Long Answer Define the term contingent contract. Discuss the rules relating to contingent contracts. Contingent Contracts Discuss the rule laid down in Hadley v. Baxendale. Kinds of Damages What is meant by a quasi-contract and the circumstances under which quasi-contractual obligations arise? Quasi Contract Explain the concept of damages and the rules for assessment of damages for breach of contract. Kinds of Damages Duty to Mitigate Part C — Problem / Case-Study Questions X finds B's purse and gives it to him. B promises to give X ₹5,000. Explain whether X will succeed in recovering the amount. (Turns on Section 168's reward rule together with the Section 25(2) exception for a promise to compensate a voluntary act already done) Rights of finder of lost goods Consideration - salient features A and B jointly owe ₹200 to C. A pays the amount to C. B, not knowing this fact, pays ₹100 over again to C. Discuss the rights of A and B as against C. Things Delivered by Mistake or Coercion A minor is supplied with necessaries of life by a grocer. He makes out a promissory note in favour of the grocer. Is the grocer entitled to claim payment under the promissory note? (The note itself is void since a minor cannot bind himself personally — the real question is what the grocer can recover under Section 68) Necessaries supplied to a person who is incapable of entering into a contract A agreed to erect a plant for B by 31st January. The contract provided that B should pay ₹500 per month for every month A took beyond the agreed date. A was late by six months. B sued A for ₹6,500, the actual loss caused to him as a result of the delay. To what damages, if any, is B entitled? (Applies the Section 74 principle in Fateh Chand v. Balkishan Dass — the named sum caps recovery even when actual proven loss is higher) Kinds of Damages Questions are drawn from previous Osmania University LL.B. examination papers for study and revision purposes only.

law-of-contract-i-u5-t2.subtitle: Sections 5 to 8 of the Specific Relief Act, 1963

en.inOneMinute: If someone throws you out of your land, the law gives you two doors. One asks you to prove that you own it (Section 5). The other asks only whether you were in possession and were removed without due process of law (Section 6). Sections 7 and 8 do the same work for goods. No one may force a person out of his property by self-help, not even the true owner. A person in settled possession can be removed only through a court. In exams, the six-month possessory suit under Section 6 is asked most often. In real life, it protects tenants, shopkeepers and farmers from being put on the street overnight.
legalProvision: Section 5. Recovery of specific immovable property. A person entitled to the possession of specific immovable property may recover it in the manner provided by the Code of Civil Procedure, 1908 (5 of 1908).

Section 6. Suit by person dispossessed of immovable property. (1) If any person is dispossessed without his consent of immovable property otherwise than in due course of law, he or any person through whom he has been in possession or any person claiming through him may, by suit, recover possession thereof, notwithstanding any other title that may be set up in such suit. (2) No suit under this section shall be brought— (a) after the expiry of six months from the date of dispossession; or (b) against the Government. (3) No appeal shall lie from any order or decree passed in any suit instituted under this section, nor shall any review of any such order or decree be allowed. (4) Nothing in this section shall bar any person from suing to establish his title to such property and to recover possession thereof.
(The words "through whom he has been in possession or any person" were inserted in sub-section (1) by Act 18 of 2018, with effect from 1 October 2018.)

Section 7. Recovery of specific movable property. A person entitled to the possession of specific movable property may recover it in the manner provided by the Code of Civil Procedure, 1908 (5 of 1908). Explanation 1. —A trustee may sue under this section for the possession of movable property to the beneficial interest in which the person for whom he is trustee is entitled. Explanation 2. —A special or temporary right to the present possession of movable property is sufficient to support a suit under this section.

Section 8. Liability of person in possession, not as owner, to deliver to persons entitled to immediate possession. Any person having the possession or control of a particular article of movable property, of which he is not the owner, may be compelled specifically to deliver it to the person entitled to its immediate possession, in any of the following cases:— (a) when the thing claimed is held by the defendant as the agent or trustee of the plaintiff; (b) when compensation in money would not afford the plaintiff adequate relief for the loss of the thing claimed; (c) when it would be extremely difficult to ascertain the actual damage caused by its loss; (d) when the possession of the thing claimed has been wrongfully transferred from the plaintiff. Explanation. —Unless and until the contrary is proved, the court shall, in respect of any article of movable property claimed under clause (b) or clause (c) of this section, presume— (a) that compensation in money would not afford the plaintiff adequate relief for the loss of the thing claimed, or, as the case may be; (b) that it would be extremely difficult to ascertain the actual damage caused by its loss.
Related provisions (Limitation Act, 1963, Schedule)

Article 64. For possession of immovable property based on previous possession and not on title, when the plaintiff while in possession of the property has been dispossessed. – Twelve years. – The date of dispossession.
Article 65. For possession of immovable property or any interest therein based on title. – Twelve years. – When the possession of the defendant becomes adverse to the plaintiff.
In simple words

Section 5: a person entitled to possess particular land or a building may sue for it in the ordinary way under the Code of Civil Procedure. Section 6: a person put out of land or a building without his consent and without due process of law may sue to get it back. The defendant cannot defend by saying he owns it. The suit must be filed within six months and cannot be against the Government. There is no appeal or review. Anyone may still file a separate suit on title. Section 7: the same as Section 5, for particular goods. A trustee may sue, and a special or temporary right to present possession is enough. Section 8: a person who holds a particular article but does not own it can be made to hand over that very article, in four cases. In two of them the court presumes that money is not enough. Articles 64 and 65: an ordinary suit on earlier possession, or on title, may be filed within 12 years.
en.meaning:
Possession here means actual control of the property. Settled possession means possession that has continued for some time with the owner's knowledge. The law protects it even against the owner. In Krishna Ram Mahale (1989) the Supreme Court held that such a person "cannot be dispossessed by the owner of the property except by recourse to law", even if he has no right to remain. The question this part of the Act answers. Who is entitled to possession, and how may he get it back? The answer for land is a choice between two suits. A title suit under Section 5 proves ownership and decides it for good. A possessory suit under Section 6 is quick, but it proves only earlier possession and unlawful removal. It does not decide who owns the land. Why the law has this rule. If every owner could retake property by force whenever he believed he was right, disputes would end in violence. The Privy Council's words, approved by the Supreme Court, are: "In India persons are not permitted to take forcible possession; they must obtain such possession as they are entitled to through a Court." Question 2: was the plaintiff in possession and removed without his consent and without due process of law? If no, file a title suit under Section 5 (12 years, Article 65). Question 3: is the suit within six months of dispossession and not against the Government? If no, file a title suit under Section 5, or a suit on earlier possession within 12 years (Article 64), where the defendant may plead title. If all answers are yes, a Section 6 suit lies: title is no defence, there is no appeal or review, and a title suit remains open under Section 6(4).
keyPoints: Section 5 is a title suit under the Code of Civil Procedure (12 years, Article 65). Section 6 is a quick suit on possession. Section 6: six months, not against the Government, no appeal or review, title no defence. Since 2018, a person through whom the dispossessed person was in possession can also sue. Section 6(4) always saves a separate suit on title. After six months, a suit on earlier possession lies within 12 years (Article 64), but the defendant may plead title. Settled possession is protected even against the true owner ( Lallu Yeshwant Singh ; Krishna Ram Mahale ). Section 7: recovery of movables. A trustee may sue, and a special or temporary right to possession is enough. Section 8: four cases where a non-owner must deliver the article, with a presumption for the plaintiff in clauses (b) and (c).

caseLaws.name: Lallu Yeshwant Singh v
caseLaws.facts: Rao Jagdish Singh (1967) Facts. Gairdakhilkar (tenant) cultivators in Gwalior district said the landlord forcibly stopped them from cultivating and had the land cultivated by others. The landlord said their rights had ended because land revenue was not paid. They sued under Section 326 of the Gwalior Qanoon Mal, which is similar to Section 9 of the Specific Relief Act, 1877. Principle. The tenants' rights did not end automatically. Under Section 9 the question of title is irrelevant, and a landlord cannot use force to throw out his tenant. AIR 1968 SC 620 : (1968) 2 SCR 203, decided 29 November 1967 (Sikri and Shah JJ). Why it matters. It is the foundation of the "no self-help" rule now in Section 6. Krishna Ram Mahale v. Shobha Venkat Rao (1989) Facts. The owner of a restaurant in Parel, Bombay had let the plaintiff conduct it under a 1956 agreement. On 15 February 1959 he took possession behind her back, in collusion with others, relying on notices she said she never received. She sued within a few weeks. Principle. A person in settled possession "cannot be dispossessed by the owner of the property except by recourse to law", even if he had no right to remain. The appeal was dismissed with costs, and the Court Receiver was appointed to take possession. (1989) 4 SCC 131 : AIR 1989 SC 2097, decided 9 August 1989. Why it matters. It states the "no self-help" rule in the clearest terms. Nair Service Society Ltd. v. K.C. Alexander (1968) Facts. The plaintiff sued in 1942 for possession of about 131 acres of Government poramboke land in former Travancore, from which he said the Society's men had removed him in October 1939. The suit was filed long after six months and was based on his earlier possession. Principle. In a suit under Section 9 of the 1877 Act the plaintiff need not prove title. After six months the defendant may raise title; the plaintiff may still sue on earlier possession within 12 years. AIR 1968 SC 1165 : (1968) 3 SCR 163 (Hidayatullah, Sikri, Hegde JJ). Why it matters. It explains how Section 6 relates to ordinary suits for possession. Sanjay Kumar Pandey v. Gulbahar Sheikh (2004) Facts. A trial court decreed a suit under Section 6 of the Specific Relief Act, 1963. The defendants filed a revision under Section 115 of the Code of Civil Procedure, and the High Court dismissed the suit. Principle. The unsuccessful party's remedy "is to file a suit based on title". A revision is available "only by way of an exception". The Supreme Court set aside the High Court's order and sent the revision back for a fresh hearing. (2004) 4 SCC 664 : AIR 2004 SC 3354, decided 2 April 2004. Why it matters. It shows how Section 6(3) and Section 6(4) work in practice.

selfTest.q: 1. Within what time must a Section 6 suit be filed?
selfTest.a: Within six months from the date of dispossession.

selfTest.q: 2. Can the defendant in a Section 6 suit plead that he is the owner?
selfTest.a: No. Section 6(1) says the suit lies notwithstanding any other title that may be set up.

selfTest.q: 3. Does an appeal lie from a decree in a Section 6 suit?
selfTest.a: No. Section 6(3) bars appeal and review. A suit on title remains open under Section 6(4).

selfTest.q: 4. A person dispossessed eight months ago has no title deed. Can he still sue?
selfTest.a: Yes. He may sue on his earlier possession within 12 years (Article 64). If the defendant proves a better title, he fails.

selfTest.q: 5. A hirer of a tractor loses it to a stranger. Can he sue under Section 7?
selfTest.a: Yes. Explanation 2 says a special or temporary right to present possession is enough.

సెక్షన్ 5: ఒక నిర్దిష్ట భూమిని లేదా భవనాన్ని స్వాధీనం చేసుకునే హక్కు ఉన్న వ్యక్తి, సివిల్ ప్రొసీజర్ కోడ్ కింద సాధారణ పద్ధతిలో దాని కోసం దావా వేయవచ్చు. సెక్షన్ 6: తన సమ్మతి లేకుండా, చట్ట ప్రక్రియ లేకుండా భూమి లేదా భవనం నుంచి బయటకు గెంటబడిన వ్యక్తి దాన్ని తిరిగి పొందడానికి దావా వేయవచ్చు. తానే యజమాని అని చెప్పి ప్రతివాది తప్పించుకోలేడు. దావా ఆరు నెలల్లో వేయాలి, ప్రభుత్వంపై వేయలేం. అప్పీల్ గానీ, రివ్యూ గానీ ఉండదు. ఎవరైనా టైటిల్‌పై వేరే దావా వేయవచ్చు. సెక్షన్ 7: నిర్దిష్ట వస్తువుల కోసం సెక్షన్ 5 లాంటిదే. ట్రస్టీ దావా వేయవచ్చు; ప్రస్తుత స్వాధీనానికి ప్రత్యేక లేదా తాత్కాలిక హక్కు ఉన్నా చాలు. సెక్షన్ 8: ఒక నిర్దిష్ట వస్తువును యజమాని కాకుండా తన దగ్గర ఉంచుకున్న వ్యక్తిని, నాలుగు సందర్భాల్లో, అదే వస్తువును అప్పగించేలా చేయవచ్చు. వాటిలో రెండింటిలో డబ్బు సరిపోదని కోర్టు ఊహిస్తుంది. ఆర్టికల్స్ 64, 65: పూర్వ స్వాధీనంపై లేదా టైటిల్‌పై సాధారణ దావాను 12 సంవత్సరాల్లో వేయవచ్చు.
te.meaning:
ఇక్కడ స్వాధీనం (possession) అంటే ఆస్తిపై వాస్తవ నియంత్రణ. స్థిరపడిన స్వాధీనం అంటే యజమానికి తెలిసి కొంతకాలం కొనసాగిన స్వాధీనం. యజమానికి వ్యతిరేకంగా కూడా చట్టం దాన్ని కాపాడుతుంది. Krishna Ram Mahale (1989) లో, అలాంటి వ్యక్తి "cannot be dispossessed by the owner of the property except by recourse to law" అని, అతనికి అక్కడ ఉండే హక్కు లేకపోయినా ఇదే నియమమని సుప్రీంకోర్టు చెప్పింది. చట్టంలోని ఈ భాగం సమాధానం చెప్పే ప్రశ్న. స్వాధీనానికి ఎవరు అర్హులు, దాన్ని ఎలా తిరిగి పొందవచ్చు? భూమికి సమాధానం రెండు దావాల మధ్య ఎంపిక. సెక్షన్ 5 కింది టైటిల్ దావా యాజమాన్యాన్ని రుజువు చేసి శాశ్వతంగా తేలుస్తుంది. సెక్షన్ 6 కింది స్వాధీన దావా త్వరితమైనది, కానీ అది పూర్వ స్వాధీనం, చట్టవిరుద్ధ తొలగింపులను మాత్రమే రుజువు చేస్తుంది. భూమి ఎవరిదో అది తేల్చదు. చట్టంలో ఈ నియమం ఎందుకు ఉంది. తాను సరైనవాడినని నమ్మిన ప్రతిసారీ ప్రతి యజమాని బలవంతంగా ఆస్తిని తిరిగి తీసుకోగలిగితే, వివాదాలు హింసలో ముగుస్తాయి. సుప్రీంకోర్టు ఆమోదించిన Privy Council మాటలు: "In India persons are not permitted to take forcible possession; they must obtain such possession as they are entitled to through a Court." ఏ దావా ఎంచుకోవాలో Diagram 1 లో చూడండి. Diagram 1. పై నుంచి ప్రతి ప్రశ్నకు సమాధానం ఇవ్వండి. "కాదు" అయితే పక్కన ఉన్న పెట్టెకు వెళ్లండి. flowchart TD Q1{"1. ఆస్తి స్థిరాస్తా
(భూమి లేదా భవనం)?"} Q1 -->|"కాదు"| M["చరాస్తి:
సె. 7, 8"] Q1 -->|"అవును"| Q2{"2. వాది స్వాధీనంలో ఉండి, సమ్మతి లేకుండా,
చట్ట ప్రక్రియ లేకుండా తొలగించబడ్డాడా?
సె. 6(1)"} Q2 -->|"కాదు"| T["టైటిల్ దావా, సె. 5
12 సంవత్సరాలు (ఆర్టి. 65)"] Q2 -->|"అవును"| Q3{"3. స్వాధీనం కోల్పోయిన ఆరు నెలల్లో,

సె. 6(2)"} Q3 -->|"కాదు"| L["టైటిల్ దావా, సె. 5, లేదా 12 సంవత్సరాల్లో
పూర్వ స్వాధీనంపై దావా (ఆర్టి. 64);
ప్రతివాది టైటిల్ వాదించవచ్చు"] Q3 -->|"అవును"| S["సె. 6 దావా నిలుస్తుంది: టైటిల్ రక్షణ కాదు;
అప్పీల్, రివ్యూ లేవు (సె. 6(3));
టైటిల్ దావా తెరిచే ఉంది (సె. 6(4))"] వచన వివరణ ప్రశ్న 1: ఆస్తి స్థిరాస్తా? కాకపోతే, చరాస్తికి సెక్షన్లు 7, 8 వాడండి. ప్రశ్న 2: వాది స్వాధీనంలో ఉండి, తన సమ్మతి లేకుండా, చట్ట ప్రక్రియ లేకుండా తొలగించబడ్డాడా? కాకపోతే, సెక్షన్ 5 కింద టైటిల్ దావా (12 సంవత్సరాలు, ఆర్టికల్ 65). ప్రశ్న 3: స్వాధీనం కోల్పోయిన ఆరు నెలల్లో, ప్రభుత్వంపై కాకుండా దావా వేస్తున్నారా? కాకపోతే, సెక్షన్ 5 కింద టైటిల్ దావా, లేదా 12 సంవత్సరాల్లో పూర్వ స్వాధీనంపై దావా (ఆర్టికల్ 64); అందులో ప్రతివాది టైటిల్ వాదించవచ్చు. అన్నీ అవును అయితే, సెక్షన్ 6 దావా నిలుస్తుంది: టైటిల్ రక్షణ కాదు, అప్పీల్ లేదా రివ్యూ లేదు, సెక్షన్ 6(4) కింద టైటిల్ దావా తెరిచే ఉంటుంది.

selfTest.q: 1. సెక్షన్ 6 దావాను ఎంత కాలంలో వేయాలి?
selfTest.a: స్వాధీనం కోల్పోయిన తేదీ నుంచి ఆరు నెలల్లో.

selfTest.q: 2. సెక్షన్ 6 దావాలో ప్రతివాది తానే యజమానినని వాదించవచ్చా?
selfTest.a: లేదు. మరే టైటిల్ వాదించినా దావా నిలుస్తుందని సెక్షన్ 6(1) చెబుతుంది.

selfTest.q: 3. సెక్షన్ 6 దావాలోని డిక్రీపై అప్పీల్ ఉంటుందా?
selfTest.a: లేదు. సెక్షన్ 6(3) అప్పీల్, రివ్యూలను నిషేధిస్తుంది. సెక్షన్ 6(4) కింద టైటిల్ దావా తెరిచే ఉంటుంది.

selfTest.q: 4. ఎనిమిది నెలల క్రితం స్వాధీనం కోల్పోయిన వ్యక్తికి టైటిల్ పత్రం లేదు. అతను ఇంకా దావా వేయగలడా?
selfTest.a: అవును. 12 సంవత్సరాల్లో తన పూర్వ స్వాధీనంపై దావా వేయవచ్చు (ఆర్టికల్ 64). ప్రతివాది మెరుగైన టైటిల్ రుజువు చేస్తే, అతను ఓడిపోతాడు.

selfTest.q: 5. ట్రాక్టర్ అద్దెకు తీసుకున్న వ్యక్తి దాన్ని ఒక అపరిచితుడి వల్ల కోల్పోతాడు. అతను సెక్షన్ 7 కింద దావా వేయగలడా?
selfTest.a: అవును. ప్రస్తుత స్వాధీనానికి ప్రత్యేక లేదా తాత్కాలిక హక్కు చాలని Explanation 2 చెబుతుంది.

అంశం సెక్షన్ 5: టైటిల్ దావా సెక్షన్ 6: స్వాధీన దావా
ఏమి రుజువు చేయాలి స్వాధీన హక్కు, సాధారణంగా మెరుగైన టైటిల్ పూర్వ స్వాధీనం, సమ్మతి లేకుండా, చట్ట ప్రక్రియ లేకుండా స్వాధీన నష్టం
ప్రతివాది టైటిల్ వాదించవచ్చా? అవును. టైటిలే మొత్తం సమస్య లేదు. సెక్షన్ 6(1) దాన్ని మూసేస్తుంది
గడువు 12 సంవత్సరాలు (Limitation Act, ఆర్టికల్ 65) స్వాధీనం కోల్పోయిన నాటి నుంచి ఆరు నెలలు
ప్రభుత్వంపై వేయవచ్చు సెక్షన్ 6(2)(b) నిషేధిస్తుంది
అప్పీల్ లేదా రివ్యూ సాధారణ పద్ధతిలో ఉంది సెక్షన్ 6(3) నిషేధిస్తుంది; రివిజన్ మినహాయింపుగా మాత్రమే
టైటిల్‌పై ప్రభావం టైటిల్‌ను తేలుస్తుంది టైటిల్‌ను తేల్చదు. సెక్షన్ 6(4) టైటిల్ దావాను కాపాడుతుంది

అంశం నియమం ఆధారం
భూమి, టైటిల్‌పై కోడ్ కింద దావా; 12 సంవత్సరాలు సెక్షన్ 5; ఆర్టికల్ 65
భూమి, స్వాధీనంపై త్వరిత దావా; టైటిల్ రక్షణ కాదు సెక్షన్ 6(1)
సెక్షన్ 6 పరిమితులు ఆరు నెలలు; ప్రభుత్వంపై కాదు; అప్పీల్, రివ్యూ లేవు సెక్షన్ 6(2), (3)
సెక్షన్ 6 తర్వాత టైటిల్ దావా ఎప్పుడూ తెరిచే ఉంటుంది సెక్షన్ 6(4)
పూర్వ స్వాధీనం, ఆరు నెలల తర్వాత 12 సంవత్సరాల్లో సాధారణ దావా; ప్రతివాది టైటిల్ వాదించవచ్చు ఆర్టికల్ 64; Nair Service Society
సొంత బలం వాడకూడదు స్థిరపడిన స్వాధీనాన్ని చట్టం ద్వారా మాత్రమే తొలగించాలి Lallu Yeshwant Singh; Krishna Ram Mahale
వస్తువులు కోడ్ కింద దావా; ట్రస్టీ లేదా తాత్కాలిక హక్కు చాలు సెక్షన్ 7
యజమాని కాని వ్యక్తి నుంచి నిర్దిష్ట వస్తువు నాలుగు సందర్భాలు; (b), (c) లో ఊహ సెక్షన్ 8

అంశం సెక్షన్ 6 దావా టైటిల్ దావా
అడిగే ప్రశ్న వాది స్వాధీనంలో ఉన్నాడా, చట్టం లేకుండా తొలగించబడ్డాడా? ఆస్తిపై మెరుగైన హక్కు ఎవరిది?
ఫలితం స్వాధీనం పునరుద్ధరణ యాజమాన్యం, స్వాధీనం తేలుతాయి
అంతిమమా? స్వాధీనం విషయంలో మాత్రమే; తర్వాత టైటిల్ దావా వేయవచ్చు అవును, అప్పీల్‌కు లోబడి

law-of-contract-i-u5-t5.subtitle: Sections 27 to 30 of the Specific Relief Act, 1963

en.inOneMinute: Rescission means undoing a contract. A person who signed a voidable contract, or a contract that is unlawful for a hidden reason, can ask the court to set it aside. The parties are then put back, as far as possible, to where they stood before the contract. Chapter IV of the Specific Relief Act, 1963 (Sections 27 to 30) deals with this. The court "may" rescind and "may" refuse, so the four bars in Section 27(2), Sections 28 and 29 and the duty to do equity matter as much as the grounds. In exams, the grounds in Section 27(1), the bars, the effect on benefits received, and the difference from cancellation and rectification are the main points. In real life, this is how a buyer cheated into a bad deal gets his money back through the court.
legalProvision: Section 27. When rescission may be adjudged or refused. (1) Any person interested in a contract may sue to have it rescinded, and such rescission may be adjudged by the court in any of the following cases, namely:— (a) where the contract is voidable or terminable by the plaintiff; (b) where the contract is unlawful for causes not apparent on its face and the defendant is more to blame than the plaintiff. (2) Notwithstanding anything contained in sub-section (1), the court may refuse to rescind the contract— (a) where the plaintiff has expressly or impliedly ratified the contract; or (b) where, owing to the change of circumstances which has taken place since the making of the contract (not being due to any act of the defendant himself), the parties cannot be substantially restored to the position in which they stood when the contract was made; or (c) where third parties have, during the subsistence of the contract, acquired rights in good faith without notice and for value; or (d) where only a part of the contract is sought to be rescinded and such part is not severable from the rest of the contract. Explanation. —In this section "contract" in relation to the territories to which the Transfer of Property Act, 1882 (4 of 1882), does not extend, means a contract in writing.

Section 28. Rescission in certain circumstances of contracts for the sale or lease of immovable property, the specific performance of which has been decreed. (1) Where in any suit a decree for specific performance of a contract for the sale or lease of immovable property has been made and the purchaser or lessee does not, within the period allowed by the decree or such further period as the court may allow, pay the purchase money or other sum which the court has ordered him to pay, the vendor or lessor may apply in the same suit in which the decree is made, to have the contract rescinded and on such application the court may, by order, rescind the contract either so far as regards the party in default or altogether, as the justice of the case may require. (2) Where a contract is rescinded under sub-section (1), the court— (a) shall direct the purchaser or the lessee, if he has obtained possession of the property under the contract, to restore such possession to the vendor or lessor, and (b) may direct payment to the vendor or lessor of all the rents and profits which have accrued in respect of the property from the date on which possession was so obtained by the purchaser or lessee until restoration of possession to the vendor or lessor, and, if the justice of the case so requires, the refund of any sum paid by the vendee or the lessee as earnest money or deposit in connection with the contract. (3) If the purchase or lessee pays the purchase money or other sum which he is ordered to pay under the decree within the period referred to in sub-section (1), the court may, on application made in the same suit, award the purchaser or lessee such further relief as he may be entitled to, including in appropriate cases all or any of the following reliefs, namely:— (a) the execution of a proper conveyance or lease by the vendor or lessor; (b) the delivery of possession, or partition and separate possession, of the property on the execution of such conveyance or lease. (4) No separate suit in respect of any relief which may be claimed under this section shall lie at the instance of a vendor, purchaser, lessor or lessee, as the case may be. (5) The costs of any proceedings under this section shall be in the discretion of the court.

Section 29. Alternative prayer for rescission in suit for specific performance. A plaintiff instituting a suit for the specific performance of a contract in writing may pray in the alternative that, if the contract cannot be specifically enforced, it may be rescinded and delivered up to be cancelled; and the court, if it refuses to enforce the contract specifically, may direct it to be rescinded and delivered up accordingly.

Section 30. Court may require parties rescinding to do equity. On adjudging the rescission of a contract, the court may require the party to whom such relief is granted to restore, so far as may be, any benefit which he may have received from the other party and to make any compensation to him which justice may require.
Related provisions (Indian Contract Act, 1872)

Section 19 (first paragraph). When consent to an agreement is caused by coercion, fraud or misrepresentation, the agreement is a contract voidable at the option of the party whose consent was so caused.
Section 19A (first paragraph). When consent to an agreement is caused by undue influence, the agreement is a contract voidable at the option of the party whose consent was so caused.

Section 64. When a person at whose option a contract is voidable rescinds it, the other party thereto need not perform any promise therein contained in which he is promisor. The party rescinding a voidable contract shall, if he have received any benefit thereunder from another party to such contract, restore such benefit, so far as may be, to the person from whom it was received.
Section 66. The rescission of a voidable contract may be communicated or revoked in the same manner, and subject to the same rules, as apply to the communication or revocation of a proposal.
In simple words

Section 27(1): any person interested in a contract may sue to have it set aside. The court may order rescission where the contract is voidable or terminable (capable of being ended) by the plaintiff, or where it is unlawful for causes not apparent on its face and the defendant is more to blame than the plaintiff. Section 27(2): the court may refuse rescission in four cases: later approval (ratification), no restoration possible, third-party rights, and a part that cannot be separated. Explanation to Section 27: where the Transfer of Property Act, 1882 does not extend, "contract" means a contract in writing. Section 28: rescission after a decree for specific performance of a sale or lease of immovable property, where the buyer or lessee does not pay. Section 29: a plaintiff in a suit for specific performance of a written contract may pray in the alternative for rescission. Section 30: the court may require the party granted rescission to restore benefits and make compensation as justice requires.
en.meaning:
Rescission is the setting aside of a contract by the court. The Act uses the word for a contract. Its word for undoing a written instrument is cancellation (Sections 31 to 33). When is a contract voidable? A contract is valid until the injured party chooses to cancel it where consent was caused by coercion , fraud or misrepresentation (Section 19, Indian Contract Act, 1872) or by undue influence (Section 19A). The question this part of the Act answers. When will the court set a contract aside, and on what terms? Two ways to rescind. The injured party can tell the other side that he rescinds, communicating it like a proposal (Section 66 of the Contract Act). Or he can ask the court under Section 27. The grounds for rescission by the court (Section 27(1)). The contract is voidable by the plaintiff (Section 27(1)(a)): coercion, fraud or misrepresentation (Contract Act, Section 19), or undue influence (Section 19A). The contract is terminable by the plaintiff (Section 27(1)(a)): he has a right to end it. The contract is unlawful for causes not apparent on its face (Section 27(1)(b)), but only if the defendant is more to blame than the plaintiff. See Diagram 1 for the grounds. Diagram 1. Second, the contract is terminable by the plaintiff (Section 27(1)(a)): he has a right to end it. Third, the contract is unlawful for causes not apparent on its face (Section 27(1)(b)), only if the defendant is more to blame than the plaintiff.
keyPoints: Rescission (Sections 27 to 30) undoes a contract. Cancellation (Sections 31 to 33) undoes an instrument. Grounds: voidable or terminable by the plaintiff; unlawful for causes not apparent on its face if the defendant is more to blame. Any person interested in the contract may sue. The court "may" rescind and "may" refuse (Section 27). Four bars: ratification, no restoration, third-party rights, part not severable. Section 28: rescission in the same suit after a decree for sale or lease if the buyer does not pay. Section 29: rescission as an alternative prayer. The injured party may rescind by communicating it (Contract Act, Sections 64 and 66) or sue under Section 27. The court may require restoration of benefits and compensation (Section 30).

caseLaws.name: Mohori Bibee v
caseLaws.facts: Dharmodas Ghose (1903) Facts. Dharmodas Ghose, a minor, mortgaged his houses to a money-lender, Brahmo Dutt, to secure ₹20,000. The lender's agent knew he was under age. The minor sued to have the mortgage declared void. Principle. A minor's agreement is void, not voidable. Sections 64 and 65 of the Contract Act assume a contract between competent parties and did not apply. Repayment was not ordered, because the lender knew of the minority. Privy Council, (1903) LR 30 IA 114. Why it matters. Rescission needs a contract. The case also shows how a court weighs restoration.

selfTest.q: 1. In which cases may the court adjudge rescission under Section 27(1)?
selfTest.a: Where the contract is voidable or terminable by the plaintiff, or unlawful for causes not apparent on its face and the defendant is more to blame.

selfTest.q: 2. Which sections of the Contract Act let a party rescind a voidable contract without going to court?
selfTest.a: Section 66 (how rescission is communicated) and Section 64 (its consequences).

selfTest.q: 4. In which suit does a seller apply for rescission under Section 28?
selfTest.a: In the same suit in which the decree for specific performance was made.

selfTest.q: 5. What may the court require of a party granted rescission?
selfTest.a: To restore any benefit received from the other party and to make any compensation that justice requires (Section 30).

legalProvision: Section 27. When rescission may be adjudged or refused. (1) Any person interested in a contract may sue to have it rescinded, and such rescission may be adjudged by the court in any of the following cases, namely:— (a) where the contract is voidable or terminable by the plaintiff; (b) where the contract is unlawful for causes not apparent on its face and the defendant is more to blame than the plaintiff. (2) Notwithstanding anything contained in sub-section (1), the court may refuse to rescind the contract— (a) where the plaintiff has expressly or impliedly ratified the contract; or (b) where, owing to the change of circumstances which has taken place since the making of the contract (not being due to any act of the defendant himself), the parties cannot be substantially restored to the position in which they stood when the contract was made; or (c) where third parties have, during the subsistence of the contract, acquired rights in good faith without notice and for value; or (d) where only a part of the contract is sought to be rescinded and such part is not severable from the rest of the contract. Explanation. —In this section "contract" in relation to the territories to which the Transfer of Property Act, 1882 (4 of 1882), does not extend, means a contract in writing.

Section 28. Rescission in certain circumstances of contracts for the sale or lease of immovable property, the specific performance of which has been decreed. (1) Where in any suit a decree for specific performance of a contract for the sale or lease of immovable property has been made and the purchaser or lessee does not, within the period allowed by the decree or such further period as the court may allow, pay the purchase money or other sum which the court has ordered him to pay, the vendor or lessor may apply in the same suit in which the decree is made, to have the contract rescinded and on such application the court may, by order, rescind the contract either so far as regards the party in default or altogether, as the justice of the case may require. (2) Where a contract is rescinded under sub-section (1), the court— (a) shall direct the purchaser or the lessee, if he has obtained possession of the property under the contract, to restore such possession to the vendor or lessor, and (b) may direct payment to the vendor or lessor of all the rents and profits which have accrued in respect of the property from the date on which possession was so obtained by the purchaser or lessee until restoration of possession to the vendor or lessor, and, if the justice of the case so requires, the refund of any sum paid by the vendee or the lessee as earnest money or deposit in connection with the contract. (3) If the purchase or lessee pays the purchase money or other sum which he is ordered to pay under the decree within the period referred to in sub-section (1), the court may, on application made in the same suit, award the purchaser or lessee such further relief as he may be entitled to, including in appropriate cases all or any of the following reliefs, namely:— (a) the execution of a proper conveyance or lease by the vendor or lessor; (b) the delivery of possession, or partition and separate possession, of the property on the execution of such conveyance or lease. (4) No separate suit in respect of any relief which may be claimed under this section shall lie at the instance of a vendor, purchaser, lessor or lessee, as the case may be. (5) The costs of any proceedings under this section shall be in the discretion of the court.

Section 29. Alternative prayer for rescission in suit for specific performance. A plaintiff instituting a suit for the specific performance of a contract in writing may pray in the alternative that, if the contract cannot be specifically enforced, it may be rescinded and delivered up to be cancelled; and the court, if it refuses to enforce the contract specifically, may direct it to be rescinded and delivered up accordingly.

Section 30. Court may require parties rescinding to do equity. On adjudging the rescission of a contract, the court may require the party to whom such relief is granted to restore, so far as may be, any benefit which he may have received from the other party and to make any compensation to him which justice may require.
సంబంధిత నిబంధనలు (Indian Contract Act, 1872)

Section 19 (first paragraph). When consent to an agreement is caused by coercion, fraud or misrepresentation, the agreement is a contract voidable at the option of the party whose consent was so caused.
Section 19A (first paragraph). When consent to an agreement is caused by undue influence, the agreement is a contract voidable at the option of the party whose consent was so caused.

Section 64. When a person at whose option a contract is voidable rescinds it, the other party thereto need not perform any promise therein contained in which he is promisor. The party rescinding a voidable contract shall, if he have received any benefit thereunder from another party to such contract, restore such benefit, so far as may be, to the person from whom it was received.
Section 66. The rescission of a voidable contract may be communicated or revoked in the same manner, and subject to the same rules, as apply to the communication or revocation of a proposal.

సెక్షన్ 27(1): కాంట్రాక్టుపై ఆసక్తి ఉన్న ఏ వ్యక్తైనా దాన్ని పక్కన పెట్టమని దావా వేయవచ్చు. కాంట్రాక్టు వాది ఇష్టం మేరకు రద్దు చేయదగినది లేదా ముగించదగినది (terminable) అయితే, లేదా బయటకు కనిపించని కారణాలతో చట్టవిరుద్ధమై, వాది కంటే ప్రతివాది ఎక్కువ తప్పు చేసి ఉంటే, కోర్టు రద్దుకు ఆదేశించవచ్చు. సెక్షన్ 27(2): నాలుగు సందర్భాల్లో కోర్టు రద్దు నిరాకరించవచ్చు: తర్వాత ఆమోదం (ratification), పూర్వ స్థితికి తీసుకురాలేకపోవడం, మూడో వ్యక్తుల హక్కులు, వేరు చేయలేని భాగం. సెక్షన్ 27 Explanation: Transfer of Property Act, 1882 వర్తించని చోట "contract" అంటే రాతపూర్వక కాంట్రాక్టు. సెక్షన్ 28: స్థిరాస్తి అమ్మకం లేదా లీజుకు నిర్దిష్ట అమలు డిక్రీ తర్వాత, కొనుగోలుదారు లేదా కౌలుదారు చెల్లించకపోతే రద్దు. సెక్షన్ 29: రాతపూర్వక కాంట్రాక్టు నిర్దిష్ట అమలు దావాలో వాది ప్రత్యామ్నాయంగా రద్దు కోరవచ్చు. సెక్షన్ 30: రద్దు పొందిన పక్షం ప్రయోజనాలను తిరిగి ఇవ్వాలని, న్యాయం కోరినంత పరిహారం చెల్లించాలని కోర్టు కోరవచ్చు.
te.meaning:
రద్దు అంటే కోర్టు ఒక కాంట్రాక్టును పక్కన పెట్టడం. చట్టం ఈ పదాన్ని కాంట్రాక్టుకు వాడుతుంది. రాతపూర్వక పత్రాన్ని తొలగించడానికి దాని పదం cancellation (సెక్షన్లు 31 నుంచి 33). కాంట్రాక్టు ఎప్పుడు రద్దు చేయదగినది? సమ్మతి బలవంతం (coercion), మోసం (fraud) లేదా తప్పుడు ప్రాతినిధ్యం (misrepresentation) వల్ల (Indian Contract Act, 1872 సెక్షన్ 19), లేదా అనుచిత ప్రభావం (undue influence) వల్ల (సెక్షన్ 19A) కలిగితే, నష్టపోయిన పక్షం రద్దు చేసుకునే వరకు కాంట్రాక్టు చెల్లుతుంది. ఈ భాగం జవాబు చెప్పే ప్రశ్న. కోర్టు ఎప్పుడు కాంట్రాక్టును పక్కన పెడుతుంది, ఏ షరతులపై? రద్దు చేయడానికి రెండు మార్గాలు. నష్టపోయిన పక్షం, ప్రతిపాదనను తెలియజేసినట్లే, తాను రద్దు చేస్తున్నానని అవతలి పక్షానికి తెలియజేయవచ్చు (Contract Act సెక్షన్ 66). లేదా సెక్షన్ 27 కింద కోర్టును అడగవచ్చు. కోర్టు రద్దు చేసే కారణాలు (సెక్షన్ 27(1)). కాంట్రాక్టు వాది ఇష్టం మేరకు రద్దు చేయదగినది (సెక్షన్ 27(1)(a)): బలవంతం, మోసం లేదా తప్పుడు ప్రాతినిధ్యం (Contract Act, సెక్షన్ 19), లేదా అనుచిత ప్రభావం (సెక్షన్ 19A). కాంట్రాక్టు వాది ముగించదగినది (సెక్షన్ 27(1)(a)): దాన్ని ముగించే హక్కు అతనికి ఉంది. కాంట్రాక్టు బయటకు కనిపించని కారణాలతో చట్టవిరుద్ధం (సెక్షన్ 27(1)(b)), కానీ ప్రతివాది వాది కంటే ఎక్కువ తప్పు చేసి ఉంటేనే. కారణాల కోసం Diagram 1 చూడండి. selfTest.q: 1. సెక్షన్ 27(1) కింద కోర్టు ఏ సందర్భాల్లో రద్దుకు ఆదేశించవచ్చు?
selfTest.a: కాంట్రాక్టు వాది రద్దు చేయదగినది లేదా ముగించదగినది అయినప్పుడు, లేదా బయటకు కనిపించని కారణాలతో చట్టవిరుద్ధమై ప్రతివాది ఎక్కువ తప్పు చేసినప్పుడు.

selfTest.q: 2. కోర్టుకు వెళ్లకుండా రద్దు చేయదగిన కాంట్రాక్టును రద్దు చేయడానికి Contract Act లోని ఏ సెక్షన్లు అనుమతిస్తాయి?
selfTest.a: సెక్షన్ 66 (రద్దును ఎలా తెలియజేయాలి), సెక్షన్ 64 (దాని పరిణామాలు).

selfTest.q: 4. సెక్షన్ 28 కింద అమ్మకందారు ఏ దావాలో రద్దుకు దరఖాస్తు చేస్తాడు?

law-of-contract-i-u5-t4.subtitle: Section 26 of the Specific Relief Act, 1963

en.inOneMinute: Sometimes two people truly agree on a deal, but the paper they sign says something else: a wrong figure, a missing clause, a misdescribed boundary. Rectification fixes the paper, not the deal. Section 26 allows it where fraud or a mutual mistake made the document fail to state the parties' real intention. The remedy is narrow and the court may refuse it. In exams, the grounds, the three routes and the contrast with rescission earn the marks. In real life, it saves a good bargain from a clerk's error.
legalProvision: Section 26. When instrument may be rectified. (1) When, through fraud or a mutual mistake of the parties, a contract or other instrument in writing [not being the articles of association of a company to which the Companies Act, 1956 (1 of 1956), applies] does not express their real intention, then— (a) either party or his representative in interest may institute a suit to have the instrument rectified; or (b) the plaintiff may, in any suit in which any right arising under the instrument is in issue, claim in his pleading that the instrument be rectified; or (c) a defendant in any such suit as is referred to in clause (b), may, in addition to any other defence open to him, ask for rectification of the instrument. (2) If, in any suit in which a contract or other instrument is sought to be rectified under sub-section (1), the court finds that the instrument, through fraud or mistake, does not express the real intention of the parties, the court may, in its discretion, direct rectification of the instrument so as to express that intention, so far as this can be done without prejudice to rights acquired by third persons in good faith and for value. (3) A contract in writing may first be rectified, and then if the party claiming rectification has so prayed in his pleading and the court thinks fit, may be specifically enforced. (4) No relief for the rectification of an instrument shall be granted to any party under this section unless it has been specifically claimed: Provided that where a party has not claimed any such relief in his pleading, the court shall, at any stage of the proceeding, allow him to amend the pleading on such terms as may be just for including such claim.
Related provisions (Indian Contract Act, 1872)

Section 20. Agreement void where both parties are under mistake as to matter of fact. Where both the parties to an agreement are under a mistake as to a matter of fact essential to the agreement, the agreement is void. Explanation. —An erroneous opinion as to the value of the thing which forms the subject-matter of the agreement, is not to be deemed a mistake as to a matter of fact.

Section 21. Effect of mistakes as to law. A contract is not voidable because it was caused by a mistake as to any law in force in India; but a mistake as to a law not in force in India has the same effect as a mistake of fact.

Section 22. Contract caused by mistake of one party as to matter of fact. A contract is not voidable merely because it was caused by one of the parties to it being under a mistake as to a matter of fact.
In simple words

Section 26(1): when fraud or a mutual mistake makes a written contract or other instrument fail to state the parties' real intention, either party or his representative in interest may sue to have it corrected. The same relief may be claimed in a pending suit, or asked for by a defendant. A company's articles of association are left out. Section 26(2): the court may, in its discretion , correct the instrument to state the real intention, so far as this does not harm rights that third persons acquired in good faith and for value. Section 26(3): a written contract may first be corrected and then, if this was prayed for and the court thinks fit, specifically enforced. Section 26(4): no relief unless it is specifically claimed, but the court shall allow an amendment of the pleading at any stage on just terms. Contract Act Sections 20 to 22: these deal with mistake in the agreement itself, not in the writing.
en.meaning:
Rectification means the court corrects the wording of a written instrument. An instrument is any document that records rights or duties, such as a sale agreement, a deed or a lease. The court does not make a new bargain. It records the bargain that was truly made. The question this section answers. When may a court correct a signed document so that it says what the parties really agreed? Why the law has this rule. The law normally treats a signed document as the final record of the deal. But if both sides agreed on one thing and the paper says another, holding them to the paper would enforce a bargain neither of them made. Rectification is a narrow exception that brings the paper back in line with the real agreement. The court asks four questions in order. Did the parties reach a concluded agreement with a real, shared intention (Section 26(1))? If not, there is nothing to rectify; the question is one of mistake or no contract. Does the writing fail to express that intention (Section 26(1))? If not, the document stands as written. Is the cause fraud or a mutual mistake, and not a one-sided mistake (Section 26(1))? If not, Section 26 does not apply. Can the correction be made without harming a third person who acquired rights in good faith and for value (Section 26(2))? If not, the court cannot rectify against that person. If all the answers are yes, the court may, in its discretion, rectify the instrument. A contract so rectified can then be specifically enforced (Section 26(3)). See Diagram 1 . Diagram 1. Go down the boxes in order. If no, there is nothing to rectify; it is a question of mistake or no contract. Question 2: does the writing fail to express that intention? If no, the document stands as written. Question 3: is the cause fraud or a mutual mistake, not a one-sided mistake? If no, Section 26 does not apply. Question 4: can it be rectified without harming a third person who acquired rights in good faith and for value? If no, the court cannot rectify against that person. If all answers are yes, the court may, in its discretion, rectify, and a contract so rectified can then be specifically enforced under Section 26(3).
keyPoints: Section 26 corrects the document, not the deal. Grounds: fraud or a mutual mistake. A one-sided mistake is not enough. Three routes: separate suit, claim in a suit, defendant's request. The court has a discretion. It cannot prejudice third persons who acted in good faith and for value. A contract can be rectified and then specifically enforced in the same suit (Section 26(3)). Rectification must be specifically claimed, but the court shall allow an amendment (Section 26(4)). Rectification records the bargain made. It does not substitute a different bargain ( Venkatesha , 2026).

caseLaws.name: Venkatesha v
caseLaws.facts: K.M. Venkatamuniyappa (2026) Facts. A 1971 sale deed conveyed land in Sy. No. 1/4. A rectification deed of 1997, made only between a later buyer and his own vendor, tried to change the survey number to Sy. No. 162. The original owner was not a party. Principle. Section 26 is "a limited equitable jurisdiction ". "Rectification, therefore, rectifies the expression of a concluded bargain; it does not substitute one bargain for another." The appeal was allowed and the dismissal of the suit restored. 2026 INSC 705, decided 14 July 2026 (Dipankar Datta and Vipul M. Pancholi JJ). Why it matters. It is a recent Supreme Court statement of what Section 26 can and cannot do. Raffles v. Wichelhaus (1864) Facts. A contract for 125 bales of Surat cotton "to arrive ex Peerless" from Bombay. Two ships called Peerless sailed, one in October and one in December. Principle. Each side meant a different ship. On demurrer, the plea was held a good answer. Where the parties never agreed on the same thing, the problem is mistake, not wrong wording. (1864) 2 H & C 906. Why it matters. It marks the line between a mistake in recording an agreement (Section 26) and no agreement at all.

selfTest.q: 1. On what two grounds may an instrument be rectified?
selfTest.a: Fraud or a mutual mistake of the parties.

selfTest.q: 2. Whose rights does Section 26(2) protect?
selfTest.a: Third persons who acquired rights in good faith and for value.

selfTest.q: 3. Can a rectified contract be specifically enforced?
selfTest.a: Yes. Section 26(3) allows a contract to be rectified and then enforced, if the party prayed for it and the court thinks fit.

selfTest.q: 4. A defendant finds a typing error in the agreement he is sued on. Must he file a separate suit?
selfTest.a: No. As a defendant he may ask for rectification in addition to any other defence (Section 26(1)(c)).

selfTest.q: 5. Can a company's articles of association be rectified under Section 26?
selfTest.a: No. Section 26(1) leaves them out.
