family-law-i-u1-t4.subtitle: Birthright and fluctuating shares in the Mitakshara against defined shares in the Dayabhaga

en.inOneMinute: The Mitakshara and the Dayabhaga are the two schools of Hindu law. They differ most on how a family holds property. Under the Mitakshara, a son gets an interest in ancestral property at birth. No one has a fixed share until partition, and on a death the interest passes to the others by survivorship . Under the Dayabhaga, a son gets nothing by birth. A coparcenary begins only on the father's death, each coparcener holds a defined share, and that share passes to his own heirs. They also differ on the basis of inheritance: nearness of blood in the Mitakshara, spiritual benefit in the Dayabhaga. The Hindu Succession Act, 1956 changed the Mitakshara side. Since 2005, Section 6 makes a daughter a coparcener by birth, replaces survivorship with succession, and ends the sons' pious obligation for new debts. Exams ask for the points of difference, the incidents of a Mitakshara coparcenary ( Ghamandi Ram ), and how Section 6 changed the law ( Gurupad , Vineeta Sharma ).
legalProvision: Section 6, Hindu Succession Act, 1956 (as substituted in 2005). Devolution of interest in coparcenary property. (1) On and from the commencement of the Hindu Succession (Amendment) Act, 2005 (39 of 2005), in a Joint Hindu family governed by the Mitakshara law, the daughter of a coparcener shall,― (a) by birth become a coparcener in her own right the same manner as the son; (b) have the same rights in the coparcenery property as she would have had if she had been a son; (c) be subject to the same liabilities in respect of the said coparcenery property as that of a son, and any reference to a Hindu Mitakshara coparcener shall be deemed to include a reference to a daughter of a coparcener: Provided that nothing contained in this sub-section shall affect or invalidate any disposition or alienation including any partition or testamentary disposition of property which had taken place before the 20th day of December, 2004. ... (3) Where a Hindu dies after the commencement of the Hindu Succession (Amendment) Act, 2005 (39 of 2005), his interest in the property of a Joint Hindu family governed by the Mitakshara law, shall devolve by testamentary or intestate succession, as the case may be, under this Act and not by survivorship, and the coparcenery property shall be deemed to have been divided as if a partition had taken place and,― (a) the daughter is allotted the same share as is allotted to a son; ... Explanation. ―For the purposes of this sub-section, the interest of a Hindu Mitakshara coparcener shall be deemed to be the share in the property that would have been allotted to him if a partition of the property had taken place immediately before his death, irrespective of whether he was entitled to claim partition or not. (4) After the commencement of the Hindu Succession (Amendment) Act, 2005 (39 of 2005), no court shall recognise any right to proceed against a son, grandson or great-grandson for the recovery of any debt due from his father, grandfather or great-grandfather solely on the ground of the pious obligation under the Hindu law, of such son, grandson or great-grandson to discharge any such debt: [proviso saves debts contracted before the 2005 Act] (5) Nothing contained in this section shall apply to a partition, which has been effected before the 20th day of December, 2004. Explanation. ―For the purposes of this section "partition" means any partition made by execution of a deed of partition duly registered under the Registration Act, 1908 (16 of 1908) or partition effected by a decree of a court.

Explanation to Section 30, Hindu Succession Act, 1956. The interest of a male Hindu in a Mitakshara coparcenary property or the interest of a member of a tarwad, tavazhi, illom, kutumba or kavaru in the property of the tarwad, tavazhi, illom, kutumba or kavaru shall, notwithstanding anything contained in this Act or in any other law for the time being in force, be deemed to be property capable of being disposed of by him or by her within the meaning of this section.

Section 6, Hindu Succession Act, 1956 (as originally enacted, quoted in Gurupad ). When a male Hindu dies after the commencement of this Act, having at the time of his death an interest in a Mitakshara coparcenary property, his interest in the property shall devolve by survivorship upon the surviving members of the coparcenary and not in accordance with this Act: Provided that, if the deceased had left him surviving a female relative specified in class I of the Schedule or a male relative specified in that class who claims through such a female relative, the interest of the deceased in the Mitakshara coparcenary property shall devolve by testamentary or intestate succession, as the case may be, under this Act and not by survivorship. Explanation 1. —For the purposes of this section, the interest of a Hindu Mitakshara coparcener shall be deemed to be the share in the property that would have been allotted to him if a partition of the property had taken place immediately before his death, irrespective of whether he was entitled to claim partition or not. ...
In simple words

Section 6(1): in a Mitakshara joint family, a daughter is a coparcener by birth, with the same rights and liabilities as a son. Dispositions and partitions made before 20 December 2004 are not disturbed. Section 6(3): when a coparcener dies after 9 September 2005, his interest goes by will or by succession under the Act, not by survivorship . To find his interest, a partition is assumed just before his death, and the daughter gets the same share as a son. Section 6(4): for debts after 2005, no court lets a creditor proceed against a son, grandson or great-grandson only on the ground of pious obligation. Debts contracted before 2005 are saved, and for that saving "son, grandson or great-grandson" means one born or adopted before the 2005 Act (Explanation to Section 6(4)). Section 6(5): Section 6 does not touch a partition made before 20 December 2004, and "partition" means only a registered partition deed or a court decree. Section 30, Explanation: a male Hindu can dispose of his interest in Mitakshara coparcenary property by will. Section 6 as enacted in 1956: survivorship was the normal rule, but if the deceased left a female Class I heir (or a male Class I heir claiming through her), his interest passed by succession, and his share was worked out by assuming a partition just before his death.
en.meaning:
Mitakshara is Vijnaneswara's running commentary on the Yajnavalkya Smriti, written in the latter part of the eleventh century. Its family law rests on the son's birthright in ancestral property. Dayabhaga is Jimutavahana's digest of all the Smriti Codes, written about the beginning of the twelfth century. Its family law rests on ownership by the father and defined shares (Mulla, section 11(3)). "The conception of a coparcenary and of coparcenary property according to the Dayabhaga law is entirely distinct from that according to the Mitakshara law" (Mulla, section 272). See Diagram 1 . Diagram 1. Mitakshara: interest at birth, survivorship (now succession). Dayabhaga: nothing at birth, defined shares that pass to heirs. flowchart TD subgraph M["Mitakshara"] M1["Son is born"] --> M2["At once a coparcener
with his father"] M2 --> M3["Interest fluctuates
with births and deaths"] M3 --> M4["On a death: survivorship
after 2005: succession, s. 6(3)"] end subgraph D["Dayabhaga"] D1["Son is born"] --> D2["No interest while
father lives"] D2 --> D3["Father dies: sons inherit
defined shares as coparceners"] D3 --> D4["On a death: share passes
to his own heirs"] end Text description Mitakshara: a son is born and at once becomes a coparcener with his father; his interest fluctuates with births and deaths; on a coparcener's death his interest passed by survivorship, and after 2005 passes by succession under Section 6(3). Dayabhaga: a son gets nothing while the father lives; on the father's death the sons inherit as heirs and hold defined shares as coparceners; on a coparcener's death his share passes to his own heirs. The question this topic answers. How does a member hold joint family property, and what happens to his interest when he or another member is born or dies? Why the two schools differ. The Dayabhaga school did not accept the Mitakshara view that a son becomes an owner at birth. For the Dayabhaga, property passes only on the owner's death. Every other difference on the joint family follows from this.
keyPoints: Mitakshara: right by birth, unity of ownership, fluctuating interest, survivorship (now replaced by succession). Dayabhaga: no birthright, defined shares, unity of possession but no unity of ownership, shares pass to heirs. A Dayabhaga coparcenary begins only on the father's death; there is none between father and sons. A Dayabhaga father has absolute power over ancestral property. Ghamandi Ram : six incidents; the coparcenary is a creature of law. Section 6(1): daughters are Mitakshara coparceners by birth; 6(3): succession replaces survivorship after 2005; 6(4): no pious obligation for new debts; 6(5): only a registered deed or a decree counts as partition. Gurupad : widow's 7/24 share under the old Section 6. Vineeta Sharma : father need not be alive on 9 September 2005; the test of a coparcener is the right to demand partition.

caseLaws.name: State Bank of India v
caseLaws.facts: Ghamandi Ram (1969) Facts. The karta of a joint Hindu family firm that had traded in what became Pakistan claimed the surplus left in the firm's bank account after Partition. The question was whether the family firm was an "individual" or a "body of individuals" under a Pakistan notification . Principle. A Mitakshara coparcenary holds property in collective ownership in a quasi-corporate capacity; the Court listed its six incidents and held it is "a creature of law". The firm was a body of individuals, the amount had vested in the Custodian in Pakistan, and the Bank's appeal was allowed. AIR 1969 SC 1330. Why it matters. It is the standard statement of the incidents of a Mitakshara coparcenary. Vineeta Sharma v. Rakesh Sharma (2020) Facts. A three-judge bench was asked whether a daughter is a coparcener under the amended Section 6 if her father died before 9 September 2005. Principle. A daughter is a coparcener by birth, born before or after the amendment; the father need not be alive on 9 September 2005; the old notional partition did not disrupt the coparcenary; oral partition is not accepted except in exceptional cases (para 129). (2020) 9 SCC 1 : [2020] 10 SCR. Why it matters. It places daughters inside the Mitakshara coparcenary on the same footing as sons and overrules Prakash v. Phulavati . Gurupad Khandappa Magdum v. Hirabai Khandappa Magdum (1978) Facts. Khandappa died in 1960 leaving his widow, two sons and three daughters, and Mitakshara joint family property. The widow sued for a 7/24 share. Principle. Under Explanation 1 to the original Section 6, the assumed partition just before death must be worked out fully; the widow takes her share on that partition (1/4) plus her share in the deceased's interest (1/24). Appeal dismissed with costs. (1978) 3 SCC 383 : AIR 1978 SC 1239. Why it matters. It shows how the 1956 Act displaced survivorship before 2005. Brij Narain v. Mangla Prasad (1923) Facts. Sita Ram, managing ancestral property for himself and his two minor sons, mortgaged it in 1908 to pay off two earlier mortgages. The sons sued to have the mortgage declared not binding on them. Principle. A manager cannot burden the estate except for necessity; a father's mortgage binds the sons only if it pays an antecedent debt, "antecedent in fact as well as in time". The mortgage here paid earlier debts, so it bound the estate; appeal allowed. Privy Council, (1924) 26 Bom LR 500. Why it matters. It shows the Mitakshara limits on the manager and the father's power over ancestral property, which the Dayabhaga does not have.

selfTest.q: 1. In which school does a son get a right by birth?
selfTest.a: The Mitakshara.

selfTest.q: 2. Does a Dayabhaga coparcener's share rise or fall with births and deaths?
selfTest.a: No. Each coparcener takes a defined share that does not fluctuate ( Vineeta Sharma , para 35).

selfTest.q: 3. Which case lists the incidents of a Mitakshara coparcenary?
selfTest.a: State Bank of India v. Ghamandi Ram (1969).

selfTest.q: 4. What did Section 6(4) do to the pious obligation?
selfTest.a: For debts after 2005, no court recognises proceedings against a son, grandson or great-grandson solely on that ground. Earlier debts are saved.

selfTest.q: 5. In Gurupad , how did the widow get 7/24?
selfTest.a: 1/4 on the assumed partition between her husband and two sons, plus 1/6 of her husband's 1/4 (that is, 1/24) as one of six Class I heirs.

selfTest.q: 6. Can a Dayabhaga son demand partition from his father?
selfTest.a: No. The father is the sole owner of the ancestral property (Mulla, section 275).

legalProvision: Section 6, Hindu Succession Act, 1956 (as substituted in 2005). Devolution of interest in coparcenary property. (1) On and from the commencement of the Hindu Succession (Amendment) Act, 2005 (39 of 2005), in a Joint Hindu family governed by the Mitakshara law, the daughter of a coparcener shall,― (a) by birth become a coparcener in her own right the same manner as the son; (b) have the same rights in the coparcenery property as she would have had if she had been a son; (c) be subject to the same liabilities in respect of the said coparcenery property as that of a son, and any reference to a Hindu Mitakshara coparcener shall be deemed to include a reference to a daughter of a coparcener: Provided that nothing contained in this sub-section shall affect or invalidate any disposition or alienation including any partition or testamentary disposition of property which had taken place before the 20th day of December, 2004. ... (3) Where a Hindu dies after the commencement of the Hindu Succession (Amendment) Act, 2005 (39 of 2005), his interest in the property of a Joint Hindu family governed by the Mitakshara law, shall devolve by testamentary or intestate succession, as the case may be, under this Act and not by survivorship, and the coparcenery property shall be deemed to have been divided as if a partition had taken place and,― (a) the daughter is allotted the same share as is allotted to a son; ... Explanation. ―For the purposes of this sub-section, the interest of a Hindu Mitakshara coparcener shall be deemed to be the share in the property that would have been allotted to him if a partition of the property had taken place immediately before his death, irrespective of whether he was entitled to claim partition or not. (4) After the commencement of the Hindu Succession (Amendment) Act, 2005 (39 of 2005), no court shall recognise any right to proceed against a son, grandson or great-grandson for the recovery of any debt due from his father, grandfather or great-grandfather solely on the ground of the pious obligation under the Hindu law, of such son, grandson or great-grandson to discharge any such debt: [proviso saves debts contracted before the 2005 Act] (5) Nothing contained in this section shall apply to a partition, which has been effected before the 20th day of December, 2004. Explanation. ―For the purposes of this section "partition" means any partition made by execution of a deed of partition duly registered under the Registration Act, 1908 (16 of 1908) or partition effected by a decree of a court.

Explanation to Section 30, Hindu Succession Act, 1956. The interest of a male Hindu in a Mitakshara coparcenary property or the interest of a member of a tarwad, tavazhi, illom, kutumba or kavaru in the property of the tarwad, tavazhi, illom, kutumba or kavaru shall, notwithstanding anything contained in this Act or in any other law for the time being in force, be deemed to be property capable of being disposed of by him or by her within the meaning of this section.

Section 6, Hindu Succession Act, 1956 (as originally enacted, quoted in Gurupad ). When a male Hindu dies after the commencement of this Act, having at the time of his death an interest in a Mitakshara coparcenary property, his interest in the property shall devolve by survivorship upon the surviving members of the coparcenary and not in accordance with this Act: Provided that, if the deceased had left him surviving a female relative specified in class I of the Schedule or a male relative specified in that class who claims through such a female relative, the interest of the deceased in the Mitakshara coparcenary property shall devolve by testamentary or intestate succession, as the case may be, under this Act and not by survivorship. Explanation 1. —For the purposes of this section, the interest of a Hindu Mitakshara coparcener shall be deemed to be the share in the property that would have been allotted to him if a partition of the property had taken place immediately before his death, irrespective of whether he was entitled to claim partition or not. ...
సరళమైన మాటల్లో

సెక్షన్ 6(1): మితాక్షర ఉమ్మడి కుటుంబంలో కూతురు పుట్టుకతోనే కోపార్సినర్ ; కొడుకుతో సమాన హక్కులు, బాధ్యతలు. 20 డిసెంబర్ 2004 కు ముందు జరిగిన అన్యాక్రాంతాలు, విభజన లను ఇది కదిలించదు. సెక్షన్ 6(3): 9 సెప్టెంబర్ 2005 తర్వాత కోపార్సినర్ మరణిస్తే, అతని హక్కు సర్వైవర్‌షిప్ ద్వారా కాకుండా వీలునామా ద్వారా లేదా చట్టం కింది వారసత్వం ద్వారా వెళ్తుంది. అతని హక్కును తెలుసుకోవడానికి మరణానికి ముందు విభజన జరిగినట్టు భావిస్తారు; కూతురికి కొడుకుతో సమాన వాటా వస్తుంది. సెక్షన్ 6(4): 2005 తర్వాతి అప్పులకు, పవిత్ర బాధ్యత ఆధారంగా మాత్రమే కొడుకు, మనవడు, మునిమనవడిపై రుణదాత చర్య తీసుకోవడాన్ని ఏ కోర్టూ అనుమతించదు. 2005 కు ముందు చేసిన అప్పులకు మినహాయింపు ఉంది; ఆ మినహాయింపు కోసం "కొడుకు, మనవడు, మునిమనవడు" అంటే 2005 చట్టానికి ముందు పుట్టినవారు లేదా దత్తత తీసుకున్నవారు (సెక్షన్ 6(4) Explanation). సెక్షన్ 6(5): 20 డిసెంబర్ 2004 కు ముందు జరిగిన విభజనను సెక్షన్ 6 తాకదు; "విభజన" అంటే రిజిస్టర్డ్ విభజన దస్తావేజు లేదా కోర్టు డిక్రీ మాత్రమే. సెక్షన్ 30, Explanation: పురుష హిందువు మితాక్షర కోపార్సినరీ ఆస్తిలో తన హక్కును వీలునామా ద్వారా ఇవ్వవచ్చు. 1956 లో అసలు సెక్షన్ 6: సర్వైవర్‌షిప్ సాధారణ నియమం; కానీ మరణించినవారికి Class I స్త్రీ వారసురాలు (లేదా ఆమె ద్వారా క్లెయిమ్ చేసే Class I పురుష వారసుడు) ఉంటే, అతని హక్కు వారసత్వం ద్వారా వెళ్ళేది; మరణానికి ముందు విభజన జరిగినట్టు భావించి అతని వాటాను లెక్కించేవారు.

మితాక్షర అంటే పదకొండో శతాబ్దం చివరి భాగంలో విజ్ఞానేశ్వరుడు యాజ్ఞవల్క్య స్మృతిపై రాసిన వరుస వ్యాఖ్యానం. దాని కుటుంబ చట్టం పూర్వీకుల ఆస్తిలో కొడుకు జన్మహక్కుపై ఆధారపడుతుంది. దాయభాగ అంటే సుమారు పన్నెండో శతాబ్దం ప్రారంభంలో జీమూతవాహనుడు రాసిన అన్ని స్మృతుల డైజెస్ట్. దాని కుటుంబ చట్టం తండ్రి యాజమాన్యం, నిర్దిష్ట వాటాలపై ఆధారపడుతుంది (ముల్లా, సెక్షన్ 11(3)). "The conception of a coparcenary and of coparcenary property according to the Dayabhaga law is entirely distinct from that according to the Mitakshara law" (ముల్లా, సెక్షన్ 272). Diagram 1 చూడండి. Diagram 1. మితాక్షర: పుట్టుకతో హక్కు, సర్వైవర్‌షిప్ (ఇప్పుడు వారసత్వం). దాయభాగ: పుట్టుకతో ఏమీ లేదు, వారసులకు వెళ్ళే నిర్దిష్ట వాటాలు. flowchart TD subgraph M["మితాక్షర"] M1["కొడుకు పుడతాడు"] --> M2["వెంటనే తండ్రితో
కోపార్సినర్"] M2 --> M3["జననాలు, మరణాలతో
హక్కు మారుతుంది"] M3 --> M4["మరణంపై: సర్వైవర్‌షిప్
2005 తర్వాత: వారసత్వం, సె. 6(3)"] end subgraph D["దాయభాగ"] D1["కొడుకు పుడతాడు"] --> D2["తండ్రి బతికి ఉండగా
హక్కు లేదు"] D2 --> D3["తండ్రి మరణం: కొడుకులు కోపార్సినర్లుగా
నిర్దిష్ట వాటాలు పొందుతారు"] D3 --> D4["మరణంపై: వాటా అతని
సొంత వారసులకు"] end వచన వివరణ మితాక్షర: కొడుకు పుట్టగానే తండ్రితో కోపార్సినర్ అవుతాడు; అతని హక్కు జననాలు, మరణాలతో మారుతుంది; కోపార్సినర్ మరణిస్తే అతని హక్కు సర్వైవర్‌షిప్ ద్వారా వెళ్ళేది, 2005 తర్వాత సెక్షన్ 6(3) కింద వారసత్వం ద్వారా వెళ్తుంది. దాయభాగ: తండ్రి బతికి ఉండగా కొడుకుకు ఏమీ రాదు; తండ్రి మరణిస్తే కొడుకులు వారసులుగా తీసుకుని కోపార్సినర్లుగా నిర్దిష్ట వాటాలు కలిగి ఉంటారు; కోపార్సినర్ మరణిస్తే అతని వాటా అతని సొంత వారసులకు వెళ్తుంది. ఈ అంశం జవాబిచ్చే ప్రశ్న. ఒక సభ్యుడు ఉమ్మడి కుటుంబ ఆస్తిని ఎలా కలిగి ఉంటాడు, అతను లేదా మరో సభ్యుడు పుట్టినప్పుడు, మరణించినప్పుడు అతని హక్కుకు ఏమవుతుంది? రెండు శాఖలు ఎందుకు విభేదిస్తాయి. కొడుకు పుట్టుకతోనే యజమాని అవుతాడనే మితాక్షర అభిప్రాయాన్ని దాయభాగ శాఖ అంగీకరించలేదు. దాయభాగ ప్రకారం యజమాని మరణించినప్పుడే ఆస్తి వెళ్తుంది. ఉమ్మడి కుటుంబంపై మిగతా తేడాలన్నీ దీని నుంచే వస్తాయి.

selfTest.q: 1. ఏ శాఖలో కొడుకుకు పుట్టుకతో హక్కు వస్తుంది?
selfTest.a: మితాక్షర.

selfTest.q: 2. దాయభాగ కోపార్సినర్ వాటా జననాలు, మరణాలతో పెరుగుతుందా, తగ్గుతుందా?
selfTest.a: లేదు. ప్రతి కోపార్సినర్‌కు మారని నిర్దిష్ట వాటా ఉంటుంది ( Vineeta Sharma , para 35).

selfTest.q: 3. మితాక్షర కోపార్సినరీ లక్షణాలను ఏ కేసు జాబితా చేస్తుంది?
selfTest.a: State Bank of India v. Ghamandi Ram (1969).

selfTest.q: 4. సెక్షన్ 6(4) పవిత్ర బాధ్యతను ఏం చేసింది?
selfTest.a: 2005 తర్వాతి అప్పులకు, ఆ కారణంతో మాత్రమే కొడుకు, మనవడు, మునిమనవడిపై చర్యను ఏ కోర్టూ గుర్తించదు. పాత అప్పులకు మినహాయింపు ఉంది.

selfTest.q: 5. Gurupad లో భార్యకు 7/24 ఎలా వచ్చింది?
selfTest.a: భర్త, ఇద్దరు కొడుకుల మధ్య ఊహించిన విభజనలో 1/4, దానికి తోడు ఆరుగురు Class I వారసుల్లో ఒకరిగా భర్త 1/4 లో 1/6 (అంటే 1/24).

selfTest.q: 6. దాయభాగ కొడుకు తండ్రి నుంచి విభజన కోరవచ్చా?
selfTest.a: లేదు. పూర్వీకుల ఆస్తికి తండ్రే ఏకైక యజమాని (ముల్లా, సెక్షన్ 275).

family-law-i-u1-t6.subtitle: Who the Karta is, how the office arises, and the limits on his power

en.inOneMinute: The Karta is the manager of a joint Hindu family . By default he is the father or, in his absence, the senior-most coparcener . The office comes from law and seniority, not from a contract or an election. The Supreme Court has said that managership goes to a person by birth and is regulated by seniority ( Tribhovandas Haribhai Tamboli , 1991). A junior member can act as manager only if the Karta gives up the office or in exceptional situations. Only a coparcener can be Karta ( Seth Govindram Sugar Mills , 1966). The Karta has no larger share than any other member. His one special power is to deal with the whole family property for purposes the law accepts, such as legal necessity . If members dislike his management, their remedy is partition . Since 2005 a daughter is a coparcener by birth. In Sujata Sharma v. Manu Gupta (2015) the Delhi High Court held that the eldest coparcener, though a woman, is the Karta.
legalProvision: No Act creates or defines the office of Karta . It is part of uncodified Mitakshara law. Three statutes touch it.

Section 6(1), Hindu Succession Act, 1956 (as substituted in 2005). On and from the commencement of the Hindu Succession (Amendment) Act, 2005 (39 of 2005), in a Joint Hindu family governed by the Mitakshara law, the daughter of a coparcener shall,― (a) by birth become a coparcener in her own right the same manner as the son; (b) have the same rights in the coparcenery property as she would have had if she had been a son; (c) be subject to the same liabilities in respect of the said coparcenery property as that of a son, and any reference to a Hindu Mitakshara coparcener shall be deemed to include a reference to a daughter of a coparcener: ...

Section 4(1)(a), Hindu Succession Act, 1956. Save as otherwise expressly provided in this Act,― (a) any text, rule or interpretation of Hindu law or any custom or usage as part of that law in force immediately before the commencement of this Act shall cease to have effect with respect to any matter for which provision is made in this Act;

Section 6, Hindu Minority and Guardianship Act, 1956 (opening words). The natural guardians of a Hindu minor, in respect of the minor's person as well as in respect of the minor's property (excluding his or her undivided interest in joint family property), are― ...

Section 12, Hindu Minority and Guardianship Act, 1956. Where a minor has an undivided interest in joint family property and the property is under the management of an adult member of the family, no guardian shall be appointed for the minor in respect of such undivided interest: Provided that nothing in this section shall be deemed to affect the jurisdiction of a High Court to appoint a guardian in respect of such interest.
In simple words

Section 6(1) makes a daughter a coparcener by birth, with the same rights and liabilities as a son. Since coparcenership is the qualification for the office, this is the basis for a woman becoming Karta. Section 4(1)(a) ends old Hindu law rules only on matters the Act provides for. The Act says nothing about who manages the family, so the classical rules on the Karta continue, read with the new Section 6. Sections 6 and 12 of the Guardianship Act keep a minor's undivided interest in joint family property out of the hands of a guardian. That interest is managed by the adult member who manages the family, which is the Karta.
en.meaning:
Mulla states the rule this way (section 236): "Property belonging to a joint family is ordinarily managed by the father or other senior member for the time being of the family. The manager of a joint family is called karta. The father is in all cases naturally, and in the case of minor sons necessarily, the manager of the joint family property." So the Karta is the member who manages the joint family and its property and represents it in dealings with outsiders. The family does not need to appoint him. The office falls on the senior member who is a coparcener. The Karta manages the joint family, which is wider than the coparcenary . Wives, widows and unmarried daughters are members of the family. But the person who holds the office must be a coparcener. See Diagram 1 . Diagram 1. The office goes to the senior-most coparcener; a junior member acts only in the exceptions; a non-coparcener cannot hold it. flowchart TD Q1{"Is the person a coparcener?

coparcener?"} Q2 -- "Yes" --> K["Karta by birth and seniority;

(Tribhovandas)"] J -- "No" --> X["Cannot act as manager
while the Karta is available"] Text description Is the person a coparcener? If no (for example a widow or wife), the person cannot be Karta. If yes, is the person the father or the senior-most coparcener? If yes, the person is Karta by birth and seniority, presumed to be manager. If no, a junior member can act as manager only if the Karta gives up the office, in distress or calamity affecting the family in his absence, or if the father is missing or far away and not expected back.
keyPoints: The Karta is the manager of the joint Hindu family; no Act creates the office. The father, or else the senior-most coparcener, is Karta by birth and seniority; the senior member is presumed to be manager. A junior member acts only if the Karta gives up the office or in exceptional circumstances ( Tribhovandas ). Coparcenership is a necessary qualification ( Seth Govindram Sugar Mills ). Since 2005 a daughter is a coparcener, so the eldest coparcener can be Karta though a woman ( Sujata Sharma ); a widow or wife cannot. The Karta has no larger share; he is not an agent; the members' remedy is partition. He accounts on partition only for what he received, unless there is fraud or misappropriation. He cannot alienate except for necessity ( Brij Narain ); he does not manage separate property or Section 8 inheritance ( Chander Sen ).

caseLaws.name: Sujata Sharma v
caseLaws.facts: Manu Gupta (2015) Facts. Sujata Sharma, the eldest coparcener of D.R. Gupta & Sons (HUF), sued for a declaration that she was its Karta. The defendants argued that Section 6 deals with inheritance, not management. Principle. After the 2005 amendment, a woman who is the eldest coparcener can be Karta; her marriage does not alter this. Delhi High Court, Najmi Waziri J., CS(OS) 2011/2006, decided 22.12.2015, paras 25, 27 and 29. Why it matters. It is the leading authority that a woman can be Karta. Commissioner of Income Tax v. Seth Govindram Sugar Mills (1966) Facts. The question was whether a widow, who is a member of the joint family but not a coparcener, could be its manager. The Nagpur High Court had allowed a mother to act as manager; the Madras High Court had not. Principle. Coparcenership is a necessary qualification for managership; a woman who is not a coparcener cannot be the manager. AIR 1966 SC 24 (as quoted in Sujata Sharma , para 26). Why it matters. It fixes the qualification for the office, which is why Sujata Sharma turned on Section 6. Tribhovandas Haribhai Tamboli v. Gujarat Revenue Tribunal (1991) Facts. The question was the position of a junior member who deals with joint family property while the Karta is available. (Only the passages quoted in Sujata Sharma were checked.) Principle. Managership goes by birth and seniority; a junior member acts only if the Karta gives up the office or in exceptional circumstances. AIR 1991 SC 1538 (as quoted in Sujata Sharma , paras 6 and 15). Why it matters. It is the Supreme Court statement of how the office arises. Surjit Lal Chhabda v. Commissioner of Income Tax (1975) Facts. A man with no son threw his house into the family hotchpot and claimed its rent should be taxed as income of the HUF of himself, his wife and unmarried daughter. Principle. Such a family is a joint Hindu family, but until a son is born the property "is really his"; the rent is his individual income. (1976) 3 SCC 142 : AIR 1976 SC 109. Why it matters. Calling oneself Karta does not turn one's own property into family property for all purposes. Commissioner of Wealth Tax, Kanpur v. Chander Sen (1986) Facts. Chander Sen inherited ₹1,85,043 standing to his father's credit in their firm. The Revenue treated it as the wealth of Chander Sen's joint family with his sons. Principle. A son inherits under Section 8 in his individual capacity, not as Karta of his own family. (1986) 3 SCC 567 : AIR 1986 SC 1753. Why it matters. It limits the property a Karta manages. Brij Narain v. Mangla Prasad (1923) Facts. Sita Ram, manager of a joint family with his two minor sons, mortgaged family property for Rs. 11,000 in 1908 to pay off two earlier mortgages. The sons, through their mother, sued to have it declared not binding. Principle. "The managing co-parcener of a joint undivided estate cannot alienate or burden the estate qua manager except for purposes of necessity" (para 17). Privy Council, (1924) 26 Bom LR 500. Why it matters. It states the basic limit on the Karta's power.

selfTest.q: 1. Who is the Karta by default?
selfTest.a: The father; in his absence, the senior-most coparcener (Mulla, section 236; Tribhovandas ).

selfTest.q: 2. When can a junior member act as manager while the Karta is alive?
selfTest.a: If the Karta gives up the office, in distress or calamity affecting the family in the Karta's absence, or if the father is missing or far away and not expected back soon ( Tribhovandas ).

selfTest.q: 3. Why could a widow not be Karta, and can she be one today?
selfTest.a: Because coparcenership is a necessary qualification and she is not a coparcener ( Seth Govindram Sugar Mills ). Section 6(1) makes daughters, not widows, coparceners, so she still cannot.

selfTest.q: 4. Which case held that a woman can be Karta, and which court decided it?
selfTest.a: Sujata Sharma v. Manu Gupta (2015), a single judge of the Delhi High Court.

selfTest.q: 5. A coparcener is unhappy with the Karta's spending on family ceremonies. What is his remedy?
selfTest.a: To demand partition (Mulla, section 237). The Karta need not economise like a trustee while he spends for family purposes.

selfTest.q: 6. Is a guardian appointed for a minor coparcener's undivided interest?
selfTest.a: No, where an adult member manages the joint family property (Section 12, Hindu Minority and Guardianship Act); a High Court's power is saved.

సెక్షన్ 6(1) కూతురిని పుట్టుకతో కోపార్సినర్ ‌గా చేస్తుంది; కొడుకుకు ఉన్న హక్కులు, బాధ్యతలే ఆమెకూ ఉంటాయి. కర్త పదవికి అర్హత కోపార్సినర్‌గా ఉండటమే కాబట్టి, స్త్రీ కర్త కావడానికి ఇదే ఆధారం. సెక్షన్ 4(1)(a) చట్టం ఏ విషయాలకు నిబంధన చేసిందో ఆ విషయాల్లో మాత్రమే పాత హిందూ చట్ట నియమాలను రద్దు చేస్తుంది. కుటుంబాన్ని ఎవరు నిర్వహించాలో చట్టం ఏమీ చెప్పలేదు. కాబట్టి కర్త గురించిన సంప్రదాయ నియమాలు కొత్త సెక్షన్ 6 తో కలిపి చదివి కొనసాగుతాయి. సంరక్షకత్వ చట్టంలోని సెక్షన్లు 6, 12 ఉమ్మడి కుటుంబ ఆస్తిలో మైనర్ అవిభక్త వాటాను సంరక్షకుని చేతుల్లో పెట్టవు. కుటుంబాన్ని నిర్వహించే వయోజన సభ్యుడు, అంటే కర్త, ఆ వాటాను నిర్వహిస్తాడు.

selfTest.q: 1. సాధారణంగా కర్త ఎవరు?

selfTest.q: 2. కర్త బతికి ఉండగా చిన్న సభ్యుడు నిర్వాహకుడిగా ఎప్పుడు వ్యవహరించవచ్చు?

selfTest.q: 3. వితంతువు ఎందుకు కర్త కాలేకపోయేది?

selfTest.q: 6. మైనర్ కోపార్సినర్ అవిభక్త వాటాకు సంరక్షకుడిని నియమిస్తారా?

family-law-i-u1-t3.subtitle: Why Hindu law has two schools, where each applies, and the four Mitakshara sub-schools

en.inOneMinute: A school of Hindu law is a body of rules built on one leading commentary and followed in one part of India. There are only two schools: the Mitakshara and the Dayabhaga . The Dayabhaga prevails in Bengal (and Assam). The Mitakshara prevails in the rest of India. The Mitakshara school has four sub-schools: Benares, Mithila, Maharashtra or Bombay, and Dravida or Madras. They all accept the Mitakshara as supreme and differ only in details, mainly of adoption and inheritance. The two schools differ mainly on inheritance and the joint family. Today the Hindu Acts apply to both schools alike, so the difference matters mainly for joint family property. Section 6 of the Hindu Succession Act speaks only of a family "governed by the Mitakshara law". Exams ask why the schools arose, the two schools and their regions, the four sub-schools with their regions and leading works, and what the schools mean today ( Vineeta Sharma , Surjit Lal Chhabda ).
legalProvision: No Act creates or lists the schools. They come from the commentaries and the courts. The Acts refer to them in a few places.

Section 6(1), Hindu Succession Act, 1956 (as substituted in 2005). On and from the commencement of the Hindu Succession (Amendment) Act, 2005 (39 of 2005), in a Joint Hindu family governed by the Mitakshara law, the daughter of a coparcener shall,― (a) by birth become a coparcener in her own right the same manner as the son; (b) have the same rights in the coparcenery property as she would have had if she had been a son; (c) be subject to the same liabilities in respect of the said coparcenery property as that of a son, and any reference to a Hindu Mitakshara coparcener shall be deemed to include a reference to a daughter of a coparcener: ...

Section 4(1), Hindu Succession Act, 1956. Overriding effect of Act. Save as otherwise expressly provided in this Act,― (a) any text, rule or interpretation of Hindu law or any custom or usage as part of that law in force immediately before the commencement of this Act shall cease to have effect with respect to any matter for which provision is made in this Act; (b) any other law in force immediately before the commencement of this Act shall cease to apply to Hindus in so far as it is inconsistent with any of the provisions contained in this Act.

Section 3(1), Hindu Women's Rights to Property Act, 1937 (a pre-1956 Act, quoted to show how statutes used the schools). When a Hindu governed by the Dayabhaga School of Hindu Law dies intestate leaving any property, and when a Hindu governed by any other school of Hindu law or by customary law dies intestate leaving separate property, his widow ... shall ... be entitled ... to the same share as a son: ...
In simple words

Section 6(1): the daughter's birthright as a coparcener applies only in a joint Hindu family "governed by the Mitakshara law". A Dayabhaga family is outside these words. Section 4(1): on every matter the Succession Act covers, the old texts and interpretations of each school stop having effect. A school's rules survive only on matters the Act does not cover. The other three Acts have the same clause (Hindu Marriage Act s. 4; Hindu Adoptions and Maintenance Act s. 4; Hindu Minority and Guardianship Act s. 5). Section 3(a), Hindu Marriage Act: a custom that is ancient, certain, reasonable and not against public policy has the force of law. A local rule of a sub-school can therefore survive as custom where the Act saves custom. 1937 Act: before codification, statutes named the schools and gave different rules to a Dayabhaga Hindu and to a Hindu of "any other school". On matters the 1956 Act covers, such earlier law ceased to apply under Section 4(1)(b).
en.meaning:
A school of Hindu law is a system of rules built on one authoritative commentary and followed in a particular region. The schools share the same ancient sources, the Smritis. They differ because each region accepted a different commentator's reading of those texts. See Diagram 1 . Diagram 1. One set of Smritis, two schools, and four Mitakshara sub-schools with their regions. flowchart TD S["Smritis: common to all schools"] S --> M["Mitakshara school
Vijnaneswara, commentary on Yajnavalkya
All India except Bengal"] S --> D["Dayabhaga school
Jimutavahana, digest of all Codes
Bengal and Assam"] M --> B1["Benares
Northern India"] M --> B2["Mithila
Tirhoot, north Bihar"] M --> B3["Maharashtra or Bombay
Western India"] M --> B4["Dravida or Madras
Southern India"] Text description The Smritis are common to all schools. Commentaries gave rise to two schools: the Mitakshara (Vijnaneswara, commentary on Yajnavalkya, all India except Bengal) and the Dayabhaga (Jimutavahana, digest, Bengal and Assam). The Mitakshara has four sub-schools: Benares (Northern India), Mithila (Tirhoot and north Bihar), Maharashtra or Bombay (Western India), Dravida or Madras (Southern India). The question this topic answers. Which body of Hindu law governs this family? The answer still matters for joint family property and coparcenary rights, and for any matter the Acts do not cover. Why the law has this rule. The Smritis sometimes conflicted. Commentators settled the conflicts in different ways. A commentator's view accepted in one region and rejected in another became the law of the region that accepted it. Courts then followed what each region had accepted.
keyPoints: The Smritis are common to all schools; the schools arose from commentaries accepted in different regions. Only two schools: Mitakshara (Vijnaneswara, commentary on Yajnavalkya) and Dayabhaga (Jimutavahana, digest of all Codes). Dayabhaga: Bengal and Assam. Mitakshara: the rest of India. The schools differ mainly on inheritance and the joint family system. Four Mitakshara sub-schools: Benares, Mithila, Maharashtra or Bombay, Dravida or Madras. Sub-school works supplement the Mitakshara; first ask what the Mitakshara says. The Mayukha overrules the Mitakshara only in Gujarat, the Island of Bombay and the North Konkan. The Hindu Acts apply to both schools alike; Section 6 of the Succession Act speaks only of the Mitakshara.

caseLaws.name: Collector of Madura v
caseLaws.facts: Moottoo Ramalinga Sathupathy (1868) Facts. Known as the Ramnad case, it concerned the validity of an adoption made by a widow. Mulla records that the Privy Council first laid down in it the rule on the consent of the husband's sapindas to such an adoption. Principle. The Smritis are common to all schools; commentaries received in one region and rejected in another gave rise to schools with conflicting doctrines. (1868) 12 M.I.A. 397. Why it matters. It is the classic explanation of how the schools arose (quoted in Mulla, section 11(1)). Vineeta Sharma v. Rakesh Sharma (2020) Facts. The question was whether a daughter is a coparcener under the amended Section 6 if her father died before 9 September 2005. Principle. The Court set out the two schools, the four Mitakshara sub-schools and their regions (paras 18–20), and held that the daughter is a coparcener by birth whether or not her father was alive on that date. (2020) 9 SCC 1 : [2020] 10 SCR. Why it matters. It is the Supreme Court's recent statement of the schools and their regions. Surjit Lal Chhabda v. Commissioner of Income Tax (1975) Facts. A man governed by the Mitakshara claimed that he, his wife and his unmarried daughter formed a Hindu undivided family for income tax. Principle. The schools differ on the coparcener's birthright and on inheritance, but a Dayabhaga family, like a Mitakshara family, is normally joint in food, worship and estate, and the basic idea of who can be a member of a Hindu undivided family is the same. (1976) 3 SCC 142 : AIR 1976 SC 109. Why it matters. It shows what the two schools have in common.

selfTest.q: 1. Who wrote the Mitakshara, and on which Smriti?
selfTest.a: Vijnaneswara, as a running commentary on the Yajnavalkya Smriti.

selfTest.q: 3. Where does the Dayabhaga prevail?
selfTest.a: In Bengal and Assam (the Bengali-speaking areas).

selfTest.q: 4. Do the schools still decide succession to a Hindu's property?
selfTest.a: No. The Hindu Succession Act applies to both schools alike, and its Section 4 overrides the old rules on matters it covers.

selfTest.q: 5. Where does the Vyavahara Mayukha overrule the Mitakshara?
selfTest.a: In Gujarat, the Island of Bombay and the North Konkan (Mulla, section 12(2)).

selfTest.q: 6. On what two main points do the schools differ?
selfTest.a: The law of inheritance and the joint family system (Mulla, section 11(6)).

సెక్షన్ 6(1): కూతురికి కోపార్సినర్ ‌గా జన్మహక్కు "governed by the Mitakshara law" అయిన ఉమ్మడి హిందూ కుటుంబం లో మాత్రమే వర్తిస్తుంది. దాయభాగ కుటుంబం ఈ పదాల బయట ఉంటుంది. సెక్షన్ 4(1): వారసత్వ చట్టం కవర్ చేసే ప్రతి విషయంలోనూ, ప్రతి శాఖ పాత గ్రంథాలు, వ్యాఖ్యానాలు అమలు కావడం ఆగిపోతాయి. చట్టం కవర్ చేయని విషయాల్లో మాత్రమే శాఖ నియమాలు మిగులుతాయి. మిగతా మూడు చట్టాల్లోనూ ఇదే క్లాజ్ ఉంది (హిందూ వివాహ చట్టం సె. 4; హిందూ దత్తత మరియు భరణ చట్టం సె. 4; హిందూ మైనారిటీ మరియు సంరక్షకత్వ చట్టం సె. 5). హిందూ వివాహ చట్టం సెక్షన్ 3(a): ప్రాచీనమైన, నిర్దిష్టమైన, సహేతుకమైన, ప్రజా విధానానికి విరుద్ధం కాని ఆచారానికి చట్టబలం ఉంటుంది. కాబట్టి చట్టం ఆచారాన్ని కాపాడిన చోట, ఒక ఉప-శాఖ స్థానిక నియమం ఆచారంగా మిగలవచ్చు. 1937 చట్టం: క్రోడీకరణకు ముందు, చట్టాలు శాఖల పేర్లు చెప్పి, దాయభాగ హిందువుకు ఒక నియమం, "any other school" హిందువుకు మరో నియమం ఇచ్చాయి. 1956 చట్టం కవర్ చేసే విషయాల్లో అలాంటి పాత చట్టం సెక్షన్ 4(1)(b) కింద వర్తించడం ఆగిపోయింది.

selfTest.q: 1. మితాక్షరను ఎవరు రాశారు, ఏ స్మృతిపై?
selfTest.a: విజ్ఞానేశ్వరుడు, యాజ్ఞవల్క్య స్మృతిపై వరుస వ్యాఖ్యానంగా.

selfTest.q: 3. దాయభాగ ఎక్కడ అమలులో ఉంది?
selfTest.a: బెంగాల్, అస్సాంలో (బెంగాలీ మాట్లాడే ప్రాంతాల్లో).

selfTest.q: 4. హిందువు ఆస్తి వారసత్వాన్ని ఇప్పటికీ శాఖలే నిర్ణయిస్తాయా?
selfTest.a: లేదు. హిందూ వారసత్వ చట్టం రెండు శాఖలకూ ఒకేలా వర్తిస్తుంది; అది కవర్ చేసే విషయాల్లో దాని సెక్షన్ 4 పాత నియమాలను అధిగమిస్తుంది.

selfTest.q: 5. వ్యవహార మయూఖ ఎక్కడ మితాక్షరను అధిగమిస్తుంది?
selfTest.a: గుజరాత్, బొంబాయి ద్వీపం, ఉత్తర కొంకణ్‌లో (ముల్లా, సెక్షన్ 12(2)).

selfTest.q: 6. శాఖలు ఏ రెండు ముఖ్య అంశాల్లో విభేదిస్తాయి?
selfTest.a: వారసత్వ చట్టం, ఉమ్మడి కుటుంబ వ్యవస్థ (ముల్లా, సెక్షన్ 11(6)).

family-law-i-u1-t8.subtitle: A son's duty to pay his father's debts, and its end under section 6(4)

en.inOneMinute: Under Mitakshara law a son, grandson and great-grandson must pay the debts of the father, grandfather and great-grandfather, provided the debts were not incurred for an illegal or immoral purpose. This is the pious obligation . It is a religious duty turned into a legal liability, and it is limited to the son's interest in the joint family property; it is not a personal liability. The Privy Council in Brij Narain v. Mangla Prasad (1923) held that the obligation exists whether the father is alive or dead, and that sons cannot resist their father's creditor, or his alienation for an antecedent debt , if the debt is not tainted with immorality. Since 2005, Section 6(4) of the Hindu Succession Act, 1956 stops courts from recognising any right to proceed against a son, grandson or great-grandson solely on the ground of pious obligation. Debts contracted before 9 September 2005 are saved, for descendants born or adopted before that date. Vineeta Sharma (2020) says Section 6(4) makes a daughter liable in the same manner as a son. Exams ask for the basis of the doctrine, the avyavaharika debts the son need not pay, antecedent debt, and the effect of Section 6(4).
legalProvision: Section 6(4), Hindu Succession Act, 1956 (as substituted in 2005). After the commencement of the Hindu Succession (Amendment) Act, 2005 (39 of 2005), no court shall recognise any right to proceed against a son, grandson or great-grandson for the recovery of any debt due from his father, grandfather or great-grandfather solely on the ground of the pious obligation under the Hindu law, of such son, grandson or great-grandson to discharge any such debt: Provided that in the case of any debt contracted before the commencement of the Hindu Succession (Amendment) Act, 2005 (39 of 2005), nothing contained in this sub-section shall affect― (a) the right of any creditor to proceed against the son, grandson or great-grandson, as the case may be; or (b) any alienation made in respect of or in satisfaction of, any such debt, and any such right or alienation shall be enforceable under the rule of pious obligation in the same manner and to the same extent as it would have been enforceable as if the Hindu Succession (Amendment) Act, 2005 (39 of 2005) had not been enacted. Explanation.―For the purposes of clause (a), the expression "son", "grandson" or "great-grandson" shall be deemed to refer to the son, grandson or great-grandson, as the case may be, who was born or adopted prior to the commencement of the Hindu Succession (Amendment) Act, 2005 (39 of 2005).
In simple words

Main rule. After the 2005 Act came into force (9 September 2005), a creditor cannot sue a son, grandson or great-grandson for the father's or ancestor's debt on the sole ground of pious obligation . Proviso (a). For a debt contracted before that date, the creditor keeps his old right against the descendants. Proviso (b). For such an earlier debt, a sale or mortgage made for it, or in satisfaction of it, remains enforceable under the old rule. Explanation. The saving in clause (a) covers only descendants born or adopted before 9 September 2005. The change is prospective : it does not reopen old debts. Vineeta Sharma (para 61) says the proviso saves the creditor's right for debts contracted before the amendment and that the rights and liabilities under Section 6 both run from its commencement.
en.meaning:
Mulla (section 290(1)) states the rule: "Where the sons are joint with their father, and debts have been contracted by the father for his own personal benefit, the sons are liable to pay the debts provided they were not incurred for an illegal or immoral purpose. The liability to pay the debts contracted by the father, though for his own benefit, arises from an obligation of religion and piety which is placed upon the sons under the Mitakshara law to discharge the father's debts, where the debts are not tainted with immorality." In Mulla, "sons" includes son's sons and son's son's sons. So the pious obligation is the liability of a son, grandson and great-grandson, arising from religious duty, to pay out of the joint family property the personal debts of the father, grandfather and great-grandfather that are not illegal or immoral ( vyavaharika debts). Brij Narain (para 12) calls it "the obligation of the son to discharge his father's debts, based on the doctrine of pious duty". See Diagram 1 . Diagram 1. A test for a creditor's claim against a son, grandson or great-grandson based on pious obligation. flowchart TD Q1{"Debt of the father, grandfather
or great-grandfather?"} Q1 -- "No" --> X["Doctrine does not apply"] Q1 -- "Yes" --> Q2{"Illegal, immoral or avyavaharika?
(son must prove it)"} Q2 -- "Yes" --> N["Son not liable
(Mulla s. 298)"] Q2 -- "No" --> Q3{"Debt contracted before
9.9.2005?"} Q3 -- "No" --> B["No claim solely on
pious obligation (s. 6(4))"] Q3 -- "Yes" --> Q4{"Descendant born or adopted
before 9.9.2005?"} Q4 -- "No" --> E["Clause (a) does not save
the claim against him (Explanation)"] Q4 -- "Yes" --> L["Liable to the extent of his interest
in joint family property, not personally
(Mulla s. 290(3))"] Text description Is the debt of the father, grandfather or great-grandfather? If no, the doctrine does not apply. If yes, was it for an illegal or immoral purpose, or is it avyavaharika (the son must prove this)? If yes, the son is not liable. If no, was it contracted before 9 September 2005? If no, no claim lies solely on pious obligation (Section 6(4)). If yes, was the descendant born or adopted before 9 September 2005? If no, clause (a) of the proviso does not save the claim against him. If yes, he is liable, but only to the extent of his interest in the joint family property, not personally.
keyPoints: Pious obligation: the duty of a son, grandson and great-grandson to pay the father's, grandfather's and great-grandfather's personal debts not tainted with immorality (Mulla s. 290; Brij Narain paras 11–12). The liability is limited to the interest in the joint family property; it is not personal. It exists whether the father is alive or dead, and lasts only while the father's liability subsists. Avyavaharika debts (liquor, gambling, lust or wrath, fines, tolls and the like) are excluded; the son must prove the taint. A father may sell or mortgage the sons' interest for an antecedent debt, antecedent in fact as well as in time. Section 6(4): after 9 September 2005, no proceeding against descendants solely on this ground; pre-2005 debts are saved for descendants born or adopted before that date. A daughter is liable in the same manner as a son ( Vineeta Sharma , para 61).

caseLaws.name: Brij Narain v
caseLaws.facts: Mangla Prasad (1923) Facts. In 1908 Sita Ram, manager of a joint family with his two minor sons, mortgaged ancestral property for Rs. 11,000 to pay off two earlier mortgages. The sons, through their mother, sued to have it declared not binding on them. Principle. The pious obligation exists whether the father is alive or dead; a father may lay the estate open to execution for his non-immoral debt; a mortgage binds only if it discharges an antecedent debt, antecedent in fact as well as in time (paras 11, 12, 14–15, 17). The earlier mortgages were antecedent debts, so the 1908 mortgage bound the estate (paras 18–19). Privy Council, (1924) 26 Bom LR 500 : (1924) 51 IA 129. Why it matters. It joins the sons' duty for the father's debt with the father's power to bind the estate. Vineeta Sharma v. Rakesh Sharma (2020) Facts. A three-judge bench heard a reference on how the substituted Section 6 applies to daughters. Principle. Section 6(4) makes a daughter liable in the same manner as a son; the proviso saves the creditor's right for debts contracted before the 2005 amendment; Section 6 is not retrospective (para 61). Why it matters. It confirms that daughters share the obligation and that Section 6(4) looks forward. Luhar Amrit Lal v. Doshi Jayantilal (1960) Facts. A father lost heavily in speculation in gold and silver and mortgaged joint family property to pay the losses. His sons and wife sued for a declaration that the mortgage decree did not bind them because the debt was immoral (as stated in Mulla, section 295). Principle. The sons must prove not only that the antecedent debt was immoral but also that the alienee had notice of it; having failed to prove notice, they failed. (1960) 3 SCR 842 : AIR 1960 SC 964. Why it matters. It places the burden of proving immorality and notice on the sons. Sidheshwar Mukherjee v. Bhubneshwar Prasad (1953) Facts. The question was whether the sons' interest in joint family property passed on an execution sale under a decree against their father, who was not the Karta. (Only the holding as stated in Mulla, section 292, was checked.) Principle. The son's liability rests entirely on the relation between father and son; if the debt was not immoral or illegal, the sons' interest passes on the sale even though the father was not the Karta and the sons were not parties. (1954) SCR 177 : AIR 1953 SC 487. Why it matters. It shows the obligation does not depend on the father being Karta.

selfTest.q: 1. Which debts can sons not resist, according to Brij Narain , para 11?
selfTest.a: Debts not tainted with immorality.

selfTest.q: 2. Which provision limits the doctrine now?
selfTest.a: Section 6(4) of the Hindu Succession Act, 1956, as substituted in 2005.

selfTest.q: 3. Is a daughter liable?
selfTest.a: Yes. Vineeta Sharma (para 61) says Section 6(4) makes a daughter liable in the same manner as a son.

selfTest.q: 4. Can the father's creditor attach the son's self-acquired flat under the pious obligation?
selfTest.a: No. The liability is limited to the son's interest in the joint family property (Mulla, section 290(3)).

selfTest.q: 6. A father borrowed in 2003; his son was born in 2007. Can the creditor proceed against the son solely on pious obligation?
selfTest.a: No. The Explanation to Section 6(4) limits the saving to descendants born or adopted before 9 September 2005.

ప్రధాన నియమం. 2005 చట్టం అమల్లోకి వచ్చిన తర్వాత (9 సెప్టెంబర్ 2005), తండ్రి లేదా పూర్వీకుని అప్పు కోసం కేవలం పవిత్ర బాధ్యత ఆధారంగా రుణదాత కొడుకు, మనవడు, మునిమనవడిపై దావా వేయలేడు. నిబంధన (a). ఆ తేదీకి ముందు చేసిన అప్పు విషయంలో వంశస్థులపై రుణదాతకు పాత హక్కు ఉంటుంది. నిబంధన (b). అలాంటి పాత అప్పు కోసం, లేదా దాని చెల్లింపుగా చేసిన అమ్మకం లేదా తాకట్టు పాత నియమం కింద అమలవుతుంది. Explanation. క్లాజ్ (a) రక్షణ 9 సెప్టెంబర్ 2005 కు ముందు పుట్టిన లేదా దత్తత తీసుకున్న వంశస్థులకు మాత్రమే. ఈ మార్పు భవిష్యత్తుకు మాత్రమే (prospective) వర్తిస్తుంది: పాత అప్పులను తిరగదోడదు. సవరణకు ముందు చేసిన అప్పులకు నిబంధన రుణదాత హక్కును కాపాడుతుందని, సెక్షన్ 6 కింద హక్కులు, బాధ్యతలు రెండూ సవరణ ప్రారంభం నుంచే వస్తాయని Vineeta Sharma (para 61) చెబుతుంది.

ముల్లా (సెక్షన్ 290(1)) నియమాన్ని ఇలా చెబుతారు: "Where the sons are joint with their father, and debts have been contracted by the father for his own personal benefit, the sons are liable to pay the debts provided they were not incurred for an illegal or immoral purpose. The liability to pay the debts contracted by the father, though for his own benefit, arises from an obligation of religion and piety which is placed upon the sons under the Mitakshara law to discharge the father's debts, where the debts are not tainted with immorality." ముల్లాలో "sons" అంటే కొడుకు కొడుకులు, కొడుకు కొడుకు కొడుకులు కూడా. కాబట్టి పవిత్ర బాధ్యత అంటే తండ్రి, తాత, ముత్తాతల చట్టవిరుద్ధం లేదా అనైతికం కాని ( vyavaharika ) వ్యక్తిగత అప్పులను ఉమ్మడి కుటుంబ ఆస్తి నుంచి చెల్లించాల్సిన, మత కర్త వ్యం నుంచి పుట్టిన, కొడుకు, మనవడు, మునిమనవడి బాధ్యత. Brij Narain (para 12) దీన్ని "the obligation of the son to discharge his father's debts, based on the doctrine of pious duty" అంటుంది. Diagram 1 చూడండి. Diagram 1. పవిత్ర బాధ్యత ఆధారంగా కొడుకు, మనవడు లేదా మునిమనవడిపై రుణదాత క్లెయిమ్‌కు ఒక పరీక్ష. flowchart TD Q1{"అప్పు తండ్రి, తాత
లేదా ముత్తాతదా?"} Q1 -- "కాదు" --> X["సిద్ధాంతం వర్తించదు"] Q1 -- "అవును" --> Q2{"చట్టవిరుద్ధం, అనైతికం లేదా అవ్యవహారికమా?
(కొడుకు రుజువు చేయాలి)"} Q2 -- "అవును" --> N["కొడుకు బాధ్యుడు కాదు

క్లెయిమ్ లేదు (సె. 6(4))"] Q3 -- "అవును" --> Q4{"వంశస్థుడు 9.9.2005 కు ముందు
పుట్టాడా లేదా దత్తత తీసుకోబడ్డాడా?"} Q4 -- "కాదు" --> E["క్లాజ్ (a) అతనిపై క్లెయిమ్‌ను
కాపాడదు (Explanation)"] Q4 -- "అవును" --> L["ఉమ్మడి కుటుంబ ఆస్తిలో తన వాటా మేరకే
బాధ్యుడు; వ్యక్తిగతంగా కాదు
(ముల్లా సె. 290(3))"] వచన వివరణ అప్పు తండ్రి, తాత లేదా ముత్తాతదా? కాకపోతే సిద్ధాంతం వర్తించదు. అవును అయితే, అది చట్టవిరుద్ధ లేదా అనైతిక ప్రయోజనం కోసమా, లేదా అవ్యవహారికమా (కొడుకు రుజువు చేయాలి)? అవును అయితే కొడుకు బాధ్యుడు కాదు. కాకపోతే, 9 సెప్టెంబర్ 2005 కు ముందు చేసినదా? కాకపోతే కేవలం పవిత్ర బాధ్యతపై క్లెయిమ్ నిలవదు (సెక్షన్ 6(4)). అవును అయితే, వంశస్థుడు 9 సెప్టెంబర్ 2005 కు ముందు పుట్టాడా లేదా దత్తత తీసుకోబడ్డాడా? కాకపోతే నిబంధన క్లాజ్ (a) అతనిపై క్లెయిమ్‌ను కాపాడదు. అవును అయితే అతను బాధ్యుడు, కానీ ఉమ్మడి కుటుంబ ఆస్తిలో తన వాటా మేరకే; వ్యక్తిగతంగా కాదు.

selfTest.q: 1. Brij Narain , para 11 ప్రకారం కొడుకులు ఏ అప్పులను అడ్డుకోలేరు?
selfTest.a: అనైతికతతో కలుషితం కాని అప్పులు.

selfTest.q: 2. ఇప్పుడు ఈ సిద్ధాంతాన్ని ఏ నిబంధన పరిమితం చేస్తుంది?
selfTest.a: 2005 లో ప్రత్యామ్నాయంగా వచ్చిన హిందూ వారసత్వ చట్టం, 1956 సెక్షన్ 6(4).

selfTest.q: 3. కూతురు బాధ్యురాలా?
selfTest.a: అవును. సెక్షన్ 6(4) కూతురిని కొడుకు లాగే బాధ్యురాలిని చేస్తుందని Vineeta Sharma (para 61) చెబుతుంది.

selfTest.q: 4. పవిత్ర బాధ్యత కింద తండ్రి రుణదాత కొడుకు స్వార్జిత ఫ్లాట్‌ను జప్తు చేయగలడా?
selfTest.a: లేదు. బాధ్యత ఉమ్మడి కుటుంబ ఆస్తిలో కొడుకు వాటాకే పరిమితం (ముల్లా, సెక్షన్ 290(3)).

selfTest.q: 6. తండ్రి 2003 లో అప్పు తీసుకున్నాడు; కొడుకు 2007 లో పుట్టాడు. కేవలం పవిత్ర బాధ్యతపై రుణదాత కొడుకుపై చర్య తీసుకోగలడా?
selfTest.a: లేదు. సెక్షన్ 6(4) Explanation రక్షణను 9 సెప్టెంబర్ 2005 కు ముందు పుట్టిన లేదా దత్తత తీసుకున్న వంశస్థులకే పరిమితం చేస్తుంది.

family-law-i-u1-t9.subtitle: Severance of status, division by metes and bounds, who can claim, reopening and section 6

en.inOneMinute: Partition ends the joint holding of coparcenary property. It has two steps. First, a coparcener separates in status by a clear and unequivocal declaration of his intention to separate, made known to the others. This is severance of status . Later, the property is divided by metes and bounds into definite lots, by agreement, arbitration or a court decree. Only a coparcener can demand partition, and since 9 September 2005 a daughter has the same right and the same share as a son (Section 6(1); Vineeta Sharma , para 79). A declaration that never reaches the others does not sever status ( Addagada Raghavamma , 1963). A partition can be reopened for fraud or mistake, or on other permissible grounds ( Vineeta Sharma , para 125). For Section 6, "partition" means only a partition by a registered deed or by a decree of a court. A partition made before 20 December 2004 is saved (Section 6(5)). An oral partition is accepted only in exceptional cases, backed by public documents ( Vineeta Sharma , paras 127–129).
legalProvision: Section 6(1), Hindu Succession Act, 1956 (as substituted in 2005). On and from the commencement of the Hindu Succession (Amendment) Act, 2005 (39 of 2005), in a Joint Hindu family governed by the Mitakshara law, the daughter of a coparcener shall,― (a) by birth become a coparcener in her own right the same manner as the son; (b) have the same rights in the coparcenery property as she would have had if she had been a son; (c) be subject to the same liabilities in respect of the said coparcenery property as that of a son, and any reference to a Hindu Mitakshara coparcener shall be deemed to include a reference to a daughter of a coparcener: Provided that nothing contained in this sub-section shall affect or invalidate any disposition or alienation including any partition or testamentary disposition of property which had taken place before the 20th day of December, 2004. Section 6(2). Any property to which a female Hindu becomes entitled by virtue of sub-section (1) shall be held by her with the incidents of coparcenary ownership and shall be regarded, notwithstanding anything contained in this Act or any other law for the time being in force, as property capable of being disposed of by her by testamentary disposition. Section 6(3). Where a Hindu dies after the commencement of the Hindu Succession (Amendment) Act, 2005 (39 of 2005), his interest in the property of a Joint Hindu family governed by the Mitakshara law, shall devolve by testamentary or intestate succession, as the case may be, under this Act and not by survivorship, and the coparcenery property shall be deemed to have been divided as if a partition had taken place and,― (a) the daughter is allotted the same share as is allotted to a son; (b) the share of the pre-deceased son or a pre-deceased daughter, as they would have got had they been alive at the time of partition, shall be allotted to the surviving child of such pre-deceased son or of such pre-deceased daughter; and (c) the share of the pre-deceased child of a pre-deceased son or of a pre-deceased daughter, as such child would have got had he or she been alive at the time of the partition, shall be allotted to the child of such pre-deceased child of the pre-deceased son or a pre-deceased daughter, as the case may be. Explanation.―For the purposes of this sub-section, the interest of a Hindu Mitakshara coparcener shall be deemed to be the share in the property that would have been allotted to him if a partition of the property had taken place immediately before his death, irrespective of whether he was entitled to claim partition or not. Section 6(5). Nothing contained in this section shall apply to a partition, which has been effected before the 20th day of December, 2004. Explanation.―For the purposes of this section "partition" means any partition made by execution of a deed of partition duly registered under the Registration Act, 1908 (16 of 1908) or partition effected by a decree of a court.
In simple words

Section 6(1). A daughter is a coparcener by birth, with the same rights and liabilities as a son. So she can demand partition and takes a son's share. The proviso keeps alive any partition, sale, gift or will made before 20 December 2004. Section 6(2). What a daughter gets under Section 6(1) she holds as coparcenary property, and she can leave it by will. Section 6(3). When a coparcener dies after 9 September 2005, his interest does not pass to the others by survivorship . It passes by will or by intestate succession . To find his interest, the law assumes a partition just before his death; the daughter is counted like a son, and the share of a pre-deceased son or daughter goes to that person's children. Section 6(5) and Explanation. Section 6 does not disturb a partition effected before 20 December 2004. For Section 6, only a partition by a registered deed or by a court decree counts as a "partition".
en.meaning:
Mulla (section 322) gives the classical idea: "According to the true notion of an undivided Mitakshara family, no individual member of that family, whilst it remains undivided, can predicate of the joint property, that he—that particular member—has a certain definite share, one-third or one-fourth. Partition, according to that law, consists in a numerical division of the property; in other words, it consists in defining the shares of the coparceners in the joint property; an actual division of the property by metes and bounds is not necessary." Vineeta Sharma (para 93, quoting Shub Karan Bubna , (2009) 9 SCC 689) describes the result: "'Partition' is a redistribution or adjustment of pre-existing rights , among co-owners/coparceners, resulting in a division of lands or other properties jointly held by them into different lots or portions and delivery thereof to the respective allottees. The effect of such division is that the joint ownership is terminated and the respective shares vest in them in severalty." So partition has two senses that students often mix up: Severance of status. A change in legal relationship only: the member ceases to be a coparcener and becomes entitled to a definite share. "That is matter of individual volition" ( Mukund Dharman Bhoir , Privy Council, quoted in Vineeta Sharma , para 87). Division by metes and bounds. "The partition or division of the joint estate, comprising the allotment of shares, which may be effected by different methods" (same passage). See Diagram 1 . Diagram 1. Severance of status comes first; division by metes and bounds may follow much later. flowchart TD A["Coparcener declares a definite, unequivocal
intention to separate, or files a partition suit"] A --> Q{"Does it reach the other
coparceners or the manager?"} Q -- "No" --> N["No severance
(Addagada Raghavamma)"] Q -- "Yes" --> S["Step 1: Severance of status
from the date of declaration or suit
(cannot affect vested rights)"] S --> T["Member holds a definite share
as tenant-in-common"] T --> D["Step 2: Division by metes and bounds
by agreement, arbitration or decree"] D --> F["Complete on final decree
and delivery of possession"] Text description A coparcener makes a definite and unequivocal declaration of intention to separate, or files a suit for partition. The declaration reaches the other coparceners or the manager; if it never reaches them, there is no severance. Status is severed from the date of the declaration or the suit, but relation back cannot affect vested rights. The member now holds a definite share as a tenant-in-common. Later the property is divided by metes and bounds by agreement, arbitration or a court decree. The partition is complete when a final decree is passed and the allottees are put in possession.
keyPoints: Partition has two steps: severance of status, then division by metes and bounds. Severance needs a clear, unequivocal declaration made known to those affected; no deed and no assent are needed. Relation back cannot affect vested rights ( Addagada Raghavamma ). A suit for partition severs status from its filing; withdrawal before trial means no severance. Partition is complete only on a final decree and possession. Every coparcener, including a daughter since 2005, can demand partition ( Vineeta Sharma , para 79). On a coparcener's death after 2005, his interest passes by succession, not survivorship (Section 6(3)). For Section 6, partition means a registered deed or a court decree; partitions before 20 December 2004 are saved. A partition can be reopened for fraud or mistake, or on other permissible grounds (para 125).

caseLaws.name: Addagada Raghavamma v
caseLaws.facts: Addagada Chenchamma (1963) Facts. Chimpirayya, by a will dated 14 January 1945, left his properties to his grandson Subbarao and a granddaughter, and died on 5 May 1945. It was argued that the will declared him separate from the family, but it was not shown that Subbarao or his guardian knew its contents before he died. Principle. A member can separate by a definite and unequivocal declaration, but it "should reach the person or persons affected"; once known, it relates back to the date of the declaration, but relation back "cannot affect vested rights". On Chimpirayya's death "his interest devolved on Subbarao", and the appeal was dismissed. AIR 1964 SC 136 : (1964) 2 SCR 933. Why it matters. It is the leading case on communication of the intention to separate and the limits of relation back. Vineeta Sharma v. Rakesh Sharma (2020) Facts. A three-judge bench answered a reference on how the substituted Section 6 applies to daughters and to earlier partitions. Principle. A daughter is a coparcener with the same rights as a son, including the right to claim partition (para 79). Only a partition by a registered deed or a final court decree before 20 December 2004 is saved; an oral partition is accepted only in exceptional cases backed by public documents (paras 126–129). Why it matters. It fixes what counts as a partition after the 2005 amendment and collects the rules on severance of status (paras 79–98, 125). Gurupad Khandappa Magdum v. Hirabai Khandappa Magdum (1978) Facts. Khandappa died in 1960, leaving his widow Hirabai, two sons and three daughters. Hirabai sued for a 7/24 share in the joint family property. Principle. The notional partition in Explanation 1 to the old Section 6 must be given full effect: the widow's share is her 1/4 share at the notional partition plus 1/24 (her share in Khandappa's 1/4 interest among six heirs), that is 7/24. AIR 1978 SC 1239 : (1978) 3 SCC 383. Why it matters. It explains how the deemed partition on death worked under the old Section 6.

selfTest.q: 1. Does severance of status need a deed?
selfTest.a: No. A clear and unequivocal declaration made known to the others is enough.

selfTest.q: 2. Which case lays down the communication rule?
selfTest.a: Addagada Raghavamma v. Addagada Chenchamma (1963).

selfTest.q: 3. What does "partition" mean in the Explanation to Section 6(5)?
selfTest.a: A partition by a deed of partition registered under the Registration Act, 1908, or a partition effected by a decree of a court.

selfTest.q: 4. Is a partition complete when a preliminary decree is passed?
selfTest.a: No. It is complete only when a final decree is passed and the allottees are put in possession ( Vineeta Sharma , paras 90, 128).

selfTest.q: 5. Can a wife demand partition?
selfTest.a: No. But if a partition takes place between her husband and his sons, she takes a share equal to a son's, except in Southern India (Mulla, section 315).

selfTest.q: 6. Raghava Rao's property is worth ₹1,20,00,000. He, his two sons and his daughter divide it in 2010. What does each get?
selfTest.a: One-fourth each, ₹30,00,000 (Mulla, section 321; Section 6(1)(b)).

Partition, according to that law, consists in a numerical division of the property; in other words, it consists in defining the shares of the coparceners in the joint property; an actual division of the property by metes and bounds is not necessary." Vineeta Sharma (para 93, Shub Karan Bubna , (2009) 9 SCC 689 ను ఉటంకిస్తూ) ఫలితాన్ని ఇలా వివరిస్తుంది: "'Partition' is a redistribution or adjustment of pre-existing rights , among co-owners/coparceners, resulting in a division of lands or other properties jointly held by them into different lots or portions and delivery thereof to the respective allottees. The effect of such division is that the joint ownership is terminated and the respective shares vest in them in severalty." కాబట్టి విభజన కు విద్యార్థులు తరచూ కలిపేసే రెండు అర్థాలు ఉన్నాయి: స్థాయి విచ్ఛేదం. చట్టపరమైన సంబంధంలో మార్పు మాత్రమే: సభ్యుడు కోపార్సినర్‌గా ఉండటం ఆగిపోయి, నిర్దిష్ట వాటాకు హక్కుదారుడవుతాడు. "That is matter of individual volition" ( Mukund Dharman Bhoir , ప్రివీ కౌన్సిల్, Vineeta Sharma , para 87 లో ఉటంకించినది). హద్దుల ప్రకారం పంపకం. "The partition or division of the joint estate, comprising the allotment of shares, which may be effected by different methods" (అదే భాగం). Diagram 1 చూడండి. Diagram 1. మొదట స్థాయి విచ్ఛేదం; హద్దుల ప్రకారం పంపకం చాలా తర్వాత రావచ్చు. flowchart TD A["కోపార్సినర్ విడిపోవాలనే నిర్దిష్టమైన, సందేహం లేని
ఉద్దేశం ప్రకటిస్తాడు, లేదా విభజన దావా వేస్తాడు"] A --> Q{"అది ఇతర కోపార్సినర్లకు లేదా
నిర్వాహకునికి చేరిందా?"} Q -- "లేదు" --> N["విచ్ఛేదం లేదు
(Addagada Raghavamma)"] Q -- "అవును" --> S["దశ 1: ప్రకటన లేదా దావా తేదీ నుంచి
స్థాయి విచ్ఛేదం
(సంక్రమించిన హక్కులను తాకదు)"] S --> T["సభ్యుడు నిర్దిష్ట వాటాను
tenant-in-common గా కలిగి ఉంటాడు"] T --> D["దశ 2: ఒప్పందం, మధ్యవర్తిత్వం లేదా డిక్రీ ద్వారా
హద్దుల ప్రకారం పంపకం"] D --> F["తుది డిక్రీ, స్వాధీనంతో
పూర్తవుతుంది"] వచన వివరణ కోపార్సినర్ విడిపోవాలనే నిర్దిష్టమైన, సందేహం లేని ప్రకటన చేస్తాడు, లేదా విభజన దావా వేస్తాడు. ప్రకటన ఇతర కోపార్సినర్లకు లేదా నిర్వాహకునికి చేరుతుంది; ఎప్పటికీ చేరకపోతే విచ్ఛేదం లేదు. ప్రకటన లేదా దావా తేదీ నుంచి స్థాయి విచ్ఛేదమవుతుంది; కానీ వెనక్కి వర్తింపు ఇప్పటికే సంక్రమించిన హక్కులను తాకదు. ఇప్పుడు సభ్యుడు నిర్దిష్ట వాటాను tenant-in-common గా కలిగి ఉంటాడు. తర్వాత ఒప్పందం, మధ్యవర్తిత్వం లేదా కోర్టు డిక్రీ ద్వారా ఆస్తిని హద్దుల ప్రకారం పంచుతారు. తుది డిక్రీ వచ్చి వాటాదారులకు స్వాధీనం ఇచ్చినప్పుడు విభజన పూర్తవుతుంది.

selfTest.q: 1. స్థాయి విచ్ఛేదానికి దస్తావేజు అవసరమా?
selfTest.a: లేదు. ఇతరులకు తెలియజేసిన స్పష్టమైన, సందేహం లేని ప్రకటన చాలు.

selfTest.q: 2. తెలియజేయాలనే నియమాన్ని ఏ కేసు చెప్పింది?
selfTest.a: Addagada Raghavamma v. Addagada Chenchamma (1963).

selfTest.q: 3. సెక్షన్ 6(5) Explanation లో "partition" అంటే ఏమిటి?
selfTest.a: Registration Act, 1908 కింద రిజిస్టర్ చేసిన విభజన దస్తావేజు ద్వారా జరిగిన విభజన, లేదా కోర్టు డిక్రీ ద్వారా జరిగిన విభజన.

selfTest.q: 4. ప్రాథమిక డిక్రీ వచ్చినప్పుడే విభజన పూర్తవుతుందా?
selfTest.a: లేదు. తుది డిక్రీ వచ్చి, వాటాదారులకు స్వాధీనం ఇచ్చినప్పుడే పూర్తవుతుంది ( Vineeta Sharma , paras 90, 128).

selfTest.q: 5. భార్య విభజన కోరవచ్చా?
selfTest.a: లేదు. కానీ ఆమె భర్త, కొడుకుల మధ్య విభజన జరిగితే, దక్షిణ భారతదేశంలో తప్ప, ఆమెకు కొడుకుతో సమాన వాటా వస్తుంది (ముల్లా, సెక్షన్ 315).

selfTest.q: 6. రాఘవరావు ఆస్తి విలువ ₹1,20,00,000. అతను, అతని ఇద్దరు కొడుకులు, కూతురు 2010 లో పంచుకున్నారు. ఒక్కొక్కరికి ఎంత?

Under Section 2 of the Hindu Marriage Act, 1955, which of the following is NOT excluded from the application of Hindu law?

Under section 3(a) of the Hindu Marriage Act, a custom must be:

Explanation. Section 3(a) requires a custom to be ancient, certain and reasonable and not against public policy.

family-law-i-u1-t10.subtitle: Father's antecedent debts, the manager's power and a coparcener's own share

en.inOneMinute: Joint family property can be transferred so as to bind the family only by certain persons and on certain grounds. The manager ( Karta ) "cannot alienate or burden the estate qua manager except for purposes of necessity" ( Brij Narain v. Mangla Prasad , para 17); Mulla adds the benefit of the estate. A father has a further power. He may, by incurring a debt that is not for an immoral purpose, lay the estate open to execution, and a mortgage by him binds the estate if it is to discharge an antecedent debt (para 17). A buyer or lender from the manager must prove legal necessity, or that he made proper and honest inquiry. An alienation without necessity is voidable, not void. A coparcener cannot give away his undivided interest; whether he can sell it depends on the school. Since 1956 he can leave it by will (Section 30). Since 2005, Section 6(4) stops any claim against a son, grandson or great-grandson solely on the ground of pious obligation for debts contracted after 9 September 2005. The Hindu rule of damdupat limits the interest recoverable at one time to the amount of the principal, in the places where it applies.
legalProvision: Section 6(4), Hindu Succession Act, 1956 (as substituted in 2005). After the commencement of the Hindu Succession (Amendment) Act, 2005 (39 of 2005), no court shall recognise any right to proceed against a son, grandson or great-grandson for the recovery of any debt due from his father, grandfather or great-grandfather solely on the ground of the pious obligation under the Hindu law, of such son, grandson or great-grandson to discharge any such debt: Provided that in the case of any debt contracted before the commencement of the Hindu Succession (Amendment) Act, 2005 (39 of 2005), nothing contained in this sub-section shall affect― (a) the right of any creditor to proceed against the son, grandson or great-grandson, as the case may be; or (b) any alienation made in respect of or in satisfaction of, any such debt, and any such right or alienation shall be enforceable under the rule of pious obligation in the same manner and to the same extent as it would have been enforceable as if the Hindu Succession (Amendment) Act, 2005 (39 of 2005) had not been enacted. Explanation.―For the purposes of clause (a), the expression "son", "grandson" or "great-grandson" shall be deemed to refer to the son, grandson or great-grandson, as the case may be, who was born or adopted prior to the commencement of the Hindu Succession (Amendment) Act, 2005 (39 of 2005). Section 6(1), proviso. Provided that nothing contained in this sub-section shall affect or invalidate any disposition or alienation including any partition or testamentary disposition of property which had taken place before the 20th day of December, 2004. Section 30, Explanation. The interest of a male Hindu in a Mitakshara coparcenary property or the interest of a member of a tarwad, tavazhi, illom, kutumba or kavaru in the property of the tarwad, tavazhi, illom, kutumba or kavaru shall, notwithstanding anything contained in this Act or in any other law for the time being in force, be deemed to be property capable of being disposed of by him or by her within the meaning of this section.
In simple words

Section 6(4). For a debt contracted after 9 September 2005, a creditor cannot proceed against the son, grandson or great-grandson merely because of the pious obligation . For an earlier debt, the creditor's old right against descendants born or adopted before that date, and any alienation made for that debt, are saved. Vineeta Sharma (para 61) adds that Section 6(4) makes a daughter liable in the same manner as a son. Section 6(1), proviso . A sale, gift, mortgage , partition or will made before 20 December 2004 is not upset by the daughter's new right. Section 30, Explanation. A coparcener can leave his undivided interest by will. The rest of this topic is judge-made Mitakshara law, as stated by the Privy Council in Brij Narain and by Mulla.
en.meaning:
Alienation is a transfer of property by sale, mortgage, gift or a similar act. Joint family property may be alienated in two ways: by a person with power to bind the whole family property, or by a coparcener dealing only with his own undivided interest. Mulla (section 255) lists who alone can alienate coparcenary property "so as to pass a good title to the alienee": (1) the whole body of coparceners, where they are all adults; (2) the manager, to the extent mentioned in § 242; (3) the father, to the extent mentioned in § 256; (4) a sole surviving coparcener in the circumstances mentioned in § 257. "No other coparcener is entitled to alienate coparcenary property so as to bind the other coparceners unless he is authorized by them to do so" (section 255). An antecedent debt is a debt of the father that is "antecedent in fact as well as in time, that is to say, that the debt must be truly independent and not part of he transaction impeached" ( Brij Narain , para 17(4)). See Diagram 1 . Diagram 1. A test for any sale or mortgage of the whole joint family property. flowchart TD Q1{"By all coparceners (all adults)

or benefit of the estate, proved by
