(Mulla ss. 242-244)"] Q2 -- "No" --> Q3{"By the father, to pay his own
antecedent debt, not immoral
or illegal?"} Q3 -- "No" --> V["Voidable at the option of the others;
binds alienor's own interest where
the school allows (ss. 242(4), 268)"] Q3 -- "Yes" --> Q4{"Debt contracted before
9.9.2005?"} Q4 -- "Yes" --> S["Binds the sons' interest
(Brij Narain; s. 6(4) proviso (b))"] Q4 -- "No" --> X["Section 6(4): pious obligation alone
cannot bind the sons' interest"] Text description Was it made by all the coparceners, all being adults, or by a sole surviving coparcener? If yes, it binds. If no, was it made by the manager for legal necessity or the benefit of the estate, with necessity or proper inquiry proved by the alienee? If yes, it binds adults and minors. If no, was it made by the father to pay his own antecedent debt, not immoral or illegal? If no, it is voidable at the option of the other coparceners and binds only the alienor's own interest where the school allows. If yes, was the debt contracted before 9 September 2005? If yes, it binds the sons' interest. If no, Section 6(4) applies and pious obligation alone cannot bind the sons' interest.
keyPoints: Only all adult coparceners, the manager, the father and a sole surviving coparcener can alienate so as to bind the family (Mulla, section 255). The manager may alienate only for legal necessity or benefit of the estate ( Brij Narain , para 17(1); Mulla, section 242). The buyer or lender must prove necessity or proper honest inquiry; he need not see to the use of the money (section 244). An alienation without necessity is voidable, not void (section 242(4)). The father may bind the estate for his own antecedent, non-immoral debt; antecedent means in time and in fact ( Brij Narain , para 17). Section 6(4) ends pious obligation as the sole ground for debts after 9 September 2005. A gift of an undivided interest is void; a sale for value is allowed in Bombay, Madras and Madhya Pradesh (sections 258–260). Damdupat: interest recoverable at one time cannot exceed the principal (section 596).

caseLaws.name: Brij Narain v
caseLaws.facts: Mangla Prasad (1923) Facts. In 1908 Sita Ram, manager of a joint family with his two minor sons, mortgaged ancestral property for Rs. 11,000 to pay off two earlier mortgages of 1905 and 1907. The sons, through their mother, sued to have it declared not binding on them. Principle. The five propositions in para 17: the manager binds the estate only for necessity; a father may lay it open to execution for a non-immoral debt; his mortgage binds only if it discharges an antecedent debt, antecedent in time and in fact; and it makes no difference whether he is alive or dead. The older mortgages were antecedent debts, so the 1908 mortgage bound the estate and the appeal was allowed (paras 18–19). Privy Council, (1924) 26 Bom LR 500 : (1924) 51 IA 129. Why it matters. It is the leading statement of the father's power over joint family property for his own debts. Hunoomanpersaud Panday v. Mussumat Babooee Munraj Koonweree (1856) Facts. A mother, managing her minor son's estate, mortgaged it (as described in Mulla, section 242). Principle. The manager's power "can only be exercised rightly in a case of need, or for the benefit of the estate"; a lender must inquire, and if he acts honestly after inquiry, the actual existence of the necessity is not a condition of his charge (quoted in Mulla, section 242). (1856) 6 Moo IA 393. Why it matters. It is the source of the "need or benefit of the estate" test and of the alienee's duty to inquire. Vineeta Sharma v. Rakesh Sharma (2020) Facts. A three-judge bench answered a reference on how the substituted Section 6 applies to daughters. Principle. Without partition only an undivided share can be sold, not specific property, and whether consent is needed depends on the school (para 81). Once a share is determined it can be sold or mortgaged as separate property (para 80). Section 6(4) makes a daughter liable in the same manner as a son (para 61). Why it matters. It states the limits on a coparcener's alienation and on debt liability after 2005.

selfTest.q: 1. What does "antecedent" mean in antecedent debt?
selfTest.a: Antecedent in fact as well as in time: truly independent and not part of the transaction challenged ( Brij Narain , para 17(4)).

selfTest.q: 2. What is the test for the father's power to expose the estate to execution?
selfTest.a: The debt must not be for an immoral purpose ( Brij Narain , para 17(2)).

selfTest.q: 3. When does a mortgage by a father bind his sons' interest?
selfTest.a: When it is to discharge an antecedent debt of his that was not for an immoral or illegal purpose ( Brij Narain , para 17(3); Mulla, section 256). For debts after 9 September 2005, see Section 6(4).

selfTest.q: 4. When does a sale by a Karta who is not the father bind the family?
selfTest.a: When it is for legal necessity or for the benefit of the estate (Mulla, sections 242, 243, 243A).

selfTest.q: 5. Who must prove legal necessity?
selfTest.a: The buyer or mortgagee, who must prove necessity in fact or proper and honest inquiry (Mulla, section 244).

selfTest.q: 6. A lent ₹1,000 and interest has run to ₹1,200. Where damdupat applies, how much interest can A recover in a suit?
selfTest.a: The amount of the principal, ₹1,000 (Mulla, section 596).

legalProvision: Section 6(4), Hindu Succession Act, 1956 (as substituted in 2005). After the commencement of the Hindu Succession (Amendment) Act, 2005 (39 of 2005), no court shall recognise any right to proceed against a son, grandson or great-grandson for the recovery of any debt due from his father, grandfather or great-grandfather solely on the ground of the pious obligation under the Hindu law, of such son, grandson or great-grandson to discharge any such debt: Provided that in the case of any debt contracted before the commencement of the Hindu Succession (Amendment) Act, 2005 (39 of 2005), nothing contained in this sub-section shall affect― (a) the right of any creditor to proceed against the son, grandson or great-grandson, as the case may be; or (b) any alienation made in respect of or in satisfaction of, any such debt, and any such right or alienation shall be enforceable under the rule of pious obligation in the same manner and to the same extent as it would have been enforceable as if the Hindu Succession (Amendment) Act, 2005 (39 of 2005) had not been enacted. Explanation.―For the purposes of clause (a), the expression "son", "grandson" or "great-grandson" shall be deemed to refer to the son, grandson or great-grandson, as the case may be, who was born or adopted prior to the commencement of the Hindu Succession (Amendment) Act, 2005 (39 of 2005). Section 6(1), proviso. Provided that nothing contained in this sub-section shall affect or invalidate any disposition or alienation including any partition or testamentary disposition of property which had taken place before the 20th day of December, 2004. Section 30, Explanation. The interest of a male Hindu in a Mitakshara coparcenary property or the interest of a member of a tarwad, tavazhi, illom, kutumba or kavaru in the property of the tarwad, tavazhi, illom, kutumba or kavaru shall, notwithstanding anything contained in this Act or in any other law for the time being in force, be deemed to be property capable of being disposed of by him or by her within the meaning of this section.

సెక్షన్ 6(4). 9 సెప్టెంబర్ 2005 తర్వాత చేసిన అప్పు కోసం కేవలం పవిత్ర బాధ్యత కారణంగా రుణదాత కొడుకు, మనవడు, మునిమనవడిపై చర్య తీసుకోలేడు. అంతకు ముందటి అప్పుకు, ఆ తేదీకి ముందు పుట్టిన లేదా దత్తత తీసుకున్న వంశస్థులపై రుణదాత పాత హక్కు, ఆ అప్పు కోసం చేసిన అన్యాక్రాంతం కాపాడబడతాయి. సెక్షన్ 6(4) కూతురిని కొడుకు లాగే బాధ్యురాలిని చేస్తుందని Vineeta Sharma (para 61) జోడిస్తుంది. సెక్షన్ 6(1) నిబంధన. 20 డిసెంబర్ 2004 కు ముందు జరిగిన అమ్మకం, బహుమతి, తాకట్టు, విభజన లేదా వీలునామా ను కూతురి కొత్త హక్కు తిరగదోడదు. సెక్షన్ 30 Explanation. కోపార్సినర్ తన అవిభక్త హక్కును వీలునామా ద్వారా ఇవ్వవచ్చు. ఈ అంశంలో మిగిలినదంతా Brij Narain లో ప్రివీ కౌన్సిల్, ముల్లా చెప్పిన న్యాయమూర్తులు రూపొందించిన మితాక్షర చట్టం.

అన్యాక్రాంతం (alienation) అంటే అమ్మకం, తాకట్టు, బహుమతి లేదా అలాంటి చర్య ద్వారా ఆస్తి బదిలీ. ఉమ్మడి కుటుంబ ఆస్తిని రెండు విధాలుగా అన్యాక్రాంతం చేయవచ్చు: మొత్తం కుటుంబ ఆస్తిని బంధించే అధికారం ఉన్న వ్యక్తి ద్వారా, లేదా తన అవిభక్త హక్కుతో మాత్రమే వ్యవహరించే కోపార్సినర్ ద్వారా. కోపార్సినరీ ఆస్తిని "so as to pass a good title to the alienee" అన్యాక్రాంతం చేయగలవారిని ముల్లా (సెక్షన్ 255) ఇలా జాబితా చేస్తారు: (1) the whole body of coparceners, where they are all adults; (2) the manager, to the extent mentioned in § 242; (3) the father, to the extent mentioned in § 256; (4) a sole surviving coparcener in the circumstances mentioned in § 257. "No other coparcener is entitled to alienate coparcenary property so as to bind the other coparceners unless he is authorized by them to do so" (సెక్షన్ 255). పూర్వపు అప్పు అంటే "antecedent in fact as well as in time, that is to say, that the debt must be truly independent and not part of he transaction impeached" అయిన తండ్రి అప్పు ( Brij Narain , para 17(4)). selfTest.q: 1. పూర్వపు అప్పులో "antecedent" అంటే ఏమిటి?
selfTest.a: సమయంలోనూ, వాస్తవంలోనూ ముందుది: నిజంగా స్వతంత్రమైనది, సవాలు చేసిన లావాదేవీలో భాగం కానిది ( Brij Narain , para 17(4)).

selfTest.q: 2. ఎస్టేట్‌ను డిక్రీ అమలుకు గురిచేసే తండ్రి అధికారానికి పరీక్ష ఏమిటి?
selfTest.a: అప్పు అనైతిక ప్రయోజనం కోసం కాకూడదు ( Brij Narain , para 17(2)).

selfTest.q: 3. తండ్రి తాకట్టు కొడుకుల హక్కును ఎప్పుడు బంధిస్తుంది?
selfTest.a: అనైతిక లేదా చట్టవిరుద్ధ ప్రయోజనం కోసం కాని అతని పూర్వపు అప్పు తీర్చడానికైతే ( Brij Narain , para 17(3); ముల్లా, సెక్షన్ 256). 9 సెప్టెంబర్ 2005 తర్వాతి అప్పులకు సెక్షన్ 6(4) చూడండి.

selfTest.q: 4. తండ్రి కాని కర్త చేసిన అమ్మకం కుటుంబాన్ని ఎప్పుడు బంధిస్తుంది?

In Surjit Lal Chhabda v. CIT (1975), the Supreme Court held that a joint Hindu family:

Explanation. The Court held a joint Hindu family is a status that can exist even with just one male member, his wife, and unmarried daughter — no property or additional coparcener required.

According to State Bank of India v. Ghamandi Ram (1969), a Mitakshara coparcenary is best described as:

Explanation. The Supreme Court described a Mitakshara coparcenary as 'a creature of law' — it cannot be created by agreement between family members.

Explanation. Coparcenary is a creature of law, not agreement — there is no requirement of any written partnership-style deed.

en.meaning:
Which of these correctly describes 'severance of status' in Hindu law?

Explanation. Severance of status is a change in legal relationship only — it needs no physical division of property at all.

In Addagada Raghavamma v. Addagada Chenchamma (1964), the Supreme Court held that severance of status requires:

Explanation. The Court held severance requires a clear, unequivocal declaration of intent to separate, which must be communicated to the other affected coparceners.

'Division by metes and bounds' refers to:

Explanation. Division by metes and bounds is the actual, physical division of property into specific, individual shares — the second stage of partition.

Which of the following can demand partition since the Hindu Succession (Amendment) Act, 2005?

Explanation. A father may, by incurring such a debt, expose the family estate to execution proceedings on a decree for that debt — one of Lord Dunedin's five propositions.

family-law-i-u1-t7.subtitle: Management, debts and alienation of joint family property, with Brij Narain

en.inOneMinute: The Karta manages the joint family and its property. His powers are wide in day-to-day matters: he controls income and spending, runs the family business, contracts debts for family purposes, makes contracts, gives receipts, compromises and refers disputes to arbitration, and sues and is sued for the family. His power to sell or mortgage family property is limited. The Privy Council in Brij Narain v. Mangla Prasad (1923) held that a managing coparcener "cannot alienate or burden the estate qua manager except for purposes of necessity". Mulla adds a second ground: benefit of the estate. An alienation outside these grounds is voidable at the option of the other coparceners. A father who is Karta has an extra power. He may, by a debt not incurred for an immoral purpose, lay the estate open to execution for that debt. A mortgage binds the estate only if it pays off an antecedent debt , antecedent "in fact as well as in time". His functions are the duties that go with the office: maintaining the members, meeting marriage and ceremony expenses, keeping the property, and accounting when the family divides. Exams ask for the Brij Narain propositions, the meaning of legal necessity , and the father's special power.
legalProvision: The Karta 's powers are not in an Act. They come from Mitakshara law and court decisions. Three provisions of the Hindu Succession Act, 1956 bear on them.

Section 6(1), proviso (as substituted in 2005). Provided that nothing contained in this sub-section shall affect or invalidate any disposition or alienation including any partition or testamentary disposition of property which had taken place before the 20th day of December, 2004.

Section 6(4). After the commencement of the Hindu Succession (Amendment) Act, 2005 (39 of 2005), no court shall recognise any right to proceed against a son, grandson or great-grandson for the recovery of any debt due from his father, grandfather or great-grandfather solely on the ground of the pious obligation under the Hindu law, of such son, grandson or great-grandson to discharge any such debt: Provided that in the case of any debt contracted before the commencement of the Hindu Succession (Amendment) Act, 2005 (39 of 2005), nothing contained in this sub-section shall affect― (a) the right of any creditor to proceed against the son, grandson or great-grandson, as the case may be; or (b) any alienation made in respect of or in satisfaction of, any such debt, and any such right or alienation shall be enforceable under the rule of pious obligation in the same manner and to the same extent as it would have been enforceable as if the Hindu Succession (Amendment) Act, 2005 (39 of 2005) had not been enacted. Explanation.―For the purposes of clause (a), the expression "son", "grandson" or "great-grandson" shall be deemed to refer to the son, grandson or great-grandson, as the case may be, who was born or adopted prior to the commencement of the Hindu Succession (Amendment) Act, 2005 (39 of 2005).

Section 30, Explanation. The interest of a male Hindu in a Mitakshara coparcenary property or the interest of a member of a tarwad, tavazhi, illom, kutumba or kavaru in the property of the tarwad, tavazhi, illom, kutumba or kavaru shall, notwithstanding anything contained in this Act or in any other law for the time being in force, be deemed to be property capable of being disposed of by him or by her within the meaning of this section.
In simple words

Section 6(1) makes a daughter a coparcener by birth, so she can be Karta and exercise all the powers in this note ( Sujata Sharma v. Manu Gupta , Delhi High Court, 2015). The proviso to Section 6(1) protects any sale, mortgage, gift, partition or will made before 20 December 2004. A Karta's earlier valid alienation therefore stands against a daughter's claim. Section 6(4) ends the pious obligation for debts taken after 9 September 2005 (the commencement of the 2005 Act). For debts taken before that date, a creditor's rights against sons, grandsons and great-grandsons born or adopted before that date are saved. Vineeta Sharma (para 61) adds that a daughter is equally bound by the pious obligation in the same way as a son. The Section 30 Explanation lets a coparcener dispose of his own undivided interest by will. That is a power of every coparcener over his own interest, not a power of the Karta over the whole property.
en.meaning:
The Karta's powers are the legal capacities that let him act for the joint family as its manager and bind the other members. His functions are the duties that come with the office. Two ideas fix the limits. First, no coparcener can claim a precise share while the property is undivided, because the interest "is fluctuating" and "increases and diminishes by death and birth in the family" ( Vineeta Sharma , para 26). So the Karta, too, holds no separate share he can deal with as his own. Second, one of the incidents of a coparcenary is "that there can be no alienation of the property without the concurrence of the other coparceners unless it be for legal necessity " ( Vineeta Sharma , para 30, quoting Controller of Estate Duty v. Alladi Kuppuswamy on Ghamandi Ram ). Mulla (section 236) puts it this way: the manager has no larger interest than any other member; "The only respect in which he has a superior right is that he has a power of disposition for causes recognised as just and proper under Hindu law of the whole family property, including the interest of the junior members." See Diagram 1 . Diagram 1. A test for any sale or mortgage of joint family property by the Karta. flowchart TD Q1{"For legal necessity or
benefit of the estate?"} Q1 -- "Yes" --> A["Binds all coparceners,
adults and minors"] Q1 -- "No" --> Q2{"All other coparceners
adults and consented?"} Q2 -- "Yes" --> B["Valid in its entirety"] Q2 -- "No" --> Q3{"Karta is the father, and mortgage
pays his antecedent debt
not for an immoral purpose?"} Q3 -- "Yes" --> C["Binds the sons' interests
(Brij Narain; s. 6(4) for debts
after 9.9.2005)"] Q3 -- "No" --> D["Voidable at the option of
the other coparceners"] Text description Was it for legal necessity or for the benefit of the estate? If yes, it binds all coparceners, adults and minors. If no, did all the other coparceners, all adults, consent? If yes, it is valid in its entirety. If no, is the Karta the father, and was it a mortgage to discharge his antecedent debt not for an immoral purpose? If yes, it binds the sons' interests (debts after 9 September 2005 cannot be recovered from sons solely on pious obligation). If no, it is voidable at the option of the other coparceners.
keyPoints: The Karta manages the family and represents it ( Tribhovandas ). He controls income; members who dislike his spending can only seek partition (Mulla s. 237). His debts for family purposes bind the family property, not other members' separate property (Mulla s. 240). He may contract, give receipts, compromise, refer to arbitration and give discharges, but cannot give up a family debt (Mulla ss. 241–250). He cannot alienate or burden the estate except for necessity ( Brij Narain , para 17) or benefit of the estate (Mulla s. 242); otherwise the alienation is voidable. A father may lay the estate open to execution for his debt not for an immoral purpose; a mortgage binds only for an antecedent debt, antecedent in fact as well as in time. Section 6(4): no recovery from sons solely on pious obligation for debts after 9 September 2005. A sole surviving coparcener may dispose of the property; the alienation stands after a son's birth ( Vineeta Sharma , para 28).

caseLaws.name: Brij Narain v
caseLaws.facts: Mangla Prasad (1923) Facts. In 1908 Sita Ram, manager of a joint family with his two minor sons, mortgaged ancestral property for Rs. 11,000 to repay two earlier mortgages. The sons, through their mother, sued to have it declared not binding on them. Principle. A managing coparcener cannot burden the estate except for necessity; a father may lay the estate open to execution for his non-immoral debt; a mortgage binds only if it discharges an antecedent debt (para 17). The earlier mortgages were antecedent debts, so the mortgage bound the estate and the mortgagee 's appeal was allowed (paras 18–19). Privy Council, (1924) 26 Bom LR 500. Why it matters. It states the limits on a manager's power and the father's special power. Hunoomanpersaud Panday v. Mussumat Babooee Munraj Koonweree (1856) Facts. A mother, as manager of her minor son's estate, mortgaged it (as described in Mulla, section 242). Principle. The power to charge an estate not one's own "can only be exercised rightly in a case of need, or for the benefit of the estate"; a lender who inquires and acts honestly is protected. (1856) 6 Moo IA 393. Why it matters. Mulla treats it as the leading case on alienation for necessity, and a Karta's power is analogous. Vineeta Sharma v. Rakesh Sharma (2020) Facts. A three-judge bench heard a reference on how the substituted Section 6 applies to daughters. Principle. No coparcener can claim a precise share (para 26); a sole coparcener may dispose of the property (para 28); no alienation without the concurrence of the coparceners unless for legal necessity (para 30); a daughter is bound by the pious obligation like a son (para 61). Why it matters. It shows the Karta's power as an exception to joint ownership. Sujata Sharma v. Manu Gupta (2015) Facts. The eldest coparcener of a Hindu undivided family, a woman, claimed to be its Karta. Principle. The Delhi High Court held that she could be Karta (para 27). The powers in this note belong to her as to any Karta. Why it matters. Women Kartas now exercise the same powers.

selfTest.q: 1. On what grounds can a Karta alienate joint family property?
selfTest.a: For legal necessity or for the benefit of the estate ( Brij Narain , para 17; Mulla, section 242).

selfTest.q: 2. When does a mortgage by a father bind the estate?
selfTest.a: Only if it discharges an antecedent debt ( Brij Narain , para 17(3)).

selfTest.q: 3. What does "antecedent" mean?
selfTest.a: Antecedent in fact as well as in time: the debt must be truly independent and not part of the transaction challenged ( Brij Narain , para 17(4)).

selfTest.q: 4. Is an alienation without legal necessity void?
selfTest.a: No. It is voidable at the option of the other coparceners; a creditor cannot repudiate it (Mulla, section 242(4)).

selfTest.q: 5. Can the bank that lent to the Karta for the family business reach the separate property of another coparcener?
selfTest.a: No, unless that coparcener was a party to the loan or later ratified it. It can reach the family property, including that member's share in it (Mulla, section 240).

selfTest.q: 6. Can a Karta write off a debt owed to the family?
selfTest.a: No. He has no power to give up a debt due to the joint family (Mulla, section 250), though he may compromise it bona fide for the family's benefit (section 248).

legalProvision: కర్త అధికారాలు ఏ చట్టంలోనూ లేవు. అవి మితాక్షర చట్టం, కోర్టు తీర్పుల నుంచి వస్తాయి. హిందూ వారసత్వ చట్టం, 1956 లోని మూడు నిబంధనలు వీటిని తాకుతాయి.

Section 6(1), proviso (as substituted in 2005). Provided that nothing contained in this sub-section shall affect or invalidate any disposition or alienation including any partition or testamentary disposition of property which had taken place before the 20th day of December, 2004.

Section 6(4). After the commencement of the Hindu Succession (Amendment) Act, 2005 (39 of 2005), no court shall recognise any right to proceed against a son, grandson or great-grandson for the recovery of any debt due from his father, grandfather or great-grandfather solely on the ground of the pious obligation under the Hindu law, of such son, grandson or great-grandson to discharge any such debt: Provided that in the case of any debt contracted before the commencement of the Hindu Succession (Amendment) Act, 2005 (39 of 2005), nothing contained in this sub-section shall affect― (a) the right of any creditor to proceed against the son, grandson or great-grandson, as the case may be; or (b) any alienation made in respect of or in satisfaction of, any such debt, and any such right or alienation shall be enforceable under the rule of pious obligation in the same manner and to the same extent as it would have been enforceable as if the Hindu Succession (Amendment) Act, 2005 (39 of 2005) had not been enacted. Explanation.―For the purposes of clause (a), the expression "son", "grandson" or "great-grandson" shall be deemed to refer to the son, grandson or great-grandson, as the case may be, who was born or adopted prior to the commencement of the Hindu Succession (Amendment) Act, 2005 (39 of 2005).

Section 30, Explanation. The interest of a male Hindu in a Mitakshara coparcenary property or the interest of a member of a tarwad, tavazhi, illom, kutumba or kavaru in the property of the tarwad, tavazhi, illom, kutumba or kavaru shall, notwithstanding anything contained in this Act or in any other law for the time being in force, be deemed to be property capable of being disposed of by him or by her within the meaning of this section.

సెక్షన్ 6(1) కూతురిని పుట్టుకతో కోపార్సినర్ ‌గా చేస్తుంది; కాబట్టి ఆమె కర్త కాగలదు, ఈ నోట్‌లోని అన్ని అధికారాలనూ వినియోగించగలదు ( Sujata Sharma v. Manu Gupta , ఢిల్లీ హైకోర్టు, 2015). 20 డిసెంబర్ 2004 కు ముందు జరిగిన అమ్మకం, తాకట్టు, దానం, విభజన , వీలునామా లను సెక్షన్ 6(1) నిబంధన ( proviso ) కాపాడుతుంది. కాబట్టి కర్త అంతకుముందు చేసిన చెల్లుబాటయ్యే అన్యాక్రాంతం కూతురి క్లెయిమ్‌కు వ్యతిరేకంగా నిలుస్తుంది. 9 సెప్టెంబర్ 2005 (2005 చట్టం అమల్లోకి వచ్చిన తేదీ) తర్వాత చేసిన అప్పులకు సెక్షన్ 6(4) పవిత్ర బాధ్యత (pious obligation) ను ముగిస్తుంది. ఆ తేదీకి ముందు చేసిన అప్పుల విషయంలో, ఆ తేదీకి ముందు పుట్టిన లేదా దత్తత తీసుకున్న కొడుకులు, మనవళ్లు, మునిమనవళ్లపై రుణదాత హక్కులు కాపాడబడ్డాయి. కూతురు కూడా కొడుకు లాగే పవిత్ర బాధ్యతకు బద్ధురాలని Vineeta Sharma (para 61) చెబుతుంది. సెక్షన్ 30 Explanation ప్రకారం కోపార్సినర్ తన అవిభక్త వాటాను వీలునామా ద్వారా ఇవ్వవచ్చు. అది ప్రతి కోపార్సినర్‌కు తన వాటాపై ఉన్న అధికారం; మొత్తం ఆస్తిపై కర్త అధికారం కాదు.
te.meaning:
కర్త అధికారాలు అంటే నిర్వాహకుడిగా కుటుంబం తరఫున వ్యవహరించి ఇతర సభ్యులను బంధించడానికి అతనికి ఉన్న చట్టపరమైన సామర్థ్యాలు. అతని విధులు అంటే ఆ పదవితో వచ్చే బాధ్యతలు. రెండు ఆలోచనలు పరిమితులను నిర్ణయిస్తాయి. మొదటిది, ఆస్తి అవిభక్తంగా ఉన్నంతకాలం ఏ కోపార్సినరూ ఖచ్చితమైన వాటాను చెప్పలేడు; ఎందుకంటే హక్కు "is fluctuating", "increases and diminishes by death and birth in the family" ( Vineeta Sharma , para 26). కాబట్టి కర్తకు కూడా తన సొంతంగా వ్యవహరించగల ప్రత్యేక వాటా ఉండదు. రెండోది, కోపార్సినరీ లక్షణాల్లో ఒకటి "that there can be no alienation of the property without the concurrence of the other coparceners unless it be for legal necessity " ( Vineeta Sharma , para 30, Ghamandi Ram పై Controller of Estate Duty v. Alladi Kuppuswamy విశ్లేషణను ఉటంకిస్తూ). ముల్లా (సెక్షన్ 236) ఇలా చెబుతారు: నిర్వాహకుడికి ఇతర సభ్యుల కంటే ఎక్కువ హక్కు లేదు; "The only respect in which he has a superior right is that he has a power of disposition for causes recognised as just and proper under Hindu law of the whole family property, including the interest of the junior members." Diagram 1 చూడండి. Diagram 1. కర్త చేసిన ఉమ్మడి కుటుంబ ఆస్తి అమ్మకం లేదా తాకట్టుకు ఒక పరీక్ష. flowchart TD Q1{"చట్టబద్ధమైన అవసరం లేదా

అప్పులకు సె. 6(4))"] Q3 -- "కాదు" --> D["ఇతర కోపార్సినర్ల ఇష్టం మేరకు
రద్దు చేయదగినది"] వచన వివరణ అది చట్టబద్ధమైన అవసరం లేదా ఎస్టేట్ ప్రయోజనం కోసమా? అవును అయితే వయోజన, మైనర్ కోపార్సినర్లందరినీ బంధిస్తుంది. కాకపోతే, ఇతర కోపార్సినర్లందరూ వయోజనులై అంగీకరించారా? అవును అయితే పూర్తిగా చెల్లుతుంది. కాకపోతే, కర్త తండ్రా, అనైతికం కాని అతని పూర్వపు అప్పు తీర్చడానికి తాకట్టా? అవును అయితే కొడుకుల వాటాలను బంధిస్తుంది (9 సెప్టెంబర్ 2005 తర్వాత అప్పులను కేవలం పవిత్ర బాధ్యతపై కొడుకుల నుంచి వసూలు చేయలేరు). కాకపోతే ఇతర కోపార్సినర్ల ఇష్టం మేరకు రద్దు చేయదగినది.

selfTest.q: 1. కర్త ఏ కారణాలపై ఉమ్మడి కుటుంబ ఆస్తిని అన్యాక్రాంతం చేయవచ్చు?
selfTest.a: చట్టబద్ధమైన అవసరం లేదా ఎస్టేట్ ప్రయోజనం కోసం ( Brij Narain , para 17; ముల్లా, సెక్షన్ 242).

selfTest.q: 2. తండ్రి చేసిన తాకట్టు ఎస్టేట్‌ను ఎప్పుడు బంధిస్తుంది?
selfTest.a: పూర్వపు అప్పు తీర్చడానికి అయితేనే ( Brij Narain , para 17(3)).

selfTest.q: 3. "Antecedent" అంటే ఏమిటి?
selfTest.a: సమయంలోనూ, వాస్తవంలోనూ ముందుది: అప్పు నిజంగా స్వతంత్రమైనదై, సవాలు చేసిన లావాదేవీలో భాగం కాకూడదు ( Brij Narain , para 17(4)).

selfTest.q: 4. చట్టబద్ధమైన అవసరం లేని అన్యాక్రాంతం శూన్యమా?
selfTest.a: కాదు. అది ఇతర కోపార్సినర్ల ఇష్టం మేరకు రద్దు చేయదగినది; రుణదాత తిరస్కరించలేడు (ముల్లా, సెక్షన్ 242(4)).

selfTest.q: 5. కుటుంబ వ్యాపారం కోసం కర్తకు అప్పు ఇచ్చిన బ్యాంకు మరో కోపార్సినర్ ప్రత్యేక ఆస్తిని చేరుకోగలదా?

family-law-i-u1-t5.subtitle: Joint Hindu family, coparcenary, ancestral and blended property, and separate property

en.inOneMinute: A joint Hindu family is a wide group of relatives descended from a common ancestor, with their wives and unmarried daughters. Membership is a status that comes by birth, marriage or adoption. The family need not own any property. A coparcenary is a smaller body inside it. Its members, the coparceners , get an interest in the ancestral property by birth and can demand partition. Traditionally it was the holder of the property and three generations of male descendants; since 2005 daughters are coparceners too. Joint family property and coparcenary property mean the same thing: ancestral property, property bought with joint funds, and separate property thrown into the common stock. A member's own earnings are self-acquired property and stay separate. Exams ask you to keep these ideas apart, to list the incidents of a coparcenary ( Ghamandi Ram ), to explain blending ( Surjit Lal Chhabda ), and to say what changed after 1956 ( Chander Sen ) and 2005 ( Vineeta Sharma ).
legalProvision: No Act defines "joint family" or " coparcenary ". Both come from the Mitakshara and from court decisions. The Hindu Succession Act changes how coparcenary property passes.

Section 6(1), Hindu Succession Act, 1956 (as substituted in 2005). On and from the commencement of the Hindu Succession (Amendment) Act, 2005 (39 of 2005), in a Joint Hindu family governed by the Mitakshara law, the daughter of a coparcener shall,― (a) by birth become a coparcener in her own right the same manner as the son; (b) have the same rights in the coparcenery property as she would have had if she had been a son; (c) be subject to the same liabilities in respect of the said coparcenery property as that of a son, and any reference to a Hindu Mitakshara coparcener shall be deemed to include a reference to a daughter of a coparcener: Provided that nothing contained in this sub-section shall affect or invalidate any disposition or alienation including any partition or testamentary disposition of property which had taken place before the 20th day of December, 2004.

Section 6(2). Any property to which a female Hindu becomes entitled by virtue of sub-section (1) shall be held by her with the incidents of coparcenary ownership and shall be regarded, notwithstanding anything contained in this Act or any other law for the time being in force, as property capable of being disposed of by her by testamentary disposition.

Section 6(3) (first part). Where a Hindu dies after the commencement of the Hindu Succession (Amendment) Act, 2005 (39 of 2005), his interest in the property of a Joint Hindu family governed by the Mitakshara law, shall devolve by testamentary or intestate succession, as the case may be, under this Act and not by survivorship, ...

Explanation to Section 30. The interest of a male Hindu in a Mitakshara coparcenary property ... shall, notwithstanding anything contained in this Act or in any other law for the time being in force, be deemed to be property capable of being disposed of by him or by her within the meaning of this section.

Section 3, Kerala Joint Hindu Family System (Abolition) Act, 1975. Birth in family not to give rise to rights in property. On and after the commencement of this Act, no right to claim any interest in any property of an ancestor during his or her lifetime which is founded on the mere fact that the claimant was born in the family of the ancestor shall be recognised in any court.
In simple words

Section 6(1): in a Mitakshara joint family, a daughter of a coparcener is a coparcener by birth, with the same rights and liabilities as a son. Partitions and dispositions before 20 December 2004 are saved. Section 6(2): what she gets she holds as coparcenary property, and she can leave it by will . Section 6(3): when a coparcener dies after 9 September 2005, his interest passes by will or by succession, not by survivorship . Section 30, Explanation: a male Hindu can leave his interest in Mitakshara coparcenary property by will. Section 8: the property of a Hindu male who dies intestate (without a will) goes to his heirs under the Act. Chander Sen shows what this means for property a son inherits from his father. Kerala Act, Section 3: in Kerala no one gets a right in an ancestor's property merely by being born in the family.
en.meaning:
Joint Hindu family . "A Joint Hindu family consists of all persons lineally descended from a common ancestor, and includes their wives and unmarried daughters. A daughter ceases to be a member of her father's family on marriage, and becomes a member of her husband's family" (Mulla, section 212(1)). It is a status, not a contract. Coparcenary. "The coparcenary consists of only those persons who have taken by birth an interest in the property of the holder and who can enforce a partition whenever they like. It is a narrower body than a joint family" ( Sunil Kumar v. Ram Parkash (1988), quoted in Vineeta Sharma , para 27). Mulla describes it as "a common male ancestor with his lineal descendants in the male line within four degrees counting from and inclusive of such ancestor (or three degrees exclusive of the ancestor)" (section 214(1)). Since 2005, daughters are coparceners by birth. Joint family property or coparcenary property. Mulla says the two terms are synonymous (section 220). It is property in which every coparcener has a joint interest and joint possession (section 221). Separate property. Property that belongs to one member alone. It includes self-acquired property (Mulla, sections 220, 222). See Diagram 1 . Diagram 1. The joint family is the widest group; the coparcenary sits inside it; coparcenary property is what the coparcenary owns. Inside it: the coparcenary, the holder and three generations of descendants, and daughters since 2005. Inside that: coparcenary property, which is ancestral property, joint acquisitions with its aid, income, and blended property. Outside, linked by a dotted line marked "blending": a member's separate or self-acquired property. The question this topic answers. Who belongs to the family, who among them has rights in the property, and which property is shared? Why the law has this rule. "The cord that knits the members of the family is not property but the relationship of one another" ( Sunil Kumar , quoted in Vineeta Sharma , para 27). Rights in property, however, belong only to the smaller group who take by birth.
keyPoints: A joint Hindu family is a status based on sapindaship and needs no property. A coparcenary is a creature of law and is smaller than the joint family; a stranger enters only by adoption. The test of a coparcener is the right to demand partition ( Vineeta Sharma , para 25). Since 2005 daughters are coparceners by birth (Section 6(1)). Joint family property and coparcenary property are synonyms: ancestral, joint acquisitions with its aid, income, blended. Self-acquired property stays separate unless blended by clear intention. A son who inherits from his father under Section 8 holds it as his own ( Chander Sen ). Kerala Act, 1975: the joint family system among Hindus is abolished; birthright ends and coparcenary property is held as tenancy in common.

caseLaws.name: Surjit Lal Chhabda v
caseLaws.facts: Commissioner of Income Tax (1975) Facts. Surjit Lal, with no son, swore before a Presidency Magistrate in 1956 that he had thrown his self-acquired Kathoke Lodge into the family hotchpot of himself, his wife and unmarried daughter, and claimed the rent was the family's income. Principle. A joint Hindu family can consist of one male, his wife and unmarried daughter; but property he throws into the common stock is still really his in the eye of Hindu law until a son is born, so its income is his individual income. Appeal dismissed. (1976) 3 SCC 142 : AIR 1976 SC 109. Why it matters. It separates the joint family from the coparcenary and shows the limits of blending by a man with no son. State Bank of India v. Ghamandi Ram (1969) Facts. The karta of a joint family firm that had traded in what became Pakistan claimed the surplus in its bank account; the question was whether the firm was an "individual" under a Pakistan notification . Principle. A Mitakshara coparcenary is a creature of law holding property in a quasi-corporate capacity; the Court listed its six incidents and held the firm a body of individuals. Bank's appeal allowed. AIR 1969 SC 1330. Why it matters. It is the standard source for the incidents of a coparcenary. Commissioner of Wealth Tax, Kanpur v. Chander Sen (1986) Facts. Rangi Lal died in 1965, leaving his son Chander Sen and grandsons; ₹1,85,043 stood to his credit in the firm. The Revenue treated it as the property of Chander Sen's joint family with his sons. Principle. A son who inherits his father's property under Section 8 takes it in his individual capacity; his sons get no right by birth in it. (1986) 3 SCC 567 : AIR 1986 SC 1753. Why it matters. It shows that property inherited from a father after 1956 is not ancestral property in the old sense. Sitabai v. Ramchandra (1969) Facts. Sitabai, widow of Bhagirath, adopted a son on 4 March 1958; Bhagirath's brother Dulichand, the sole surviving coparcener, died on 13 March 1958. Dulichand's illegitimate son took possession of the family property. Principle. Joint family property does not lose its character in the hands of a sole surviving coparcener while a widow entitled to maintenance is alive; a son adopted by a widow under the 1956 Act becomes a coparcener with her husband's surviving brother. AIR 1970 SC 343. Why it matters. It shows that a joint family can continue with a single coparcener and revive through adoption. Addagada Raghavamma v. Addagada Chenchamma (1963) Facts. Chimpirayya's will said he was a divided member and left his property to his grandson and a granddaughter. The question was whether the will severed his joint status although it was not communicated to his grandson's guardian before his death. Principle. A clear, unequivocal, unilateral declaration is enough to sever joint status, but it takes effect only when it reaches the members affected. Appeal dismissed with costs. AIR 1964 SC 136. Why it matters. It shows how the joint status of a coparcener ends. Vineeta Sharma v. Rakesh Sharma (2020) Facts. The question was whether a daughter is a coparcener if her father died before 9 September 2005. Principle. The Court described the joint family, the coparcenary and coparcenary property (paras 22–35) and held that a daughter is a coparcener by birth, whether or not her father was alive on that date. (2020) 9 SCC 1 : [2020] 10 SCR. Why it matters. It is the current Supreme Court statement of the whole topic.

selfTest.q: 1. Can a joint family exist without property?
selfTest.a: Yes. It is a status, and the family need not own anything (Mulla, section 212(2)).

selfTest.q: 2. Can members create a coparcenary by agreement?
selfTest.a: No. It is created by law. A stranger joins only by adoption.

selfTest.q: 3. What is the doctrine of blending?
selfTest.a: A coparcener voluntarily throws his separate property into the common stock, giving up his separate claim; it becomes joint family property.

selfTest.q: 4. Is property inherited from a maternal grandfather coparcenary property?
selfTest.a: No. Only property inherited from the father, grandfather or great-grandfather is ( Vineeta Sharma , para 24; Mulla, section 218).

selfTest.q: 5. Is a married daughter a coparcener today?
selfTest.a: Yes. She leaves her father's joint family on marriage, but Section 6(1) speaks of "the daughter of a coparcener" without distinguishing married and unmarried daughters, and Vineeta Sharma (para 129(i)) applies it to daughters born before or after 2005.

selfTest.q: 6. In Surjit Lal Chhabda , why was the rent taxed as Surjit Lal's own income?
selfTest.a: He had no son. Though he threw the lodge into the common stock, in the eye of Hindu law it remained really his, with full power to sell or give it away.

సెక్షన్ 6(1): మితాక్షర ఉమ్మడి కుటుంబంలో కోపార్సినర్ కూతురు పుట్టుకతోనే కోపార్సినర్; కొడుకుతో సమాన హక్కులు, బాధ్యతలు. 20 డిసెంబర్ 2004 కు ముందు జరిగిన విభజన లు, అన్యాక్రాంతాలు కాపాడబడతాయి. సెక్షన్ 6(2): ఆమె పొందినదాన్ని కోపార్సినరీ ఆస్తిగా కలిగి ఉంటుంది; వీలునామా ద్వారా ఇవ్వవచ్చు. సెక్షన్ 6(3): 9 సెప్టెంబర్ 2005 తర్వాత కోపార్సినర్ మరణిస్తే, అతని హక్కు సర్వైవర్‌షిప్ ద్వారా కాకుండా వీలునామా లేదా వారసత్వం ద్వారా వెళ్తుంది. సెక్షన్ 30, Explanation: పురుష హిందువు మితాక్షర కోపార్సినరీ ఆస్తిలో తన హక్కును వీలునామా ద్వారా ఇవ్వవచ్చు. సెక్షన్ 8: వీలునామా లేకుండా మరణించిన హిందూ పురుషుని ఆస్తి చట్టం కింద అతని వారసులకు వెళ్తుంది. కొడుకు తండ్రి నుంచి పొందిన ఆస్తికి దీని అర్థం ఏమిటో Chander Sen చూపిస్తుంది. కేరళ చట్టం, సెక్షన్ 3: కేరళలో కుటుంబంలో పుట్టినంత మాత్రాన ఎవరికీ పూర్వీకుని ఆస్తిలో హక్కు రాదు.

ఉమ్మడి హిందూ కుటుంబం . "A Joint Hindu family consists of all persons lineally descended from a common ancestor, and includes their wives and unmarried daughters. A daughter ceases to be a member of her father's family on marriage, and becomes a member of her husband's family" (ముల్లా, సెక్షన్ 212(1)). ఇది ఒప్పందం కాదు, హోదా. కోపార్సినరీ. "The coparcenary consists of only those persons who have taken by birth an interest in the property of the holder and who can enforce a partition whenever they like. It is a narrower body than a joint family" ( Sunil Kumar v. Ram Parkash (1988), Vineeta Sharma para 27 లో ఉటంకించినది). ముల్లా దీన్ని "a common male ancestor with his lineal descendants in the male line within four degrees counting from and inclusive of such ancestor (or three degrees exclusive of the ancestor)" అని వర్ణిస్తారు (సెక్షన్ 214(1)). 2005 నుంచి కూతుళ్లు పుట్టుకతోనే కోపార్సినర్లు. ఉమ్మడి కుటుంబ ఆస్తి లేదా కోపార్సినరీ ఆస్తి. ఈ రెండు పదాలు పర్యాయపదాలని ముల్లా చెబుతారు (సెక్షన్ 220). ప్రతి కోపార్సినర్‌కు ఉమ్మడి హక్కు, ఉమ్మడి స్వాధీనం ఉన్న ఆస్తి ఇది (సెక్షన్ 221). ప్రత్యేక ఆస్తి. ఒక్క సభ్యునికి మాత్రమే చెందిన ఆస్తి. స్వార్జిత ఆస్తి దీనిలో భాగం (ముల్లా, సెక్షన్లు 220, 222). "కలపడం" .-> P classDef hide fill:none,stroke:none,color:transparent class SP,SQ hide వచన వివరణ బయటి పెట్టె: ఉమ్మడి హిందూ కుటుంబం, సపిండత్వంపై ఆధారపడిన హోదా, భార్యలు, పెళ్లికాని కూతుళ్లు సహా. దాని లోపల: కోపార్సినరీ, ఆస్తి కలిగినవారు, మూడు తరాల వంశస్థులు, 2005 నుంచి కూతుళ్లు. దాని లోపల: కోపార్సినరీ ఆస్తి, అంటే పూర్వీకుల ఆస్తి, దాని సహాయంతో సంపాదించినది, ఆదాయం, కలిపిన ఆస్తి. బయట, "కలపడం" అని గుర్తించిన చుక్కల గీతతో కలిపి: సభ్యుని ప్రత్యేక లేదా స్వార్జిత ఆస్తి. ఈ అంశం జవాబిచ్చే ప్రశ్న. కుటుంబంలో ఎవరు ఉంటారు, వారిలో ఎవరికి ఆస్తిలో హక్కులు ఉంటాయి, ఏ ఆస్తి ఉమ్మడి? చట్టంలో ఈ నియమం ఎందుకు ఉంది. "The cord that knits the members of the family is not property but the relationship of one another" ( Sunil Kumar , Vineeta Sharma para 27 లో). అయితే ఆస్తిలో హక్కులు పుట్టుకతో పొందే చిన్న సమూహానికే చెందుతాయి.

selfTest.q: 1. ఆస్తి లేకుండా ఉమ్మడి కుటుంబం ఉండగలదా?
selfTest.a: అవును. అది హోదా; కుటుంబానికి ఏమీ ఉండనక్కర్లేదు (ముల్లా, సెక్షన్ 212(2)).

selfTest.q: 2. సభ్యులు ఒప్పందం ద్వారా కోపార్సినరీని సృష్టించగలరా?
selfTest.a: లేదు. అది చట్టం ద్వారా ఏర్పడుతుంది. అపరిచితుడు దత్తత ద్వారా మాత్రమే చేరతాడు.

selfTest.q: 3. బ్లెండింగ్ సిద్ధాంతం అంటే ఏమిటి?
selfTest.a: కోపార్సినర్ తన ప్రత్యేక హక్కును వదులుకుని, తన ప్రత్యేక ఆస్తిని స్వచ్ఛందంగా ఉమ్మడి నిల్వలో కలపడం; అది ఉమ్మడి కుటుంబ ఆస్తి అవుతుంది.

selfTest.q: 4. తల్లి తండ్రి నుంచి వచ్చిన ఆస్తి కోపార్సినరీ ఆస్తా?
selfTest.a: కాదు. తండ్రి, తాత లేదా ముత్తాత నుంచి వచ్చిన ఆస్తి మాత్రమే ( Vineeta Sharma , para 24; ముల్లా, సెక్షన్ 218).

selfTest.q: 5. ఈరోజు పెళ్లయిన కూతురు కోపార్సినరా?
selfTest.a: అవును. పెళ్లితో ఆమె తండ్రి ఉమ్మడి కుటుంబాన్ని వదులుతుంది; కానీ సెక్షన్ 6(1) పెళ్లయిన, కాని కూతుళ్ల మధ్య తేడా చూపకుండా "the daughter of a coparcener" అంటుంది; 2005 కు ముందు లేదా తర్వాత పుట్టిన కూతుళ్లకు Vineeta Sharma (para 129(i)) దాన్ని వర్తింపజేస్తుంది.

selfTest.q: 6. Surjit Lal Chhabda లో అద్దెపై సుర్జిత్ లాల్ సొంత ఆదాయంగా ఎందుకు పన్ను వేశారు?
selfTest.a: అతనికి కొడుకు లేడు. లాడ్జిని ఉమ్మడి నిల్వలో కలిపినా, హిందూ చట్టం దృష్టిలో అది నిజానికి అతనిదే; దాన్ని అమ్మడానికి, దానం చేయడానికి అతనికి పూర్తి అధికారం ఉంది.

family-law-i-u2-t1.subtitle: Meaning of Hindu marriage: a sacrament with contract-like features, and the Gandharva form

en.inOneMinute: No Act defines Hindu marriage in one sentence. The definition has to be built from the classical law and from the sections of the Hindu Marriage Act, 1955. Classical law. Marriage was a sacrament , "a holy union for the performance of religious duties" (Mulla). In Tikait Mon Mohini Jemadai v. Basanta Kumar Singh (1901) the Calcutta High Court said that "though marriage under the Hindu Law is a contract, it is also a sacrament"; it is "more religious than secular in character" and "the union is indissoluble ". Under the 1955 Act. Mulla's commentary defines a Hindu marriage as "a union of one man with one woman to the exclusion of all others" made by the customary rites and ceremonies of either party. Once made, it creates "a relation and a status not imposed or defined by contract but by law". It is a sacred, ceremonial and monogamous union, which the law can now declare void, annul or dissolve. What exams ask. The sacrament and contract debate; Tikait ; the ceremonies required by Section 7 ( Bhaurao , Dolly Rani ); the contract-like features added in 1955; the eight classical forms; and the civil marriage under the Special Marriage Act, 1954.
legalProvision: The Act has no definition clause for "marriage". These sections together show what a Hindu marriage is in law.

Section 5, Hindu Marriage Act, 1955. Conditions for a Hindu marriage. A marriage may be solemnized between any two Hindus, if the following conditions are fulfilled, namely:— (i) neither party has a spouse living at the time of the marriage; (ii) at the time of the marriage, neither party— (a) is incapable of giving a valid consent to it in consequence of unsoundness of mind; or (b) though capable of giving a valid consent, has been suffering from mental disorder of such a kind or to such an extent as to be unfit for marriage and the procreation of children; or (c) has been subject to recurrent attacks of insanity; (iii) the bridegroom has completed the age of twenty-one years and the bride, the age of eighteen years at the time of the marriage; (iv) the parties are not within the degrees of prohibited relationship unless the custom or usage governing each of them permits of a marriage between the two; (v) the parties are not sapindas of each other, unless the custom or usage governing each of them permits of a marriage between the two;

Section 7. Ceremonies for a Hindu marriage. (1) A Hindu marriage may be solemnized in accordance with the customary rites and ceremonies of either party thereto. (2) Where such rites and ceremonies include the Saptapadi (that is, the taking of seven steps by the bridegroom and the bride jointly before the sacred fire), the marriage becomes complete and binding when the seventh step is taken.

Section 4. Overriding effect of Act. Save as otherwise expressly provided in this Act,— (a) any text rule or interpretation of Hindu law or any custom or usage as part of that law in force immediately before the commencement of this Act shall cease to have effect with respect to any matter for which provision is made in this Act; (b) any other law in force immediately before the commencement of this Act shall cease to have effect in so far as it is inconsistent with any of the provisions contained in this Act.
Section 8(5). Notwithstanding anything contained in this section, the validity of any Hindu marriage shall in no way be affected by the omission to make the entry.

Section 29(4). Nothing contained in this Act shall be deemed to affect the provisions contained in the Special Marriage Act, 1954 (43 of 1954) with respect to marriages between Hindus solemnized under that Act, whether before or after the commencement of this Act.

Section 12(2) proviso, Special Marriage Act, 1954. Provided that it shall not be complete and binding on the parties unless each party says to the other in the presence of the Marriage Officer and the three witnesses and in any language understood by the parties,—"I, (A), take thee (B), to be my lawful wife (or husband)".
In simple words

Section 5: a Hindu marriage can be made only between two Hindus who meet the conditions: no living spouse, sound mind, the minimum ages (21 and 18), and no prohibited relationship or sapinda relationship unless a custom governing each of them allows it. (Clause (vi), on the consent of the bride's guardian, was omitted in 1978.) Section 7: the marriage is made by the customary rites and ceremonies of either the bride's side or the bridegroom's side. If those rites include the saptapadi , the marriage is complete and binding when the seventh step is taken. Section 4: on every matter the Act deals with, the old texts, rules and customs of Hindu law stop applying. Other older laws stop applying only where they are inconsistent with the Act. Section 8(5): a Hindu marriage is not invalid only because it was not registered. Section 29(4): two Hindus may still marry under the Special Marriage Act, 1954, and that Act then governs their marriage. Special Marriage Act, Section 12(2): a civil marriage is complete only when each party makes the stated declaration to the other before the Marriage Officer and three witnesses.
en.meaning:
The question this topic answers. What is a Hindu marriage in law: a religious sacrament, a contract , or something else? Classical meaning. Mulla states the law before 1955 in these words: "Marriage, according to the Hindu law, is a holy union for the performance of religious duties. It is not a contract" (Mulla, section 427). The Introductory Note to the Hindu Marriage Act in Mulla adds: "In Hindu law marriage is treated as a samskara or a sacrament. It is the last of ten sacraments, enjoined by the Hindu religion for regeneration of men and obligatory in case of every Hindu who does not desire to adopt the life of a Sanyasi." Meaning under the Act (Mulla's definition). Mulla's commentary on Section 5 says: "A Hindu marriage under the Act, it is submitted, is not entirely or necessarily a sacrament (sanskara) but a union of one man with one woman to the exclusion of all others satisfied by solemnization of the customary rites and ceremonies of either party essential for a marriage: and directly it exists, creates a relation and a status not imposed or defined by contract but by law." The same passage says: "It is also not possible to say that the legal concept of marriage under the Act is one of contract." The four parts of this definition. See Diagram 1 . Diagram 1. Mulla's definition, read with Sections 5 and 7: a ceremonial, monogamous union that creates a status fixed by law. flowchart TD M["Hindu marriage under the Act
(no statutory definition)"] M --> A["1. Union of one man
with one woman"] M --> B["2. To the exclusion of all others
no living spouse: s. 5(i)"] M --> C["3. Made by customary rites
of either party: s. 7"] M --> D["4. Creates a status
fixed by law, not by contract"] Text description A Hindu marriage under the Act has four parts: a union of one man with one woman; to the exclusion of all others, because neither party may have a living spouse under Section 5(i); made by the customary rites and ceremonies of either party under Section 7; and creating a status fixed by law, not by contract. A union of one man with one woman. It is between a bridegroom and a bride (Sections 5(iii) and 7(2) use these words). To the exclusion of all others. It is monogamous: neither party may have a living spouse (Section 5(i)). Made by ceremonies. It must be solemnized by the customary rites and ceremonies of either party (Section 7). Without them there is no Hindu marriage. It creates a status fixed by law. The rights and duties of husband and wife come from law, not from any agreement between them. Why the law has this rule. Marriage decides the status of the spouses, the legitimacy of children, maintenance and succession. The law therefore fixes how a marriage is made and what it means, and does not leave this to private agreement.
keyPoints: The Hindu Marriage Act has no definition of marriage; its meaning comes from Sections 5 and 7. Classical law: "a holy union for the performance of religious duties. It is not a contract" (Mulla, s. 427). Tikait (1901): "though ... a contract, it is also a sacrament"; "the union is indissoluble"; a pre-marriage deed varying marital rights is against public policy. Mulla's definition under the Act: a union of one man with one woman to the exclusion of all others, by the customary rites of either party, creating a status fixed by law, not by contract. Bhaurao (1965): without proper ceremonies there is no "solemnized" marriage, even in the Gandharva form. Dolly Rani (2024): no ceremony, no marriage; registration is only proof. The Act added consent, nullity, divorce, restitution, judicial separation and remarriage. Eight classical forms; only Brahma and Asura recognised before 1955; the Act names no form. Special Marriage Act, 1954: civil marriage between any two persons, by declaration before the Marriage Officer and three witnesses.

caseLaws.name: Tikait Mon Mohini Jemadai v
caseLaws.facts: Basanta Kumar Singh (1901) Facts. The parties married in 1885 as minors. At the marriage, a deed said the husband would never take his wife from her father's house and would obey her mother. After about fifteen years there, disputes arose, and he sued to make her live with him in his own house. Principle. Marriage "though ... a contract ... is also a sacrament" and "the union is indissoluble" (para 16). The rights and duties of marriage are fixed by law and cannot be varied by agreement (Banerjee, quoted at para 32); the deed was "opposed to public policy" (para 40). Appeal dismissed with costs. (1901) ILR 28 Cal 751. Why it matters. It is the classic authority for the sacramental view, and for the rule that the incidents of marriage are fixed by law. Bhaurao Shankar Lokhande v. State of Maharashtra (1965) Facts. Bhaurao, married to Indubai in about 1956, married Kamlabai in 1962 while Indubai was alive, and was convicted of bigamy. The State said the second marriage was a Gandharva marriage as modified by custom; the invocation before fire and the saptapadi were not performed. Principle. "Solemnize" means to celebrate with proper ceremonies and in due form; the two essential ceremonies are part of a Gandharva marriage too unless custom has modified them. The second marriage was not "solemnized", so the convictions were set aside. AIR 1965 SC 1564 : (1965) 2 SCR 837. Why it matters. It shows that consent without the essential ceremonies does not make a Hindu marriage. Dolly Rani v. Manish Kumar Chanchal (2024) Facts. Two pilots obtained a society's marriage certificate in 2021 and registered the marriage under the Uttar Pradesh rules, planning the ceremony for 2022. No rites were performed. Disputes and cases followed, and both told the Court that no marriage had been solemnized. Principle. Without the Section 7 ceremonies there is no Hindu marriage; a certificate or registration "would neither confirm any marital status ... nor establish a marriage". A Hindu marriage "is a samskara and a sacrament"; "A marriage is not a commercial transaction." The Court declared there was no marriage and quashed the cases. 2024 INSC 355. Why it matters. It restates, for today, that a Hindu marriage is a ceremonial and sacred union, and that registration is only proof.

selfTest.q: 1. Does the Hindu Marriage Act define "marriage"?
selfTest.a: No. Its meaning is gathered from Sections 5 and 7, the case law and Mulla.

selfTest.q: 2. What did the Calcutta High Court say about Hindu marriage in Tikait?
selfTest.a: "Though marriage under the Hindu Law is a contract, it is also a sacrament"; it is more religious than secular, and the union is indissoluble (para 16).

selfTest.q: 4. Is a Gandharva marriage made by consent alone?
selfTest.a: No. The essential ceremonies are needed in this form too, unless custom has modified them (Mulla; Bhaurao ).

selfTest.q: 5. A couple registers their marriage but performs no ceremony. Are they married under the Act?
selfTest.a: No. Without Section 7 ceremonies there is no Hindu marriage, and registration cannot create one ( Dolly Rani ; Section 8(5) only protects a marriage that was solemnized but not registered).

selfTest.q: 6. Which two classical forms were recognised before 1955, and what was the difference?
selfTest.a: The Brahma form, a gift of the bride without consideration, and the Asura form, where the guardian received shulka (bride's price).

Feature Provision of the 1955 Act
Capacity and consent Section 5(ii): neither party may be incapable of valid consent because of unsoundness of mind, or suffer from the stated mental disorder or recurrent attacks of insanity. Section 12(1)(c): the marriage is voidable if the petitioner's consent was obtained "by force or by fraud as to the nature of the ceremony or as to any material fact or circumstances concerning the respondent".
Restitution of conjugal rights Section 9: when either spouse has, without reasonable excuse, withdrawn from the society of the other, the aggrieved party may petition; the burden of proving reasonable excuse is on the person who withdrew.
Judicial separation Section 10: either party may seek it on any ground in Section 13(1), and a wife also on a ground in Section 13(2).
Nullity Section 11 (void marriages) and Section 12 (voidable marriages).
Divorce Section 13 (stated grounds) and Section 13B (mutual consent, after living separately for one year or more; the joint motion is made not earlier than six months and not later than eighteen months after the petition).
Remarriage Section 15: a divorced person may marry again once there is no right of appeal, or the time for appeal has expired with no appeal, or the appeal has been dismissed.

Group Forms
Approved Brahma, Daiva, Arsha, Prajapatya
Unapproved Asura, Gandharva, Rakshasa, Paishacha

Section 5, Hindu Marriage Act, 1955. Conditions for a Hindu marriage. A marriage may be solemnized between any two Hindus, if the following conditions are fulfilled, namely:— (i) neither party has a spouse living at the time of the marriage; (ii) at the time of the marriage, neither party— (a) is incapable of giving a valid consent to it in consequence of unsoundness of mind; or (b) though capable of giving a valid consent, has been suffering from mental disorder of such a kind or to such an extent as to be unfit for marriage and the procreation of children; or (c) has been subject to recurrent attacks of insanity; (iii) the bridegroom has completed the age of twenty-one years and the bride, the age of eighteen years at the time of the marriage; (iv) the parties are not within the degrees of prohibited relationship unless the custom or usage governing each of them permits of a marriage between the two; (v) the parties are not sapindas of each other, unless the custom or usage governing each of them permits of a marriage between the two;

Section 7. Ceremonies for a Hindu marriage. (1) A Hindu marriage may be solemnized in accordance with the customary rites and ceremonies of either party thereto. (2) Where such rites and ceremonies include the Saptapadi (that is, the taking of seven steps by the bridegroom and the bride jointly before the sacred fire), the marriage becomes complete and binding when the seventh step is taken.

Section 4. Overriding effect of Act. Save as otherwise expressly provided in this Act,— (a) any text rule or interpretation of Hindu law or any custom or usage as part of that law in force immediately before the commencement of this Act shall cease to have effect with respect to any matter for which provision is made in this Act; (b) any other law in force immediately before the commencement of this Act shall cease to have effect in so far as it is inconsistent with any of the provisions contained in this Act.
Section 8(5). Notwithstanding anything contained in this section, the validity of any Hindu marriage shall in no way be affected by the omission to make the entry.

Section 29(4). Nothing contained in this Act shall be deemed to affect the provisions contained in the Special Marriage Act, 1954 (43 of 1954) with respect to marriages between Hindus solemnized under that Act, whether before or after the commencement of this Act.

(వధువు సంరక్షకుని సమ్మతి గురించిన క్లాజు (vi) 1978 లో తొలగించబడింది.) సెక్షన్ 7: వధువు పక్షం లేదా వరుడి పక్షం, ఏదో ఒకరి ఆచార కర్మలు, వేడుకలతో వివాహం జరుగుతుంది. ఆ కర్మల్లో సప్తపది ఉంటే, ఏడో అడుగు వేసినప్పుడు వివాహం పూర్తై, కట్టుబడి ఉంటుంది. సెక్షన్ 4: చట్టం వ్యవహరించే ప్రతి విషయంలో, హిందూ చట్టపు పాత గ్రంథాలు, నియమాలు, ఆచారాలు వర్తించడం ఆగిపోతుంది. ఇతర పాత చట్టాలు చట్టానికి విరుద్ధంగా ఉన్నంత వరకే వర్తించడం ఆగిపోతాయి. సెక్షన్ 8(5): రిజిస్టర్ చేయలేదనే కారణం మాత్రాన హిందూ వివాహం చెల్లకుండా పోదు. సెక్షన్ 29(4): ఇద్దరు హిందువులు ఇప్పటికీ ప్రత్యేక వివాహ చట్టం, 1954 కింద పెళ్లి చేసుకోవచ్చు; అప్పుడు ఆ చట్టమే వారి వివాహాన్ని పాలిస్తుంది. ప్రత్యేక వివాహ చట్టం, సెక్షన్ 12(2): మ్యారేజ్ ఆఫీసర్, ముగ్గురు సాక్షుల సమక్షంలో ప్రతి పక్షం మరొకరికి పేర్కొన్న ప్రకటన చేసినప్పుడే పౌర వివాహం పూర్తవుతుంది.

నిర్ణయించే హోదా ఏర్పడుతుంది"] వచన వివరణ చట్టం ప్రకారం హిందూ వివాహానికి నాలుగు భాగాలు: ఒక పురుషుడు, ఒక స్త్రీ కలయిక; సెక్షన్ 5(i) ప్రకారం ఎవరికీ జీవించి ఉన్న జీవిత భాగస్వామి ఉండకూడదు కాబట్టి ఇతరులందరినీ మినహాయించి; సెక్షన్ 7 ప్రకారం ఏదో ఒక పక్షం ఆచార కర్మలు, వేడుకలతో జరిగేది; ఒప్పందం కాకుండా చట్టం నిర్ణయించే హోదాను సృష్టించేది. ఒక పురుషుడు, ఒక స్త్రీ కలయిక. ఇది వరుడు, వధువు మధ్య జరిగేది (సెక్షన్లు 5(iii), 7(2) ఈ పదాలు వాడతాయి). ఇతరులందరినీ మినహాయించి. ఇది ఏకపత్నీ వివాహం: ఏ పక్షానికీ జీవించి ఉన్న జీవిత భాగస్వామి ఉండకూడదు (సెక్షన్ 5(i)). వేడుకలతో జరిగేది. ఏదో ఒక పక్షం ఆచార కర్మలు, వేడుకలతో దీనిని నిర్వహించాలి (సెక్షన్ 7). అవి లేకుండా హిందూ వివాహం లేదు. చట్టం నిర్ణయించే హోదాను సృష్టిస్తుంది. భార్యాభర్తల హక్కులు, బాధ్యతలు వారి మధ్య ఒప్పందం నుంచి కాదు, చట్టం నుంచి వస్తాయి. చట్టం ఈ నియమం ఎందుకు పెట్టింది. వివాహం భార్యాభర్తల హోదాను, పిల్లల చట్టబద్ధతను, భరణాన్ని, వారసత్వాన్ని నిర్ణయిస్తుంది. అందుకే వివాహం ఎలా జరుగుతుందో, దాని అర్థం ఏమిటో చట్టమే నిర్ణయిస్తుంది; దానిని వ్యక్తిగత ఒప్పందానికి వదలదు.

selfTest.q: 1. హిందూ వివాహ చట్టం "వివాహం" ను నిర్వచిస్తుందా?
selfTest.a: లేదు. దాని అర్థాన్ని సెక్షన్లు 5, 7, కేసు చట్టం, ముల్లా నుంచి కూర్చుకోవాలి.

selfTest.q: 2. Tikait లో కలకత్తా హైకోర్టు హిందూ వివాహం గురించి ఏమి చెప్పింది?
selfTest.a: "Though marriage under the Hindu Law is a contract, it is also a sacrament"; అది లౌకికం కంటే ఎక్కువ మతపరమైనది, ఆ కలయిక విడదీయరానిది (పేరా 16).

selfTest.q: 4. గాంధర్వ వివాహం సమ్మతి మాత్రంతో జరుగుతుందా?
selfTest.a: లేదు. ఆచారం మార్చకపోతే ఈ రూపంలో కూడా ముఖ్యమైన వేడుకలు అవసరం (ముల్లా; Bhaurao ).

selfTest.q: 5. ఒక జంట వివాహాన్ని రిజిస్టర్ చేసింది, కానీ ఏ వేడుకా జరపలేదు. వారు చట్టం కింద వివాహితులా?
selfTest.a: కాదు. సెక్షన్ 7 వేడుకలు లేకుండా హిందూ వివాహం లేదు, రిజిస్ట్రేషన్ దానిని సృష్టించలేదు ( Dolly Rani ; సెక్షన్ 8(5) జరిగి రిజిస్టర్ కాని వివాహాన్ని మాత్రమే కాపాడుతుంది).

selfTest.q: 6. 1955 కి ముందు గుర్తించిన రెండు సంప్రదాయ రూపాలు ఏవి, వాటి తేడా ఏమిటి?
selfTest.a: బ్రహ్మ రూపం, ప్రతిఫలం లేకుండా వధువు దానం; అసుర రూపం, సంరక్షకుడు శుల్కం (వధువు ధర) తీసుకునేది.

ఎలా జరుగుతుంది మతపరమైన వేడుకలు; వధువు దానం, స్వీకారం పక్షాల అంగీకారం ఏదో ఒక పక్షం ఆచార కర్మలు, వేడుకలు (సె. 7)
సమ్మతి దానం స్వీకరించడానికి అవసరం; మైనారిటీ వివాహాన్ని చెల్లకుండా చేయలేదు తప్పనిసరి; మైనర్ ఒప్పందం శూన్యం సామర్థ్యం అవసరం (సె. 5(ii)); బలవంతం లేదా మోసం ఉంటే రద్దు చేయదగినది (సె. 12(1)(c))

family-law-i-u2-t2.subtitle: Why the law protects marriage: religious, social and legal importance, and the presumption in its favour

en.inOneMinute: Marriage is the base of the Hindu family, and its importance is of three kinds. Religious. Hindu law treats marriage as a samskara , a sacrament. In Tikait (1901) the Calcutta High Court called it "more religious than secular in character". Social. In Sarla Mudgal (1995) the Supreme Court said: "Marriage is an institution in the maintenance of which the public at large is deeply interested. It is the foundation of the family and in turn of the society without which no civilisation can exist." Legal. Many rights flow from the status of husband and wife: maintenance, legitimacy of children, succession, a right to reside, and the matrimonial remedies. Because so much depends on it, the law protects marriage. It keeps children legitimate even when a marriage is void or annulled (Section 16). It also presumes a valid marriage where a man and a woman have lived together for a long time as husband and wife ( Badri Prasad , 1978). The presumption can be rebutted.
legalProvision: Section 16, Hindu Marriage Act, 1955. Legitimacy of children of void and voidable marriages. (1) Notwithstanding that a marriage is null and void under section 11, any child of such marriage who would have been legitimate if the marriage had been valid, shall be legitimate, whether such child is born before or after the commencement of the Marriage Laws (Amendment) Act, 1976 (68 of 1976), and whether or not a decree of nullity is granted in respect of that marriage under this Act and whether or not the marriage is held to be void otherwise than on a petition under this Act. (2) Where a decree of nullity is granted in respect of a voidable marriage under section 12, any child begotten or conceived before the decree is made, who would have been the legitimate child of the parties to the marriage if at the date of the decree it had been dissolved instead of being annulled, shall be deemed to be their legitimate child notwithstanding the decree of nullity. (3) Nothing contained in sub-section (1) or sub-section (2) shall be construed as conferring upon any child of a marriage which is null and void or which is annulled by a decree of nullity under section 12, any rights in or to the property of any person, other than the parents, in any case where, but for the passing of this Act, such child would have been incapable of possessing or acquiring any such rights by reason of his not being the legitimate child of his parents.

Section 24. Maintenance pendente lite and expenses of proceedings. Where in any proceeding under this Act it appears to the court that either the wife or the husband, as the case may be, has no independent income sufficient for her or his support and the necessary expenses of the proceeding, it may, on the application of the wife or the husband, order the respondent to pay to the petitioner the expenses of the proceeding, and monthly during the proceeding such sum as, having regard to the petitioner's own income and the income of the respondent, it may seem to the court to be reasonable.

Section 25(1). Permanent alimony and maintenance. Any court exercising jurisdiction under this Act may, at the time of passing any decree or at any time subsequent thereto, on application made to it for the purpose by either the wife or the husband, as the case may be, order that the respondent shall pay to the applicant for her or his maintenance and support such gross sum or such monthly or periodical sum for a term not exceeding the life of the applicant as, having regard to the respondent's own income and other property, if any, the income and other property of the applicant, the conduct of the parties and other circumstances of the case, it may seem to the court to be just, and any such payment may be secured, if necessary, by a charge on the immovable property of the respondent.
Section 8(5). Notwithstanding anything contained in this section, the validity of any Hindu marriage shall in no way be affected by the omission to make the entry.

Section 18(1), Hindu Adoptions and Maintenance Act, 1956. Subject to the provisions of this section, a Hindu wife, whether married before or after the commencement of this Act, shall be entitled to be maintained by her husband during her life time.
In simple words

Section 16(1): a child of a void marriage is legitimate, as if the marriage had been valid. No decree of nullity is needed for this. Section 16(2): when a voidable marriage is annulled, a child begotten or conceived before the decree is legitimate. Section 16(3): such a child gets rights in the property of the parents only, not of other relatives, where the child would otherwise have had no such right. Section 24: during a case under the Act, a spouse (wife or husband) without enough income may get the expenses of the case and a monthly sum. The proviso adds that the application should, as far as possible, be decided within sixty days from service of notice. Section 25(1): when or after the court passes a decree, either spouse may get maintenance for life at most, as a gross sum or a periodical sum, which may be secured by a charge on the other's immovable property. Section 8(5): not registering a marriage does not make it invalid. HAMA Section 18(1): a Hindu wife is entitled to be maintained by her husband for her whole life.
en.meaning:
Meaning. The importance of the institution of marriage is the set of religious, social and legal functions it performs for the spouses, their children and society. Mulla's Introductory Note to the Hindu Marriage Act says: "Marriage is necessarily the basis of social organisation and the foundation of important legal rights and obligations." The question this topic answers. Why does Hindu law treat marriage as an institution to be protected, and how does it protect it? The two halves of the answer. See Diagram 1 . Diagram 1. Three kinds of importance, and four ways the law protects marriage. flowchart TD M["Institution of marriage"] M --> W["Why it matters"] M --> P["How the law protects it"] W --> R["Religious: samskara
(Tikait, Mulla)"] W --> S["Social: public deeply interested
(Sarla Mudgal)"] W --> L["Legal: rights flow from
the status of spouse"] P --> P1["Rights: maintenance, succession,
residence, remedies"] P --> P2["Children legitimate
even if marriage fails: s. 16"] P --> P3["Presumption from
long cohabitation (Badri Prasad)"] P --> P4["Registration as proof:
s. 8 (Seema)"] Text description Marriage has religious importance (a samskara), social importance (the public is deeply interested in it) and legal importance (rights flow from the status of spouse). The law protects it by attaching rights of maintenance, succession and residence and the matrimonial remedies; by keeping children legitimate under Section 16; by presuming a marriage from long cohabitation; and by registration as proof. Why marriage matters: its religious, social and legal importance. How the law protects it: by the rights it attaches to marriage, by protecting children when a marriage fails, by the presumption in favour of marriage, and by providing for proof through registration. Why the law has this rule. Marriage is a status that others rely on: the spouses, their children, their families and the public. Mulla, explaining the meaning of status, quotes: the relation of the parties and their status "are not imposed or defined by contract or agreement but by law". If marriage could be easily denied, the wife's maintenance and the children's legitimacy and inheritance would be put at risk.
keyPoints: Marriage has religious, social and legal importance. Tikait : "more religious than secular in character"; Mulla: the last of ten sacraments. Sarla Mudgal : "the public at large is deeply interested" in maintaining marriage. Maintenance (HMA ss. 24–25 for either spouse; HAMA s. 18 for the wife; BNSS s. 144) and succession (HSA ss. 8, 15) depend on the status of spouse. Section 16 keeps children of void and voidable marriages legitimate; their property rights are limited to the parents' property. Long open cohabitation raises a strong but rebuttable presumption of marriage; a heavy burden lies on the person who denies it ( Badri Prasad ). Registration helps to prove a marriage but does not decide validity (s. 8(5); Seema ).

caseLaws.name: Badri Prasad v
caseLaws.facts: Deputy Director of Consolidation (1978) Facts. A man and a woman lived together as husband and wife for about fifty years. The petitioner challenged the fact of their marriage, in proceedings to which the Deputy Director of Consolidation was a party, arguing that no priest or other witness of the ceremony had been examined. The Allahabad High Court rejected the challenge. Principle. A strong presumption of wedlock arises from a long spell of living together as husband and wife; it is rebuttable, but a heavy burden lies on the person who denies it; "Law leans in favour of legitimacy and frowns upon bastardy." Special leave petitions dismissed. AIR 1978 SC 1557 : (1978) 3 SCC 527. Why it matters. It is the leading statement of the presumption in favour of marriage. Sarla Mudgal v. Union of India (1995) Facts. Hindu husbands with living Hindu wives converted to Islam and married again. One wife, Meena Mathur, learnt that her husband had married a second time after both he and the second woman converted. Principle. "Marriage is an institution in the maintenance of which the public at large is deeply interested"; the second marriage of a Hindu husband after conversion, without dissolving the first, is void and he is guilty under Section 494 IPC. (1995) 3 SCC 635 : AIR 1995 SC 1531. Why it matters. It is the leading statement of the social importance of marriage. Seema v. Ashwani Kumar (2006) Facts. While hearing a transfer petition, the Supreme Court noted that persons were denying the existence of marriages because most States kept no official record. It heard the States and the National Commission for Women on registration. Principle. Registration is not proof of a valid marriage "per se" and does not decide validity, but "it has a great evidentiary value"; marriages of all citizens should be made compulsorily registrable, and the States were directed to notify rules. Decided 14 February 2006. Why it matters. It explains the place of registration in protecting marriage, especially for women.

selfTest.q: 1. Which section protects the legitimacy of children of void marriages?
selfTest.a: Section 16(1) of the Hindu Marriage Act.

selfTest.q: 2. What does long, open cohabitation as husband and wife raise?
selfTest.a: A strong presumption of marriage, which is rebuttable; a heavy burden lies on the person who denies it ( Badri Prasad ).

selfTest.q: 3. Does non-registration affect validity?
selfTest.a: No. Section 8(5).

selfTest.q: 4. Can a husband claim maintenance under the Hindu Marriage Act?
selfTest.a: Yes. Sections 24 and 25 allow "either the wife or the husband" to apply.

selfTest.q: 5. Does "wife" in BNSS Section 144 include a divorced woman?
selfTest.a: Yes, if she has not remarried (Explanation to Section 144(1)).

selfTest.q: 6. Is the Hindu Widows' Remarriage Act, 1856 still in force?
selfTest.a: No. It was repealed in 1983. A widow's remarriage is now governed by the Hindu Marriage Act.

Right Source and rule
Maintenance during the case HMA Section 24: in any proceeding under the Act, a wife or husband without independent income sufficient for support and for the expenses of the case may get those expenses and a monthly sum; the application should, as far as possible, be decided within sixty days of service of notice.
Permanent alimony HMA Section 25: at or after a decree, either spouse may get a gross or periodical sum for a term not beyond the applicant's life, having regard to the incomes and property of both, the conduct of the parties and other circumstances. The court may vary, modify or rescind it on a change of circumstances (Section 25(2)). It may also vary, modify or rescind it if the receiving party has re-married, or, if the receiving party is the wife, she has not remained chaste, or, if the husband, he has had sexual intercourse with any woman outside wedlock (Section 25(3)).
Wife's maintenance HAMA Section 18: a Hindu wife is entitled to be maintained by her husband for life. She may live separately without losing the claim if he is guilty of desertion, has treated her with cruelty causing reasonable apprehension of harm, has any other wife living, keeps a concubine in the same house or habitually resides with one elsewhere, has ceased to be a Hindu by conversion, or there is any other cause justifying her living separately. She is not entitled to separate residence and maintenance if she is unchaste or ceases to be a Hindu by conversion (Section 18(3)).
Widowed daughter-in-law HAMA Section 19: after her husband's death she is entitled to be maintained by her father-in-law, to the extent she cannot maintain herself from her own earnings or property, or obtain maintenance from her husband's, father's or mother's estate, or from her son or daughter or their estate. The obligation is not enforceable if the father-in-law has no means from coparcenary property in his possession out of which she has not obtained a share. It ceases on her remarriage.
Order by a Magistrate BNSS Section 144(1)(a): if a person having sufficient means neglects or refuses to maintain his wife unable to maintain herself, a Magistrate of the first class may order a monthly allowance. Under the Explanation, "wife" includes a woman who has been divorced by, or has obtained a divorce from, her husband and has not remarried. (The BNSS repealed the Code of Criminal Procedure, 1973 (BNSS Section 531); Section 144 BNSS is the provision corresponding to Section 125 CrPC.)
Succession Hindu Succession Act, 1956: the widow is a Class I heir of a male Hindu (Section 8 and the Schedule); the husband takes, with the sons and daughters, first in the property of a female Hindu dying intestate (Section 15(1)(a)).
Matrimonial remedies HMA Sections 9 (restitution of conjugal rights), 10 (judicial separation), 13 and 13B (divorce). They are available only to the parties to a marriage.
